{{Short description|none}}
{{see also|List of logicians}}
{{wiktionary|Appendix:Glossary of logic}}

This is a '''glossary of logic'''. [[Logic]] is the study of the principles of valid reasoning and argumentation.

{{Compact TOC|short1|seealso=yes}}

==A==
{{glossary}}

{{term |1=A-proposition}}
{{defn |1=A type of standard-form categorical proposition, asserting that all members of the subject category are included in the predicate category; symbolized as "All S are P".<ref>{{Cite web |title=A-proposition |url=https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/a-proposition |website=Collins Dictionary}}</ref><ref name="IEP_Square">{{Cite web |title=Square of Opposition {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/sqr-opp/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |language=en-US}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Abductive reasoning|abduction]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of reasoning characterized by drawing a conclusion based on the best available explanation for a set of premises. Often used in hypothesis formation.}}

{{term |1=Abelian logic}}
{{defn |1=A type of [[relevance logic]] that rejects {{glossary link internal|contraction}} and accepts that ((A → B) → B) → A.<ref>{{Citation |last=Schechter |first=Eric |title=Classical and Nonclassical Logics |chapter=Chapter 26 Abelian logic |date=2020-10-06 |pages=437–440 |chapter-url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/9780691220147-026/html |access-date=2024-04-29 |publisher=Princeton University Press |language=en |doi=10.1515/9780691220147-026 |isbn=978-0-691-22014-7}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Paoli |first1=Francesco |last2=Spinks |first2=Matthew |last3=Veroff |first3=Robert |date=2008-10-01 |title=Abelian Logic and the Logics of Pointed Lattice-Ordered Varieties |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11787-008-0034-2 |journal=Logica Universalis |language=en |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=209–233 |doi=10.1007/s11787-008-0034-2 |issn=1661-8300|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Butchart |first1=Sam |last2=Rogerson |first2=Susan |date=2014 |title=On the Algebraizability of the Implicational Fragment of Abelian Logic |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/43649671 |journal=Studia Logica|volume=102 |issue=5 |pages=981–1001 |doi=10.1007/s11225-013-9515-2 |jstor=43649671 |issn=0039-3215|hdl=1959.3/365633 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Absorption (logic)|absorption]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical rule stating that if a proposition implies another, then adding any additional conjunction to the first proposition does not change the implication. Symbolized as <math>P \rightarrow Q \equiv (P \land R) \rightarrow Q</math>.}}

{{term |1=[[abstract object]]}}
{{defn |1=An object that does not exist at any particular time or place but rather exists as a type of thing—i.e., an idea, or abstraction.}}

{{term |1=[[abstraction]]}}
{{defn |1=The process or result of generalization by reducing the information content of a concept or an observable phenomenon, typically to retain only information which is relevant for a particular purpose.}}

{{term |1=abstraction operator}}
{{defn |1=The function implicitly defined by an {{glossary link internal|abstraction principle}}.<ref name="CookDictionary">{{Cite book |last=Cook |first=Roy T. |date=2009-03-20 |title=A Dictionary of Philosophical Logic |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1515/9780748631971 |doi=10.1515/9780748631971|isbn=978-0-7486-3197-1 }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=abstraction principle}}
{{defn |1=A formula of the form (∀α)(∀β)(Abst(α) = Abst(β) ↔ Equ(α, β)), where Abst is an {{glossary link internal|abstraction operator}} mapping the type of entities ranged over by α and β to objects, and “Equ” is an equivalence relation on the type of entities ranged over by α and β.<ref name="CookDictionary" /> For instance, {{glossary link internal|Hume's principle}}, and {{glossary link internal|Basic Law V}}.}}

{{term |1=[[accessibility relation]]}}
{{defn |1=In modal logic, a relation that describes which worlds are accessible from other worlds in the semantics of possible world models.}}

{{term |1=[[actual world]]}}
{{defn |1=In modal logic, the world that is considered to be the real world, as opposed to possible worlds which are considered in modal reasoning.}}

{{term |1=[[disjunction introduction|addition]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule of inference in formal logic where from any proposition, a disjunction can be formed by disjoining it with any other proposition. Symbolized as <math>P \vdash P \lor Q</math>.}}

{{term |1=[[ad hominem]]}}
{{defn |1=A fallacy in argumentation that targets the person making an argument rather than the argument itself.}}

{{term |1=[[ad ignorantium]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical fallacy where a proposition is considered true because it has not been proven false or vice versa.}}

{{term |1=[[ad infinitum]]}}
{{defn |1=An argument or process that is supposed to continue indefinitely, without ever reaching an end or conclusion.}}

{{term |1=adjunction}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|conjunction introduction}}.}}

{{term |1=[[affine logic]]s}}
{{defn |1=A subfield of linear logic focusing on the study of affine transformations and their implications in logical reasoning.}}

{{term |1=affirmative proposition}}
{{defn |1=A proposition that asserts the truth of a statement, as opposed to negating it.<ref name="comfsm">{{Cite web |title=Categorical Propositions |url=http://www.comfsm.fm/~dleeling/geometry/categorical_propositions.xhtml |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=www.comfsm.fm}}</ref><ref name="elemen38">{{Cite web |title=Elements of Logic 38 |url=https://www3.nd.edu/~maritain/jmc/etext/logic-38.htm |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=www3.nd.edu}}</ref><ref name="lander-quantqual">{{Cite web |title=Standard Form Categorical Propositions: Quantity, Quality, and Distribution |url=https://philosophy.lander.edu/logic/prop.html |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=philosophy.lander.edu}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[affirming the consequent]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical fallacy in which a conditional statement is incorrectly used to infer its converse. For example, from "If P then Q" and "Q", concluding "P".}}

{{term |1=[[alethic modal logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A type of modal logic that deals with modalities of truth, such as necessity and possibility.}}

{{term |1=[[ambiguity]]}}
{{defn |1=The property of a statement or phrase having more than one meaning or interpretation.}}

{{term |1=[[amphiboly]]}}
{{defn |1=A type of ambiguity resulting from ambiguous grammatical structure, rather than the ambiguity of individual words.}}

{{term |1=analethic logic}}
{{defn |1=A {{glossary link internal|three-valued logic}} where the third truth value is the {{glossary link internal|truth-value gap}} "neither true nor false" ("N"), and the {{glossary link internal|designated value|designated values}} are "true" and "neither true nor false."<ref name="WrongWithTonk">{{Cite journal |last=Cook |first=Roy T. |date=2005 |title=What's Wrong with Tonk(?) |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/30226839 |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=221 |doi=10.1007/s10992-004-7805-x |jstor=30226839 |issn=0022-3611}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=analysis}}
{{defn |no=1|1=[[Analysis]], the process of breaking a concept down into more simple parts, so that its logical structure is displayed.}}
{{defn |no=2|1=[[Mathematical analysis]]}}

{{term |1=[[Analytic–synthetic distinction|analytic]]}}
{{defn |1=A statement that is true by virtue of its meaning, such as definitions or statements grounded in logical laws.}}

{{term |1=[[Anaphora (linguistics)|anaphora]]}}
{{defn |1=A rhetorical device that consists of repeating a sequence of words at the beginnings of neighboring clauses, thereby lending them emphasis.}}

{{term |1=[[ancestral relation|ancestral]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic and mathematics, the [[transitive closure]] of a relation, capturing the idea of indirect relationships across generations or iterations.}}

{{term |1=[[Antecedent (logic)|antecedent]]}}
{{defn |1=The first part of a conditional statement, the "if" clause, which specifies a condition for the consequent.}}

{{term |1=anti-extension}}
{{defn |1=In set theory and logic, the complement of the extension of a concept or predicate, consisting of all objects that do not fall under the concept.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bennett |first1=Karen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3TtoAgAAQBAJ |title=Oxford Studies in Metaphysics volume 7 |last2=Zimmerman |first2=Dean W. |date=2012-10-25 |publisher=OUP Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-163357-7 |pages=86 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Howson |first=Colin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Y4WGAgAAQBAJ |title=Logic with Trees: An Introduction to Symbolic Logic |date=2005-10-11 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-78550-6 |pages=159 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xQvoCAAAQBAJ |title=Handbook of Philosophical Logic |last2=Guenthner |first2=Franz |date=2013-03-14 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-017-0460-1 |pages=339 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=antilogism}}
{{defn |1=A syllogism with three premises leading to a contradiction, showing the inconsistency of the premises.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dictionary.com {{!}} Meanings & Definitions of English Words |url=https://www.dictionary.com/browse/antilogism |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=Dictionary.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Definition of ANTILOGISM |url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/antilogism |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=www.merriam-webster.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ladd-Franklin |first=C. F. |date=1928 |title=The Antilogism |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2249740 |journal=Mind |volume=37 |issue=148 |pages=532–534 |doi=10.1093/mind/XXXVII.148.532 |jstor=2249740 |issn=0026-4423}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[antinomy]]}}
{{defn |1=A contradiction between two beliefs or conclusions that are in themselves reasonable; a paradox.}}

{{term |1=[[Antisymmetric relation|antisymmetry]]}}
{{defn |1=A property of a relation <math>R</math>, where for any two elements <math>a</math> and <math>b</math>, if <math>aRb</math> and <math>bRa</math>, then <math>a = b</math>.}}

{{term |1=[[A priori and a posteriori|a posteriori]]}}
{{defn |1=Knowledge or justification is said to be a posteriori if it depends on empirical evidence or experience.}}

{{term |1=[[A priori and a posteriori|a priori]]}}
{{defn |1=Knowledge or justification is said to be a priori if it is independent of empirical evidence or experience, such as logic or mathematics.}}

{{term |1=[[argument]]}}
{{defn |1=A series of statements typically used to persuade someone of something or to present reasons for accepting a conclusion.}}

{{term |1=Aristotelian comprehension schema}}
{{defn |1=This formula in [[second-order logic]]: (∃x)Φ → (∃Y)(∀x)(Yx ↔ Φ).<ref name="CookDictionary" />}}

{{term |1=[[Aristotelian logic]]}}
{{defn |1=The traditional logic developed by Aristotle, based on the study of syllogism and the principle of non-contradiction.}}

{{term |1=[[Aristotle's sea battle argument|Aristotle's sea battle]]}}
{{defn |1=A thought experiment by Aristotle to explore the concept of future contingents and the problem of determinism and free will.}}

{{term |1=Aristotle's theses}}
{{defn |1=The formulas ¬ (¬ A → A) and ¬ (A → ¬A) in [[propositional logic]]; they are theorems in [[connexive logic]] but not in [[classical logic]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Giordani |first1=Alessandro |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gDgKEAAAQBAJ |title=Logic in High Definition: Trends in Logical Semantics |last2=Malinowski |first2=Jacek |date=2020-11-19 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-53487-5 |pages=55 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Banerjee |first1=Mohua |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=25KvEAAAQBAJ |title=Logic and Its Applications: 10th Indian Conference, ICLA 2023, Indore, India, March 3–5, 2023, Proceedings |last2=Sreejith |first2=A. V. |date=2023-02-22 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-031-26689-8 |pages=189 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UULl07dutBwC |title=British Logic in the Nineteenth Century |last2=Woods |first2=John |date=2008-03-10 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-08-055701-4 |pages=561 |language=en}}</ref> See also {{glossary link internal|Boethius' theses}}.
}}

{{term |1=[[arity]]}}
{{defn |1=The number of arguments or operands that a function, operation, or relation takes. In logic, it refers to the number of terms that a predicate has.}}

{{term |1=assertion}}
{{defn |1=The principle, or axiom, that (A ∧ (A → B)) → B.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Vanderveken |first=Daniel |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A1Rvqg7_ywQC |title=Logic, Thought and Action |date=2005-06-23 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4020-3167-0 |pages=275 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cintula |first1=Petr |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=M2ZXEAAAQBAJ |title=Logic and Implication: An Introduction to the General Algebraic Study of Non-classical Logics |last2=Noguera |first2=Carles |date=2022-01-01 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-85675-5 |pages=451 |language=en}}</ref> Also called {{glossary link internal|pseudo modus ponens}}.}}

{{term |1=[[associativity]]}}
{{defn |1=A property of some binary operations in which the grouping of operations does not affect the result. For example, in arithmetic, addition and multiplication are associative.}}

{{term |1=[[asymmetry]]}}
{{defn |1=A relation between two entities where if the first is related to the second, the second is not related to the first.}}

{{term |1=[[atomic formula]]}}
{{defn |1=The simplest type of formula in logic, consisting of a single predicate applied to a sequence of terms without any logical connectives.}}

{{term |1=[[atomic sentence]]}}
{{defn |1=A sentence that contains no logical connectives or quantifiers, expressing a basic statement about objects.}}

{{term |1=[[Autological word|autological]]}}
{{defn |1=A term that describes itself. For example, the word "short" is autological because it is a short word.}}

{{term |1=[[automaton]]}}
{{defn |1=A self-operating machine or, in computer science, a theoretical model of computation that performs tasks according to a set of rules or a program.}}

{{term |1=[[automorphism]]}}
{{defn |1=An isomorphism from a mathematical object to itself, preserving all the structure of the object. In logic, it often refers to symmetries within logical structures.}}

{{term |1=axiological logic}}
{{defn |1=A branch of logic that deals with the study of value, including ethical and aesthetic values, often in the context of modal logic.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hartman |first=Robert S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1UX7DwAAQBAJ |title=The Structure of Value: Foundations of Scientific Axiology |date=2011-12-15 |publisher=Wipf and Stock Publishers |isbn=978-1-7252-3067-5 |pages=300 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Lowe |first1=E. J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bqbCBQAAQBAJ |title=Truth and Truth-making |last2=Rami |first2=A. |date=2014-12-05 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-317-49268-9 |pages=40 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gensler |first1=Harry J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FwMOA6kh2-QC |title=Historical Dictionary of Ethics |last2=Spurgin |first2=Earl W. |date=2008-08-22 |publisher=Scarecrow Press |isbn=978-0-8108-6271-5 |pages=168 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[axiom]]}}
{{defn |1=A statement or proposition that is accepted as true without proof, serving as a starting point for further reasoning and arguments.}}

{{glossary end}}

==B==
{{glossary}}

{{term |1=bad company objection}}
{{defn |1=An objection to mathematical abstractionism that points out the difficulty in distinguishing between legitimate and illegitimate forms of abstraction, particularly in the context of Frege's Basic Law V and the paradoxes it generates.<ref>{{Citation |last=Tennant |first=Neil |title=Logicism and Neologicism |date=2023 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2023/entries/logicism/ |access-date=2024-04-29 |edition=Winter 2023 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Shapiro |first1=Stewart |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hPztJzVE8j0C |title=The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Mathematics and Logic |last2=Wainwright |first2=William J. |date=2005-02-10 |publisher=Oxford University Press, USA |isbn=978-0-19-514877-0 |pages=181 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hale |first1=Bob |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PsDmCwAAQBAJ |title=The Reason's Proper Study: Essays Towards a Neo-Fregean Philosophy of Mathematics |last2=Wright |first2=Crispin |date=2003 |publisher=Clarendon Press |isbn=978-0-19-926632-6 |pages=17 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=barbara}}
{{defn |1=A standard form of categorical syllogism in Aristotelian logic, where all three propositions (major premise, minor premise, and conclusion) are universal affirmatives, symbolized as AAA. The form is: All M are P, All S are M, therefore All S are P.<ref>{{Cite web |title=History of logic - Syllogisms, Aristotle, Reasoning {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-logic/Syllogisms |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Lagerlund |first=Henrik |title=Medieval Theories of the Syllogism |date=2022 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2022/entries/medieval-syllogism/ |access-date=2024-04-29 |edition=Summer 2022 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mabbott |first=J. D. |date=1939 |title=Two Notes on Syllogism |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2250441 |journal=Mind |volume=48 |issue=191 |pages=326–337 |doi=10.1093/mind/XLVIII.191.326 |jstor=2250441 |issn=0026-4423}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Barcan formula]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle in modal logic that asserts the interchangeability of quantification and possibility: necessarily, if there exists something, then there necessarily exists something.}}

{{term |1=[[Basic Law V]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle proposed by Gottlob Frege in his attempt to reduce arithmetic to logic, stating that the extension of a concept is determined by the objects falling under the concept. It leads to Russell's paradox.}}

{{term |1=[[basis step|basis]]}}
{{defn |1=The initial case in a proof by mathematical induction.}}

{{term |1=[[Bayes' theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A theorem in probability theory used to update the probability for a hypothesis as more evidence or information becomes available.}}

{{term |1=[[begging the question]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical fallacy where the conclusion of an argument is assumed in the premise, making the argument circular.}}

{{term |1=[[Bew (mathematical logic)|Bew]]}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|provability predicate}}.}}

{{term |1=[[BHK interpretation|BHK-interpretation]]}}
{{defn |1=The Brouwer-Heyting-Kolmogorov interpretation, a constructivist interpretation of intuitionistic logic, where the truth of a statement is equated with the existence of a proof for it.}}

{{term |1=[[Bias (statistics)|bias]]}}
{{defn |1=A systematic deviation from neutrality, objectivity, or fairness, often resulting from a particular tendency or inclination, especially in statistical or cognitive contexts.}}

{{term |1=[[Logical biconditional|biconditional]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical connective between statements, where both statements imply each other; often denoted as <math>P \leftrightarrow Q</math>, meaning "P if and only if Q".}}

{{term |1=[[Bijection|bijective]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that is both injective (no two elements of the domain map to the same element of the codomain) and surjective (every element of the codomain is mapped to by some element of the domain), establishing a one-to-one correspondence between the domain and codomain.}}

{{term |1=[[binary function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that takes two arguments. In logic and mathematics, this is often a function that combines two values to produce a third value, such as addition or multiplication in arithmetic.}}

{{term |1=[[binary relation]]}}
{{defn |1=A relation involving two terms or elements, defining a particular relationship between pairs of objects from two sets (or from one set to itself).}}

{{term |1=[[Principle of bivalence|bivalence]]}}
{{defn |1=The principle that any proposition is either true or false, with no middle ground; foundational to classical logic.}}

{{term |1=Boethius' theses}}
{{defn |1=The formulas (A → B) → ¬ (A → ¬ B) and (A → ¬ B) → ¬ (A → B) in [[propositional logic]]; they are theorems in [[connexive logic]] but not in [[classical logic]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9mwtRDXVM2wC |title=Logic: A History of its Central Concepts |last2=Pelletier |first2=Francis Jeffry |last3=Woods |first3=John |date=2012-12-31 |publisher=Newnes |isbn=978-0-08-093170-8 |pages=427 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Omori |first1=Hitoshi |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m5PHDwAAQBAJ |title=New Essays on Belnap-Dunn Logic |last2=Wansing |first2=Heinrich |date=2020-01-01 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-31136-0 |pages=7 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Mares |first=Edwin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6YbtEAAAQBAJ |title=The Logic of Entailment and its History |date=2024-02-15 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-009-37531-3 |pages=46 |language=en}}</ref> See also {{glossary link internal|Aristotle's theses}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Boolean algebra]]}}
{{defn |1=An area of algebra in which the values of the variables are the truth values true and false, typically used in computer science, logic, and mathematical logic.}}

{{term |1=Boolean negation}}
{{defn |1=A form of [[negation]] where the negation of a non-true proposition is true, and the negation of a non-false proposition is false.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aG3uCAAAQBAJ |title=What is Negation? |last2=Wansing |first2=Heinrich |date=2013-06-29 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-015-9309-0 |pages=72 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Restall |first=Greg |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z3AsBgAAQBAJ |title=An Introduction to Substructural Logics |date=2002-09-11 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-11131-1 |pages=340 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Mares |first=Edwin D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fOM-TvZ3SecC |title=Relevant Logic: A Philosophical Interpretation |date=2004-02-26 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-82923-6 |pages=92 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Boolean operator (Boolean algebra)|Boolean operator]]}}
{{defn |1=An operator used in logic and computer science that performs logical operations on its operands, such as AND, OR, and NOT.}}

{{term |1=borderline case}}
{{defn |1=A situation or instance that falls at the boundary between categories or classifications, often challenging strict definitions or distinctions.<ref name="SEP_Vagueness">{{Citation |last=Sorensen |first=Roy |title=Vagueness |date=2023 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2023/entries/vagueness/ |access-date=2024-04-22 |edition=Winter 2023 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Alxatib |first1=Sam |last2=Pelletier |first2=Francis Jeffry |date=June 2011 |title=The Psychology of Vagueness: Borderline Cases and Contradictions |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1468-0017.2011.01419.x |journal=Mind & Language |language=en |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=287–326 |doi=10.1111/j.1468-0017.2011.01419.x|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Shafer-Landau |first=Russ |date=1995 |title=Vagueness, Borderline Cases and Moral Realism |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/20009807 |journal=American Philosophical Quarterly |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=83–96 |jstor=20009807 |issn=0003-0481}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Bones |first=Inga |chapter=What Is Vagueness? |date=2020-09-22 |title=How to Swim in Sinking Sands |pages=12–56 |chapter-url=https://brill.com/display/book/9783957437549/BP000010.xml |access-date=2024-04-29 |publisher=Brill mentis |language=en |doi=10.30965/9783957437549_003 |isbn=978-3-95743-754-9|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Up tack|bottom]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic, the symbol used to represent a contradiction or an absurdity; often denoted by the symbol <math>\bot</math>.}}

{{term |1=[[bound variable]]}}
{{defn |1=A variable that is quantified over in a logical expression, as opposed to a free variable, which is not bound by a quantifier.}}

{{term |1=[[bounded quantifier]]}}
{{defn |1=A quantifier that operates within a specific domain or set, as opposed to an unbounded or universal quantifier that applies to all elements of a particular type.}}

{{term |1=[[branching quantifier]]}}
{{defn |1=A type of quantifier in formal logic that allows for the expression of dependencies between different quantified variables, representing more complex relationships than can be expressed with standard linear quantification.}}

{{term |1=Brouwerian modal logic}}
{{defn |1=A form of modal logic that incorporates principles of intuitionism, as developed by [[L.E.J. Brouwer]], focusing on the notion of possibility grounded in constructivist or intuitionist mathematics.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wright |first=G. H. von |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PiBeDwAAQBAJ |title=Philosophical Logic: Philosophical Papers |date=2018-05-31 |publisher=Cornell University Press |isbn=978-1-5017-1731-4 |pages=135 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Oliveira |first=Anjolina G. de |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aFO6CgAAQBAJ |title=The Functional Interpretation of Logical Deduction |date=2012 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-4360-96-8 |pages=217 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Rusza |first=Imre |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=s7vnCAAAQBAJ |title=Modal Logic with Descriptions |date=2013-04-17 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-017-2294-0 |pages=128 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=Buridan's sophismata}}
{{defn |1=A collection of paradoxes and logical exercises attributed to the medieval philosopher Jean Buridan, designed to challenge logical and linguistic intuitions.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Saxonia |first=Albertus de |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n6W0liV33WcC |title=Albert of Saxony's Twenty-Five Disputed Questions on Logic: A Critical Edition of His Quaestiones Circa Logicam |date=2002 |publisher=BRILL |isbn=978-90-04-12513-1 |pages=29 |language=la}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Beklemishev |first=Lev D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Q8xNyJlpvQ0C |title=Provability, Computability and Reflection |date=2000-04-01 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-08-095731-9 |pages=7 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Klima |first=Gyula |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tnw8DwAAQBAJ |title=John Buridan |date=2009 |publisher=Oxford University Press, USA |isbn=978-0-19-517622-3 |pages=329 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[busy beaver problem]]}}
{{defn |1=A problem in computability theory that seeks the Turing machine with the largest possible behavior (e.g., producing the most output, running the longest) among all Turing machines of a certain size, illustrating limits of computability.}}

{{glossary end}}

==C==
{{glossary}}

{{term |1=Caesar problem}}
{{defn |1=A problem in the philosophy of language and logic regarding the applicability of mathematical concepts to non-mathematical objects, famously illustrated by Gottlob Frege's question of whether the concept of being a successor in number applies to Julius Caesar.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Linnebo |first=Øystein |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780199641314.003.0009 |title=Thin objects: an abstractionist account |date=2018 |publisher=Oxford university press |isbn=978-0-19-964131-4 |location=Oxford |chapter=The Julius Caesar Problem|volume=1 |doi=10.1093/oso/9780199641314.003.0009 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Greimann |first=Dirk |date=2003 |title=What is Frege's Julius Caesar Problem? |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/42971497 |journal=Dialectica |volume=57 |issue=3 |pages=261–278 |doi=10.1111/j.1746-8361.2003.tb00271.x |jstor=42971497 |issn=0012-2017}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Heck |first=Richard G. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=55G9P870S1YC |title=Frege's Theorem |date=2011-09-29 |publisher=OUP Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-969564-5 |pages=107 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Carnap-Ramsey sentence]]}}
{{defn |1=A sentence formulated to express the empirical content of a theory in logical positivism, named after Rudolf Carnap and Frank P. Ramsey, aimed at separating theoretical terms from observational terms.}}

{{term |1=[[Categorical theory|categorical]]}}
{{defn |1=A theory is categorical if all its models are isomorphic, meaning they describe the same mathematical structures in different ways.}}

{{term |1=[[categorical logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of logic that studies the categorization of objects and the logical foundations of categories, often using the framework of category theory.}}

{{term |1=[[categorical proposition]]}}
{{defn |1=A proposition that asserts or denies that all or some of the members of one category are included in another category, fundamental in syllogistic reasoning.}}

{{term |1=[[categorical syllogism]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of deductive reasoning in Aristotelian logic consisting of three categorical propositions that involve three terms and deduce a conclusion from two premises.}}

{{term |1=[[Category (mathematics)|category]]}}
{{defn |1=In mathematics and logic, a collection of objects and morphisms between them that satisfies certain axioms, fundamental to category theory.}}

{{term |1=[[category theory]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of mathematics that deals with abstract algebraic structures and relationships between them, providing a unifying framework for various areas of mathematics.}}

{{term |1=causal logic}}
{{defn |1=A branch of logic concerned with the study of causal relationships, including the representation and reasoning about causes and effects.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9mwtRDXVM2wC |title=Logic: A History of its Central Concepts |last2=Pelletier |first2=Francis Jeffry |last3=Woods |first3=John |date=2012-12-31 |publisher=Newnes |isbn=978-0-08-093170-8 |pages=437 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Sion |first=Avi |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t5WFOzkk5nYC |title=The Logic of Causation: Definition, Induction and Deduction of Deterministic Causality |date=2010-05-17 |publisher=Avi Sion |isbn=978-2-9700091-3-9 |pages=58 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=causal modal logic}}
{{defn |1=An extension of modal logic that includes modalities for necessity and possibility along with causal relations, allowing for the formal analysis of causal statements.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bowen |first=Paul D. |date=1983-10-01 |title=Causation in classical physics |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01064064 |journal=Synthese |language=en |volume=57 |issue=1 |pages=1–20 |doi=10.1007/BF01064064 |issn=1573-0964|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Simon |first=Herbert A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iCvpCAAAQBAJ |title=Models of Discovery: and Other Topics in the Methods of Science |date=2012-12-06 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-010-9521-1 |pages=52 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=chronological logic}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|temporal modal logic}}.<ref>{{Citation |last=Rescher |first=Nicholas |chapter=Chronological Logic |date=1968 |title=Topics in Philosophical Logic |pages=196–228 |editor-last=Rescher |editor-first=Nicholas |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-017-3546-9_12 |access-date=2024-04-29 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-94-017-3546-9_12 |isbn=978-94-017-3546-9|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Gensler |first=Harry J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-lrWH-aZw7QC |title=The A to Z of Logic |date=2010 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-0-8108-7596-8 |pages=233 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Church's theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A theorem establishing the undecidability of certain decision problems in logic, such as the Entscheidungsproblem, proving that there is no consistent, complete, and effectively calculable logic.}}

{{term |1=[[Church–Turing thesis]]}}
{{defn |1=A hypothesis proposing that any function that can be naturally regarded as computable by a human being can be computed by a Turing machine, thereby defining the limits of what can be computed.}}

{{term |1=[[Proof by exhaustion|classical dilemma]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of argument presenting two alternatives, both leading to the same conclusion, often used in classical rhetoric and logic to demonstrate inevitability.}}

{{term |1=[[classical logic]]}}
{{defn |1=The traditional framework of logic based on principles of bivalence, non-contradiction, and excluded middle, primarily focusing on propositional and predicate logic.}}

{{term |1=classical reductio ad absurdum}}
{{defn |1=A stronger form of [[reductio ad absurdum]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hale |first=Bob |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=L7poAgAAQBAJ |title=Necessary Beings: An Essay on Ontology, Modality, and the Relations Between Them |date=2013-09-19 |publisher=OUP Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-164834-2 |pages=106 |language=en}}</ref> where instead of only deriving <math>\neg P</math> from showing that <math>P</math> leads to a contradiction, one can also derive <math>P</math> from showing that <math>\neg P</math> leads to a contradiction.}}

{{term |1=coextensive}}
{{defn |1=Having the same scope or range, especially referring to two terms or concepts that apply to the same set of objects.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Goldfarb |first=Warren D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ywNo3rl4tS4C |title=Deductive Logic |date=2003-01-01 |publisher=Hackett Publishing |isbn=978-0-87220-660-1 |pages=94 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Frigg |first=Roman |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OSl3EAAAQBAJ |title=Models and Theories: A Philosophical Inquiry |date=2022-06-28 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-1-000-60953-0 |pages=55 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=cogent inductive argument}}
{{defn |1=A {{glossary link internal|strong inductive argument}} where all the premises are true.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Nat |first=Arnold vander |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aXGLAgAAQBAJ |title=Simple Formal Logic: With Common-Sense Symbolic Techniques |date=2010-03-05 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-21870-6 |pages=325 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Banks |first=Sinclair |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EiZXEAAAQBAJ |title=The Solution to an Injustice in Trials: A fallacy unmasked |date=2019-03-01 |publisher=Sinclair Banks |isbn=978-0-578-46220-2 |pages=364 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Stanlick |first1=Nancy A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qvr3BgAAQBAJ |title=Asking Good Questions: Case Studies in Ethics and Critical Thinking |last2=Strawser |first2=Michael J. |date=2015-03-05 |publisher=Hackett Publishing |isbn=978-1-58510-755-1 |pages=68 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Bogdan |first=R. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q6vzCAAAQBAJ |title=Local Induction |date=2012-12-06 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-011-9799-1 |pages=122 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[coherence theory of truth]]}}
{{defn |1=A theory that holds truth as coherence among a set of beliefs or statements, rather than correspondence with reality or facts.}}

{{term |1=[[Combinatory logic|combinator]]}}
{{defn |1=A function or expression in combinatory logic that acts on arguments to produce results without the need for variable bindings.}}

{{term |1=combinatorialism}}
{{defn |1=Combinatorialism is the view that any arbitrary combination of elements constitutes a legitimate mathematical structure, whether that structure is definable or not.<ref>{{Citation |last=Menzel |first=Christopher |title=Possible Worlds |date=2023 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2023/entries/possible-worlds/ |access-date=2024-04-29 |edition=Fall 2023 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Hansen |first=Casper Storm |chapter=Classical Mathematics and Plenitudinous Combinatorialism |date=2021 |title=Founding Mathematics on Semantic Conventions |series=Synthese Library |volume=446 |pages=9–27 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-030-88534-2_2 |access-date=2024-04-29 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-88534-2_2 |isbn=978-3-030-88533-5|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kim |first=Jaegwon |date=1986 |title=Possible Worlds and Armstrong's Combinatorialism |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40231493 |journal=Canadian Journal of Philosophy |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=595–612 |doi=10.1080/00455091.1986.10717138 |jstor=40231493 |issn=0045-5091}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[combinatory logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of mathematical logic that seeks to eliminate the need for variables in mathematical expressions by using combinators.}}

{{term |1=combinatory terms}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|combinator}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Commutative property|commutativity]]}}
{{defn |1=A property of binary operations where the order of the operands does not change the result, as in addition and multiplication in arithmetic.}}

{{term |1=[[compactness theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A theorem in logic stating that if every finite subset of a set of sentences has a model, then the entire set has a model.}}

{{term |1=[[Completed infinity|complete infinity]]}}
{{defn |1=A concept in philosophy and mathematics referring to an actual infinity that is considered as a completed whole, contrasting with potential infinities that are indefinitely extendable.}}

{{term |1=[[Completeness (logic)|completeness]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic, the property of a logical system whereby every logically valid formula can be derived using the system's axioms and inference rules.}}

{{term |1=[[complexity class]]}}
{{defn |1=A classification of decision problems based on their inherent computational complexity, grouping problems that can be solved within similar resource constraints.}}

{{term |1=[[Complexity theory (computation)|complexity theory]]}}
{{defn |1=The study of the inherent difficulty of computational problems, focusing on the resources needed to solve them, such as time and memory.}}

{{term |1=[[Function composition|composition]]}}
{{defn |1=The act of combining simple objects or ideas into a complex whole, or the resulting combination itself.}}

{{term |1=[[compositionality]]}}
{{defn |1=The principle in semantics that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its constituent expressions and the rules used to combine them.}}

{{term |1=compound formula}}
{{defn |1=A formula representing a {{glossary link internal|compound statement}}.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tomassi |first=Paul |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5Funj1Zaau0C |title=Logic |date=2013-05-13 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-70591-7 |pages=39 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=compound statement}}
{{defn |1=A statement in logic that is formed by combining two or more statements with logical connectives, allowing for the construction of more complex statements from simpler ones.<ref name="IntroLogic2">{{Cite web |title=Introduction to Logic - Chapter 2 |url=http://intrologic.stanford.edu/chapters/chapter_02.html |access-date=2024-03-22 |website=intrologic.stanford.edu}}</ref><ref name="IEP_PropositionalLogic">{{Cite web |title=Introduction to Propositional Logic |url=https://www.cs.odu.edu/~toida/nerzic/content/logic/prop_logic/implications/implication_proof.html |access-date=2024-04-28 |website=www.cs.odu.edu}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[unrestricted comprehension|comprehension schema]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle in set theory and logic allowing for the formation of sets based on a defining property or condition.}}

{{term |1=[[computable function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function for which there exists an algorithm that can compute the function's value for any valid input within a finite amount of time.}}

{{term |1=[[computation]]}}
{{defn |1=The process of performing a sequence of calculations or logical operations systematically to obtain a result.}}

{{term |1=[[concept]]}}
{{defn |1=An abstract idea representing the fundamental characteristics of what it describes.}}

{{term |1=[[logical conclusion|conclusion]]}}
{{defn |1=The statement that logically follows from the premises of an argument, serving as the argument's final claim.}}

{{term |1=[[abstract and concrete|concrete object]]}}
{{defn |1=An object that exists in physical reality, as opposed to abstract objects which do not have a physical existence.}}

{{term |1=[[Conditional (disambiguation)|conditional]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical connective that represents a "if... then..." relationship between two statements.}}

{{term |1=conditional logic}}
{{defn |1=A branch of logic that studies the properties of the conditional connective and related logical concepts.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Nute |first=Donald |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C6-1BwAAQBAJ |title=Topics in Conditional Logic |date=2012-12-06 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-009-8966-5 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Egré |first1=Paul |title=The Logic of Conditionals |date=2021 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2021/entries/logic-conditionals/ |access-date=2024-04-29 |edition=Winter 2021 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Rott |first2=Hans}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[conditional probability]]}}
{{defn |1=The probability of an event occurring given that another event has already occurred.}}

{{term |1=[[conditional proof]]}}
{{defn |1=A method in logic for proving a conditional statement by assuming the antecedent and showing that the consequent follows.}}

{{term |1=conditionalization}}
{{defn |1=The conditional obtained by taking the conjunction of the premises of the argument as antecedent and the conclusion of the argument as consequent. For instance, the conditionalization of modus ponens, <math>P \to Q, P \vdash Q</math>, is the formula <math>((P \to Q) \land P) \to Q</math>, called {{glossary link internal|pseudo modus ponens}}.<ref name="CookDictionary" />}}

{{term |1=[[congruence relation]]}}
{{defn |1=An equivalence relation that respects the operations of the algebraic structure it is defined on, such as addition or multiplication in a group.}}

{{term |1=conjunct}}
{{defn |1=A component statement within a conjunction, each of which must be true for the entire conjunction to be true.<ref name="beallbasics1ed">{{Cite book |last=Beall |first=Jeffrey C. |title=Logic: the basics |date=2010 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-203-85155-5 |edition=1. publ |location=London |pages=17, 57 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Logical conjunction|conjunction]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical connective that represents the "and" relationship between two statements, requiring both to be true.}}

{{term |1=[[conjunction elimination]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule of inference in propositional logic that allows one to infer a conjunct from a conjunction.}}

{{term |1=[[conjunction introduction]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule of inference that allows the formation of a conjunction from two individual statements.}}

{{term |1=[[conjunctive normal form]]}}
{{defn |1=A way of expressing a logical formula as a conjunction of clauses, where each clause is a disjunction of literals.}}

{{term |1=[[connected relation|connected]]}}
{{defn |1=A property of a graph in which there is a path between any two vertices, or a property of a topological space in which it cannot be divided into two disjoint nonempty open sets.}}

{{term |1=[[connexive logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of logic that studies principles of connection between propositions, such as the relation between a statement and its contrapositive.}}

{{term |1=[[consequence relation]]}}
{{defn |1=A relation between sets of sentences or propositions, where the truth of the first set (the premises) necessitates the truth of the second set (the consequences).}}

{{term |1=[[consequent]]}}
{{defn |1=The second part of a conditional statement, indicating the result or outcome if the antecedent condition is met.}}

{{term |1=[[consequentia mirabilis]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle in classical logic stating that if the negation of a proposition leads to a contradiction, then the proposition itself must be true.}}

{{term |1=[[conservative extension]]}}
{{defn |1=A property of a theory that is expanded by new axioms or rules without changing the truth values of statements in the original theory.}}

{{term |1=[[Constant (mathematics)|constant]]}}
{{defn |1=A symbol in logic and mathematics that represents a fixed and unchanging value.}}

{{term |1=[[constant function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that always returns the same value, regardless of the input.}}

{{term |1=[[constructive dilemma]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of argument where, given two conditional statements and evidence that at least one of their antecedents is true, one can conclude that at least one of the consequents is true.}}

{{term |1=[[constructive logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of logic that emphasizes the constructive proof of existence, requiring an explicit construction of an object to assert its existence rather than relying on indirect arguments.}}

{{term |1=[[constructive mathematics]]}}
{{defn |1=A philosophy of mathematics that requires mathematical objects to be constructible and computable, rejecting non-constructive proofs such as those involving the law of excluded middle in its full generality.}}

{{term |1=[[constructive proof]]}}
{{defn |1=A proof that demonstrates the existence of a mathematical object by providing a method to construct it explicitly, as opposed to proving indirectly by contradiction.}}

{{term |1=[[contextualism]]}}
{{defn |1=The theory that the context in which an assertion is made is essential for understanding its truth conditions and meaning.}}

{{term |1=[[Contingency (philosophy)|contingency]]}}
{{defn |1=The property of being neither necessarily true nor necessarily false, depending on some conditions or on the state of the world.}}

{{term |1=[[Contraction (logic)|contraction]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic and mathematics, the process of eliminating duplicates in expressions or equations to simplify them.}}

{{term |1=[[contradiction]]}}
{{defn |1=A statement or proposition that asserts both a statement and its negation, considered universally false in classical logic.}}

{{term |1=[[contradictory]]}}
{{defn |1=Referring to a pair of statements or propositions where one is the negation of the other, such that they cannot both be true or both be false.}}

{{term |1=[[contraposition]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical principle that states that a conditional statement is logically equivalent to its contrapositive, transforming "If P, then Q" into "If not Q, then not P".}}

{{term |1=[[Contraposition|contrapositive]]}}
{{defn |1=The statement resulting from swapping the antecedent and consequent of a conditional statement and negating both, maintaining logical equivalence.}}

{{term |1=[[Contrary (logic)|contrary]]}}
{{defn |1=Referring to a pair of statements or propositions that cannot both be true, but can both be false.}}

{{term |1=[[convention T]]}}
{{defn |1=A criterion of truth proposed by Alfred Tarski, stating that a sentence is true if and only if it corresponds to the facts or reality it describes.}}

{{term |1=[[Converse (logic)|converse]]}}
{{defn |1=The statement formed by reversing the antecedent and consequent of a conditional statement, not necessarily maintaining logical equivalence.}}

{{term |1=converse domain}}
{{defn |1=In set theory and logic, the set of all elements that are related to any element of a given set under a specific relation.<ref name="LemmonLogic">{{Cite book |last=Lemmon |first=E. J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qkmG04_ecLMC |title=Beginning Logic |date=1971-09-30 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-0-412-38090-7 |pages=47–48, 53, 69–70, 187 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Converse Barcan formula|converse barcan formula]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle in modal logic suggesting that possibility precedes existence, the converse of the Barcan formula.}}

{{term |1=[[Converse (logic)|conversion]]}}
{{defn |1=The logical operation of swapping the subject and predicate of a categorical proposition, sometimes affecting its truth.}}

{{term |1=[[Copula (linguistics)|copula]]}}
{{defn |1=The part of a proposition that links the subject to the predicate, typically represented by forms of the verb "to be".}}

{{term |1=[[co-referential]]}}
{{defn |1=Referring to different expressions that denote the same object or entity in the world.}}

{{term |1=[[Coreflexive relation|coreflexivity]]}}
{{defn |1=A property of a binary relation where every element is related to itself, implying reflexivity.}}

{{term |1=[[corollary]]}}
{{defn |1=A proposition that follows directly from another proposition or theorem with little or no additional proof.}}

{{term |1=[[correspondence theory of truth]]}}
{{defn |1=The philosophical doctrine that the truth or falsity of a statement is determined by how it relates to the world and whether it accurately describes (corresponds with) that world.}}

{{term |1=[[counterexample]]}}
{{defn |no=1|1=(''broadly'') An example that disproves a statement or proposition, showing that it is not universally true.}}
{{defn |no=2|1=(''to an argument form'') A counterexample to an [[argument form]], or [[sequent]], is an argument in the same [[logical form]] where the premises are clearly true but the conclusion is clearly false, showing that the form is [[Validity (logic)|invalid]], since it lacks {{glossary link internal|semantic validity}}.<ref name="AllenHand">{{Cite book |last1=Allen |first1=Colin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RSTYAgAAQBAJ |title=Logic Primer, second edition |last2=Hand |first2=Michael |date=2001-01-16 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-30396-5 |pages=53, 99 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[counterfactual conditional]]}}
{{defn |1=A conditional statement (if...then...) concerning an event that did not actually happen but is considered for the sake of argument.}}

{{term |1=counterfactual logic}}
{{defn |1=A branch of logic that studies counterfactual conditionals and their implications, often used in philosophical discussions about causality and decision theory.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Moreland |first1=J. P. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yTufCgAAQBAJ |title=Philosophical Foundations for a Christian Worldview |last2=Craig |first2=William Lane |date=2009-09-20 |publisher=InterVarsity Press |isbn=978-0-8308-7649-5 |pages=54 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Iemhoff |first1=Rosalie |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=b_-eDwAAQBAJ |title=Logic, Language, Information, and Computation: 26th International Workshop, WoLLIC 2019, Utrecht, The Netherlands, July 2-5, 2019, Proceedings |last2=Moortgat |first2=Michael |last3=Queiroz |first3=Ruy de |date=2019-06-23 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-662-59533-6 |pages=248 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Elgin |first=Samuel Z. |date=2021-02-01 |title=Counterfactual Logic and the Necessity of Mathematics |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10992-020-09563-8 |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |language=en |volume=50 |issue=1 |pages=97–115 |doi=10.1007/s10992-020-09563-8 |issn=1573-0433|url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=countermodel}}
{{defn |1=A countermodel of an argument is a model in which the premises are true and the conclusion false, showing that the argument is not valid.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Boghossian |first1=Paul Artin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mn_nCwAAQBAJ |title=New Essays on the a Priori |last2=Peacocke |first2=Christopher |date=2000 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-924126-2 |pages=202 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="GodelIntro">{{Cite book |last=Smith |first=Peter |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y8tqY5qU330C |title=An Introduction to Gödel's Theorems |date=2007-07-26 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-85784-0 |pages=10,331 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="AllenHand" />}}

{{term |1=counternecessary conditional}}
{{defn |1=A conditional statement that considers a situation against a necessarily true backdrop, exploring implications in hypothetical scenarios that contradict necessary truths; also known as counterpossible.<ref>{{Citation |last=Baker |first=Alan |chapter=Counterpossibles in Mathematical Practice: The Case of Spoof Perfect Numbers |date=2020 |title=Handbook of the History and Philosophy of Mathematical Practice |pages=1–27 |editor-last=Sriraman |editor-first=Bharath |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-19071-2_24-1 |access-date=2024-04-29 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-19071-2_24-1 |isbn=978-3-030-19071-2|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[counterpart theory]]}}
{{defn |1=A philosophical theory proposed by Lewis that addresses the semantics of modal logic, suggesting that objects in possible worlds have counterparts in other possible worlds.}}

{{term |1=[[Course-of-values recursion|course of values recursion]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle in mathematics and logic that defines a function based on the values it takes on smaller arguments, essential for defining functions like factorials and other recursive functions.}}

{{term |1=[[Curry's paradox|Curry paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A paradox in logic that arises when considering a statement that asserts its own unprovability, leading to contradictions in certain systems of formal logic.}}

{{term |1=[[cut rule|cut]]}}
{{defn |1=In proof theory, a rule or step in a deductive proof that introduces an intermediate conclusion, which is later used to derive further conclusions.}}

{{term |1=[[Cut-elimination theorem|cut elimination]]}}
{{defn |1=A procedure in proof theory that systematically removes cuts from a proof, simplifying it and showing that any result that can be proved with cuts can also be proved without them.}}

{{glossary end}}

==D==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=dagger}}
{{defn |1=A name for the [[joint denial]], or [[logical NOR]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Sheffer Stroke {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/sheffers/ |access-date=2024-04-28 |language=en-US}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Decidability (logic)|decidable theory]]}}
{{defn |1=A theory for which there exists a decision procedure, meaning that for any statement within the theory, it is possible to algorithmically determine whether the statement is true or false within the theory.}}

{{term |1=[[decision procedure]]}}
{{defn |1=An algorithm or systematic method that can decide whether given statements are theorems (true) or non-theorems (false) in a logical system or mathematical theory.}}

{{term |1=[[De dicto and de re|de dicto]]}}
{{defn |1=Referring to the way a statement attributes a property to a noun phrase as a whole, often contrasted with de re, which attributes a property to the thing itself.}}

{{term |1=[[Deduction (logic)|deduction]]}}
{{defn |1=The process of reasoning from one or more statements (premises) to reach a logically certain conclusion.}}

{{term |1=[[deduction theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A theorem stating that if a statement can be derived from a set of premises together with another statement, then the conclusion can be derived from the premises alone by adding the statement as a conditional.}}

{{term |1=[[Deductive reasoning|deductive argument]]}}
{{defn |1=An argument where the conclusion necessarily follows from the premises, intended to provide conclusive proof of the conclusion.}}

{{term |1=deductive consequence}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|syntactic consequence}}.<ref name="IEP_Compactness">{{Cite web |title=Compactness {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/compactness/ |access-date=2024-03-22 |language=en-US}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[deductive validity]]}}
{{defn |no=1|1=The property of a deductive argument where, if the premises are true, the conclusion must also be true.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Priest |first=Graham |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1-4BLLgo0A8C |title=Logic: A Very Short Introduction |date=2000-10-12 |publisher=OUP Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-289320-8 |pages=4 |language=en}}</ref>}}
{{defn |no=2|1={{glossary link internal|Proof-theoretic validity}}, where a proof follows from the rules of the formal system.<ref name="SEP_ProofTheoreticSemantics">{{Citation |last=Schroeder-Heister |first=Peter |title=Proof-Theoretic Semantics |date=2024 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2024/entries/proof-theoretic-semantics/ |access-date=2024-04-28 |edition=Summer 2024 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref> (See {{glossary link internal|proof-theoretic semantics}}.)}}

{{term |1=deductively equivalent}}
{{defn |1=Two theories are deductively equivalent if they prove the same theorems.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Iacona |first=Andrea |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O5EtEAAAQBAJ |title=LOGIC: Lecture Notes for Philosophy, Mathematics, and Computer Science |date=2021-05-10 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-64811-4 |pages=77 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hájek |first1=Petr |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rTMoDgAAQBAJ |title=Metamathematics of First-Order Arithmetic |last2=Pudlák |first2=Pavel |date=2017-03-02 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-16841-1 |pages=166 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Leblanc |first1=Hugues |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=G9H3CAAAQBAJ |title=Foundations: Logic, Language, and Mathematics |last2=Mendelson |first2=Elliott |last3=Orenstein |first3=A. |date=2013-04-17 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-017-1592-8 |pages=93 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[deductivism]]}}
{{defn |1=The philosophical stance that emphasizes deduction as the primary method of reasoning or acquiring knowledge.}}

{{term |1=[[definiendum]]}}
{{defn |1=The term or phrase that is being defined in a definition.}}

{{term |1=[[definiens]]}}
{{defn |1=The words or phrases that are used to provide the definition of the definiendum.}}

{{term |1=[[definite description]]}}
{{defn |1=A phrase that uniquely identifies a particular individual or concept, often using "the" to specify uniqueness.}}

{{term |1=[[definition]]}}
{{defn |1=A statement that explains the meaning of a term or concept, providing its essence or specifying its characteristics.}}

{{term |1=[[deflationism]]}}
{{defn |1=A theory of truth that argues the role of the term "true" is merely to allow the expression of propositions that cannot be expressed otherwise, without implying a substantive property of truth.}}

{{term |1=degree-theoretic semantics}}
{{defn |1=An approach in semantics where the truth of sentences is measured in degrees, rather than as strictly true or false, applicable in fuzzy logic and some theories of vagueness.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Almeida |first=Michael J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QLaSAgAAQBAJ |title=The Metaphysics of Perfect Beings |date=27 February 2012 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-135-89462-7 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Wellwood |first=Alexis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GZOwDwAAQBAJ |title=The Meaning of More |date=2019-09-26 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-252681-6 |pages=157 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Garrett |first=Brian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IoBgEAAAQBAJ |title=Time, Identity and the Self: Essays on Metaphysics |date=2022-02-21 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-85517-8 |pages=175 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=demonstration}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|proof}}.}}

{{term |1=[[demonstrative]]}}
{{defn |1=A word that indicates what object is being referred to, such as "this", "that", "him", "her", and "they".}}

{{term |1=[[De Morgan duality]]}}
{{defn |1=The principle stating that the negation of a conjunction is equivalent to the disjunction of the negations, and vice versa, reflecting the duality between the logical operators AND and OR.}}

{{term |1=De Morgan negation}}
{{defn |1=A [[Augustus De Morgan|de Morgan]] negation is a simple negation satisfying [[double negation elimination]]: <math>\neg A</math> is false if and only if <math>A</math> is true, and <math>\neg A</math> is true if and only if <math>A</math> is false.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Restall |first=Greg |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NQTm_bRupAgC |title=An Introduction to Substructural Logics |date=2002-09-11 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-136-79930-3 |pages=65 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Horsten |first1=Leon |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xqVOBAAAQBAJ |title=The Bloomsbury Companion to Philosophical Logic |last2=Pettigrew |first2=Richard |date=2014-09-25 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=978-1-4725-2273-3 |pages=213 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aG3uCAAAQBAJ |title=What is Negation? |last2=Wansing |first2=Heinrich |date=2013-06-29 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-015-9309-0 |pages=26 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[De Morgan's rules]]}}
{{defn |1=Two transformation rules stating that the negation of a conjunction is the disjunction of the negations, and the negation of a disjunction is the conjunction of the negations.}}

{{term |1=[[denotation]]}}
{{defn |1=The direct reference or literal meaning of a word or phrase, as opposed to its connotation or implied meaning.}}

{{term |1=[[Dense relation|dense]]}}
{{defn |1=A relation is dense if, for any two elements, there exists a third element that lies between them according to the relation.}}

{{term |1=[[denumerable]]}}
{{defn |1=Equivalent to countably infinite; a set is denumerable if its elements can be put into a one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers.}}

{{term |1=[[denying the antecedent]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical fallacy in which the invalid argument form of "If P then Q, not P, therefore not Q" is used.}}

{{term |1=[[deontic modal logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of modal logic concerned with obligation, permission, and related modalities.}}

{{term |1=derivable rule}}
{{defn |1=A rule that can be inferred from the axioms and inference rules of a logical system, as opposed to being an axiom or primitive rule of the system.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Plato |first=Jan von |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QrdEAgAAQBAJ |title=Elements of Logical Reasoning |date=2013 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-03659-8 |pages=47 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Manzano |first=Maria |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GYSZ0AdppgMC |title=Extensions of First-Order Logic |date=1996-03-29 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-35435-6 |pages=80 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hurd |first1=Joe |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-NrzBwAAQBAJ |title=Theorem Proving in Higher Order Logics: 18th International Conference, TPHOLs 2005, Oxford, UK, August 22-25, 2005, Proceedings |last2=Melham |first2=Tom |date=2005-08-29 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-31820-0 |pages=36 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=designated value}}
{{defn |1=A semantic value that plays the same role for logical consequence as the role played by truth in classical logic, so that, for the consequence to hold, a designated value must be assigned to the conclusion if it is assigned to the premises.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Rieger |first1=Adam |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eZPHDwAAQBAJ |title=Dialetheism and its Applications |last2=Young |first2=Gareth |date=2020-01-01 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-30221-4 |pages=63 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3TNj1ZkP3qEC |title=The Many Valued and Nonmonotonic Turn in Logic |last2=Woods |first2=John |date=2007-08-13 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-08-054939-2 |pages=98 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Makridis |first=Odysseus |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DoBgEAAAQBAJ |title=Symbolic Logic |date=2022-02-21 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-67396-3 |pages=16 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[destructive dilemma]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of argument involving two conditional statements and their negated consequents, leading to the negation of at least one of the antecedents.}}

{{term |1=[[determiner]]}}
{{defn |1=A word, phrase, or affix that specifies the reference of a noun or noun phrase, such as "the", "some", "every".}}

{{term |1=deterministic polynomial time}}
{{defn |1=A complexity class (P) consisting of decision problems that can be solved by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Edixhoven |first1=Bas |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=X2aYDwAAQBAJ |title=Computational Aspects of Modular Forms and Galois Representations: How One Can Compute in Polynomial Time the Value of Ramanujan's Tau at a Prime (AM-176) |last2=Couveignes |first2=Jean-Marc |date=2011-06-20 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-14201-2 |pages=97 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Johnson |first1=R. H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c-bthgk3DQAC |title=Handbook of the Logic of Argument and Inference: The Turn Towards the Practical |last2=Ohlbach |first2=H. J. |last3=Gabbay |first3=Dov M. |last4=Woods |first4=John |date=2002-09-11 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-08-053291-2 |pages=90 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Eiter |first1=Thomas |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cc26BQAAQBAJ |title=Reasoning Web - Semantic Technologies for Advanced Query Answering: 8th International Summer School 2012, Vienna, Austria, September 3-8, 2012. Proceedings |last2=Krennwallner |first2=Thomas |date=2012-08-18 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-642-33158-9 |pages=167 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[deterministic Turing machine]]}}
{{defn |1=A theoretical computing machine that, for any given state and input symbol, has a single defined transition to a new state.}}

{{term |1=[[deviant logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A term used to describe non-standard or alternative logical systems that deviate from classical logic.}}

{{term |1=[[diagonalization lemma]]}}
{{defn |1=A lemma used in the proof of Gödel's incompleteness theorems, stating that for any formula with one free variable, there exists a sentence that asserts its own unprovability.}}

{{term |1=[[dialetheism]]}}
{{defn |1=The belief that there are true contradictions, i.e., statements that are both true and false at the same time.}}

{{term |1=[[Dialetheic logic|dialethic logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A logic that allows for the existence of true contradictions, challenging the principle of non-contradiction.}}

{{term |1=[[dilemma]]}}
{{defn |1=A situation in which a difficult choice must be made between two or more alternatives, often equally undesirable.}}

{{term |1=[[weakening (logic)|dilution]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic, the weakening of a statement by adding disjunctive clauses that do not affect the original statement's truth.}}

{{term |1=[[directed relation|directed]]}}
{{defn |1=A relation is directed if, for every pair of elements, there is a third element related to both, ensuring a kind of coherence or consistency within the set.}}

{{term |1=discharge}}
{{defn |1=The act of eliminating an assumption in a logical derivation, often by using it to prove a conditional statement.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Glossary Discharge {{!}} Logic Notes - ANU |url=https://users.cecs.anu.edu.au/~jks/LogicNotes/glossary/g_discharge.html |access-date=2024-04-28 |website=users.cecs.anu.edu.au}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Natural Deduction {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/natural-deduction/ |access-date=2024-04-28 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Braüner |first=Torben |date=2004 |title=Two Natural Deduction Systems for Hybrid Logic: A Comparison |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40180365 |journal=Journal of Logic, Language and Information |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=1–23 |doi=10.1023/A:1026187215321 |jstor=40180365 |issn=0925-8531}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=disjunct}}
{{defn |1=One of the component propositions in a [[Logical disjunction|disjunction]], each of which is an alternative to the others.<ref name="beallbasics1ed" />}}

{{term |1=[[disjunction]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical connective that represents the "or" relationship between two statements, requiring at least one to be true.}}

{{term |1=[[disjunction elimination]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule of inference that allows deriving a conclusion from a disjunction and conditional statements—if <math>P \lor Q</math> and both <math>P \rightarrow R</math> and <math>Q \rightarrow R</math>, then <math>R</math>.}}

{{term |1=[[disjunction introduction]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical principle allowing the introduction of a disjunction from any single proposition— from <math>P</math>, infer <math>P \lor Q</math>.}}

{{term |1=[[disjunction property]]}}
{{defn |1=A property in intuitionistic logic stating that if a disjunction <math>P \lor Q</math> is provable, then either <math>P</math> is provable or <math>Q</math> is provable.}}

{{term |1=[[disjunctive normal form]]}}
{{defn |1=A standardization of logical formulae in which a formula is expressed as a disjunction of conjunctive clauses.}}

{{term |1=[[disjunctive syllogism]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of deductive reasoning that concludes one disjunct must be false if the other is true and a disjunction is given (if <math>P \lor Q</math> and not <math>P</math>, then <math>Q</math>).}}

{{term |1=[[disquotationalism]]}}
{{defn |1=A theory of truth that focuses on the disquotation principle, which suggests that the function of the truth predicate is to remove quotation marks to form equivalent sentences.}}

{{term |1=[[distribution of terms|distribution]]}}
{{defn |1=A term is distributed within a [[categorical proposition]] if, and only if, that proposition says something about all objects instantiating that term.}}

{{term |1=distribution axiom}}
{{defn |no=1|1=In [[modal logic]], the axiom (called K) that {{math|□(''p'' → ''q'') → (□''p'' → □''q'')}}.<ref name="SEP_ModalLogic">{{Citation |last=Garson |first=James |title=Modal Logic |date=2024 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/spr2024/entries/logic-modal/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=Spring 2024 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>}}
{{defn |no=2|1=In [[epistemic modal logic]], the axiom (also called K) that <math>(K_i\varphi \land K_i(\varphi \implies \psi)) \implies K_i\psi</math>.}}

{{term |1=distributive laws}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|distributivity}}.}}

{{term |1=distributive predication}}
{{defn |1=A property of predicates in logic that allows them to be applied to each element of a subject class individually rather than to the class as a whole.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kamareddine |first=Fairouz |date=1995 |title=A Type Free Theory and Collective/Distributive Predication |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40180063 |journal=Journal of Logic, Language and Information |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=85–109 |doi=10.1007/BF01048616 |jstor=40180063 |issn=0925-8531}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=de Vries |first=Hanna |date=2017 |title=Two kinds of distributivity |journal=Natural Language Semantics |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=173–197 |doi=10.1007/s11050-017-9133-z |jstor=26636691 |issn=0925-854X|doi-access=free }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[distributivity]]}}
{{defn |1=The characteristic of certain binary operations to be able to distribute over others in a specific algebraic structure, maintaining equivalence.}}

{{term |1=division}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|fallacy of division}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Domain of a function|domain]]}}
{{defn |1=The set of all possible inputs for a function, or more generally, the subject matter or universe of discourse in a logical argument.}}

{{term |1=[[domain of discourse]]}}
{{defn |1=The collection of objects being discussed in a particular logical context, which determines the range of quantifiers.}}

{{term |1=dominant connective}}
{{defn |1=The connective with the largest {{glossary link internal|scope}} in a formula.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Suppes |first1=Patrick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=38LCAgAAQBAJ |title=First Course in Mathematical Logic |last2=Hill |first2=Shirley |date=2012-04-30 |publisher=Courier Corporation |isbn=978-0-486-15094-9 |pages=23–26 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Kirk |first=Donna |url=https://openstax.org/books/contemporary-mathematics/pages/2-2-compound-statements |title=Contemporary Mathematics |date=2023-03-22 |publisher=OpenStax |chapter=2.2. Compound Statements}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[double negation]]}}
{{defn |1=The application of negation twice to a proposition, which in classical logic results in the original proposition (<math>\neg \neg P \equiv P</math>).}}

{{term |1=[[double negation elimination]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle in classical logic stating that the double negation of a statement can be removed without changing its truth value (<math>\neg \neg P</math> is equivalent to <math>P</math>).}}

{{term |1=[[double negation introduction]]}}
{{defn |1=The principle that for any proposition <math>P</math>, <math>P</math> implies <math>\neg \neg P</math>, reinforcing the assertion of <math>P</math> by denying its negation.}}

{{term |1=[[double turnstile]]}}
{{defn |1=A symbol (<math>\models</math>) used in logic to denote semantic entailment or logical consequence, indicating that the truth of some propositions necessitates the truth of another.}}

{{term |1=[[downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=Part of the {{glossary link internal|Löwenheim–Skolem theorem}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Doxastic logic|doxastic modal logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of modal logic that deals with the logic of belief, modeling the beliefs of rational agents.}}

{{term |1=dual}}
{{defn |1=The dual of a truth-table is obtained by interchanging the truth values "true" and "false" (or 0 and 1) throughout the table. Connectives are dual if their truth-tables are dual: conjunction and disjunction are dual, and negation is self-dual.<ref name="OmodeoComputability">{{Cite book |last1=Omodeo |first1=Eugenio G. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GlgLDgAAQBAJ |title=Martin Davis on Computability, Computational Logic, and Mathematical Foundations |last2=Policriti |first2=Alberto |date=2017-01-27 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-319-41842-1 |pages=384 |language=en}}</ref> The dual of a formula is obtained by replacing each connective by its dual,<ref name="OmodeoComputability" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Bimbo |first=Katalin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=M5dBBAAAQBAJ |title=Proof Theory: Sequent Calculi and Related Formalisms |date=2014-08-20 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-4665-6466-4 |pages=193 |language=en}}</ref> e.g., for a formula containing only conjunction, disjunction, and negation (such as a formula in [[disjunctive normal form]]), its dual is the result of replacing each conjunction with a disjunction, and each disjunction with a conjunction. (For a formula in disjunctive normal form, its dual is a formula in [[conjunctive normal form]].)<ref>{{Cite book |last=Church |first=Alonzo |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JDLQOMKbdScC |title=Introduction to Mathematical Logic |date=1996 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-02906-1 |pages=166 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Igarashi |first1=Yoshihide |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=58ySAwAAQBAJ |title=Computing: A Historical and Technical Perspective |last2=Altman |first2=Tom |last3=Funada |first3=Mariko |last4=Kamiyama |first4=Barbara |date=2014-05-27 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-4822-2741-3 |pages=127 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=dynamic modal logic}}
{{defn |1=A branch of [[modal logic]] that studies necessary and possible connections between events.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=De Rijke |first=Maarten |date=1998 |title=A System of Dynamic Modal Logic |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/30227100 |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |volume=27 |issue=2 |pages=109–142 |doi=10.1023/A:1004295308014 |jstor=30227100 |issn=0022-3611}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=van Eijck |first1=J |url=https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/1963 |title=Dynamic modal predicate logic |last2=Cepparello |first2=G |date=January 1994 |publisher=CSLI Publishers, Stanford}}</ref>}}

{{glossary end}}

==E==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=[[effective procedure]]}}
{{defn |1=A method or process that guarantees a solution to a particular problem or class of problems, typically through a finite number of steps that can be precisely followed.}}

{{term |1=[[effectively computable|effectively computable function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function for which there exists an algorithm or mechanical procedure that can compute the function's value for any valid input in a finite amount of time.}}

{{term |1=effectively decidable relation}}
{{defn |1=A binary relation for which there exists a mechanical method to determine, for any given pair of elements, whether the relation holds between them.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Boolos |first1=George S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0LpsXQV2kXAC |title=Computability and Logic |last2=Burgess |first2=John P. |last3=Jeffrey |first3=Richard C. |date=2002-03-04 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-00758-0 |pages=73–74 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Feferman |first=Solomon |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QYdJAQAAMAAJ |title=Formal Consistency Proofs and Interpretability of Theories |date=1957 |publisher=University of California, Berkeley |pages=21 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=effectively decidable theory}}
