{{defn |1=A theory in which there exists an algorithm capable of determining whether any given statement within the theory is true or false.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Blondel |first1=Vincent D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-OwmYdZySwAC |title=Unsolved Problems in Mathematical Systems and Control Theory |last2=Megretski |first2=Alexandre |date=2009-04-11 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1-4008-2615-5 |pages=305 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="GodelIntro" />}}

{{term |1=[[elementary equivalence]]}}
{{defn |1=A relationship between two structures in logic and mathematics where they satisfy the same first-order sentences.}}

{{term |1=[[elementary topos]]}}
{{defn |1=A concept in category theory generalizing set theory concepts within a more abstract framework, allowing for the definition of mathematical structures in different contexts.}}

{{term |1=[[elimination of quantifiers]]}}
{{defn |1=A process in logical deduction where quantifiers are removed from logical expressions while preserving equivalence, often used in the theory of real closed fields.}}

{{term |1=[[elimination rule]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule in logical inference that allows the derivation of simpler formulas from more complex ones, often by removing logical connectives or quantifiers.}}

{{term |1=empty concept}}
{{defn |1=A concept that does not have any instantiation in reality or does not refer to any existing object or group of objects.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kiyoki |first=Yasushi |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ghtWcQy2DysC |title=Information Modelling and Knowledge Bases XV |date=2004 |publisher=IOS Press |isbn=978-1-58603-396-5 |pages=202 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Boniolo |first=G. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WnKGDAAAQBAJ |title=On Scientific Representations: From Kant to a New Philosophy of Science |date=2007-04-25 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-0-230-20657-1 |pages=60 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[endomorphism]]}}
{{defn |1=A function from a mathematical object to itself that preserves the object's structure.}}

{{term |1=[[entailment]]}}
{{defn |1=The logical relationship where the truth of one set of statements (the premises) necessitates the truth of another statement (the conclusion).}}

{{term |1=[[enthymeme]]}}
{{defn |1=A rhetorical argument that is presented with one or more premises left implied rather than explicitly stated.}}

{{term |1=[[Entscheidungsproblem]]}}
{{defn |1=The decision problem, a challenge posed by David Hilbert asking for an algorithm to determine the truth or falsity of any given mathematical statement. The problem was proven to be unsolvable by Alan Turing and Alonzo Church.}}

{{term |1=[[Epimenides paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A self-referential paradox involving a statement made by Epimenides, a Cretan, who stated that all Cretans are liars, leading to a logical contradiction if taken to be true.}}

{{term |1=[[epimorphism]]}}
{{defn |1=A morphism in category theory that is right-cancellable, meaning it behaves like a surjective function in the context of sets.}}

{{term |1=epistemic constraint}}
{{defn |1=The principle that truths must be knowable. It is brought up in the context of [[verificationism]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Knowles |first=William Bondi |date=2024-01-09 |title=Knowability paradox, decidability solution? |journal=Ratio |volume=37 |issue=2–3 |pages=102–111 |language=en |doi=10.1111/rati.12396 |issn=0034-0006|doi-access=free }}</ref> and [[Fitch's paradox of knowability]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cook |first=Roy T. |title=Paradoxes |date=2013 |publisher=Polity |isbn=978-0-7456-4943-6 |series=Polity key concepts in philosophy |location=Cambridge Malden (Mass.) |pages=163}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[epistemic modal logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of modal logic that deals with reasoning about knowledge and belief, using modalities to express what is known and what is believed.}}

{{term |1=epistemic paradox}}
{{defn |1=A paradox arising from basic intuitions regarding knowledge, belief, or related epistemic notions. For instance, the {{glossary link internal|knower paradox}} and the {{glossary link internal|Fitch paradox}}.}}

{{term |1=epistemic vagueness}}
{{defn |1=The view that [[vagueness]] is a feature of human knowledge, rather than of the world or of language.<ref name="VaguenessGuide">{{Cite book |last=Ronzitti |first=Giuseppina |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WhutdYQz6mMC |title=Vagueness: A Guide |date=2011-03-03 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-007-0375-9 |pages=62, 83, 88 |language=en}}</ref> Contrast {{glossary link internal|in rebus vagueness}} and {{glossary link internal|semantic vagueness}}.}}

{{term |1=[[epistemicism]]}}
{{defn |1=The philosophical position that there are truths that cannot be known, typically applied to discussions of vagueness and the sorites paradox.}}

{{term |1=E-proposition}}
{{defn |1=In traditional logic, a universal negative categorical proposition, stating that no members of one class are members of another class.<ref>{{Cite web |title=E-proposition |url=https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/e-proposition |website=Collins Dictionary}}</ref><ref name="IEP_Square" />}}

{{term |1=equivalence}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|deductively equivalent}}, {{glossary link internal|logically equivalent}}, {{glossary link internal|materially equivalent}}.}}

{{term |1=[[equivalence relation]]}}
{{defn |1=A binary relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, indicating that elements it relates are in some sense "equivalent."}}

{{term |1=equivalent}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|deductively equivalent}}, {{glossary link internal|logically equivalent}}, {{glossary link internal|materially equivalent}}.}}

{{term |1=[[equivocation]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical fallacy involving the use of a word with more than one meaning throughout an argument, leading to a misleading or unsound conclusion.}}

{{term |1=[[erotetic logic]]}}
{{defn |1=The logic of questions, including the study of the forms and principles of questions and their relationships to answers.}}

{{term |1=[[Eubulides' paradox|Eubulides paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A paradox presented by Eubulides of Miletus, including the liar paradox, which involves a statement declaring itself to be false, creating a contradiction.}}

{{term |1=[[Euclidean relation|Euclidean]]}}
{{defn |1=A relation R where, for any objects x, y, and z, it is true that if Rxy and Rxz, then Ryz.}}

{{term |1=exchange}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|permutation}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Law of excluded middle|excluded middle]]}}
{{defn |1=The principle that for any proposition, either that proposition is true or its negation is true, with no middle ground.}}

{{term |1=exclusion negation}}
{{defn |1=In [[three-valued logic]], form of negation that strictly excludes the possibility of something being true, as opposed to constructive negation which asserts the truth of an opposite proposition.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Stone |first=John David |date=1981 |title=Meaninglessness and Paradox: Some Remarks on Goldstein's Paper |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25001063 |journal=Linguistics and Philosophy |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=423–429 |doi=10.1007/BF00304404 |jstor=25001063 |issn=0165-0157}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Horn |first1=Laurence R. |title=Negation |date=2022 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2022/entries/negation/ |access-date=2024-04-28 |edition=Winter 2022 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Wansing |first2=Heinrich |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[exclusive disjunction]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical operation that is true if and only if exactly one of its operands is true, also known as "xor" or "exclusive or."}}

{{term |1=[[exclusive or]]}}
{{defn |1=A binary logical operation that returns true only when the inputs are different; symbolized as XOR or <math>\oplus</math>.}}

{{term |1=[[ex falso quodlibet]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle in classical logic stating that from a falsehood, any conclusion can be derived, also known as the principle of explosion.}}

{{term |1=existence predicate}}
{{defn |1=A predicate, usually occurring in [[free logic]]s, that asserts the existence of the referent of a constant.<ref>{{Citation |last=Nolt |first=John |title=Free Logic |date=2021 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2021/entries/logic-free/ |access-date=2024-04-28 |edition=Fall 2021 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pavlović |first1=Edi |last2=Gratzl |first2=Norbert |date=2021-02-01 |title=A More Unified Approach to Free Logics |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |language=en |volume=50 |issue=1 |pages=117–148 |doi=10.1007/s10992-020-09564-7 |issn=1573-0433|doi-access=free }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[existential generalization]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule of inference allowing the conclusion that something exists with a certain property, based on the existence of a particular example.}}

{{term |1=[[existential import]]}}
{{defn |1=The implication that something exists by the assertion of a particular kind of statement, especially relevant in traditional syllogistic logic.}}

{{term |1=[[existential instantiation]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical rule that allows one to infer the existence of a particular individual from a statement asserting the existence of such an individual generically.}}

{{term |1=[[existential introduction]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule of inference that introduces an existential quantifier, asserting the existence of at least one entity that satisfies a given property.}}

{{term |1=[[existential quantifier]]}}
{{defn |1=A quantifier used in predicate logic to indicate that there exists at least one member of the domain for which the predicate holds true.}}

{{term |1=existential variable}}
{{defn |1=A variable in predicate logic that is bound by an [[existential quantifier]], representing an unspecified member of the domain that satisfies the predicate.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Metakides |first1=G. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1BZW9m5ScQoC |title=Principles of Logic and Logic Programming |last2=Nerode |first2=A. |date=1996-06-13 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-08-053964-5 |pages=130 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Prolog |url=https://www.cs.gordon.edu/courses/cs323/PROLOG/prolog.html |access-date=2024-04-28 |website=www.cs.gordon.edu}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Explanandum and explanans|explanandum]]}}
{{defn |1=The statement or phenomenon that is being explained in an explanation.}}

{{term |1=[[explanans]]}}
{{defn |1=The statement or set of statements that provide the explanation for the phenomenon or statement referred to by the explanandum.}}

{{term |1=[[explanation]]}}
{{defn |1=The act of clarifying, elucidating, or making something understandable through detailing reasons, causes, or justifications.}}

{{term |1=explicit definition}}
{{defn |1=A definition that provides a means for replacing each occurrence of the {{glossary link internal|definiendum}} with an appropriate instance of the {{glossary link internal|definiens}}.<ref name="Springer_Implicit">{{Cite journal |last1=Giovannini |first1=Eduardo N. |last2=Schiemer |first2=Georg |date=2021-12-01 |title=What are Implicit Definitions? |journal=Erkenntnis |language=en |volume=86 |issue=6 |pages=1661–1691 |doi=10.1007/s10670-019-00176-5 |issn=1572-8420|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Winnie |first=John A. |date=1965 |title=Theoretical Terms and Partial Definitions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/186527 |journal=Philosophy of Science |volume=32 |issue=3/4 |pages=324–328 |doi=10.1086/288056 |jstor=186527 |issn=0031-8248}}</ref> Contrast {{glossary link internal|implicit definition}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Explosion (logic)|explosion]]}}
{{defn |1=The principle in logic that from a contradiction, any statement can be proven, related to the principle of ex falso quodlibet.}}

{{term |1=exportation}}
{{defn |1=A logical principle that transforms a statement of the form <math>(P \land Q) \rightarrow R</math> into the equivalent form <math>P \rightarrow (Q \rightarrow R)</math>, essentially redistributing the logical operations.<ref name="IEP_PropositionalLogic" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Propositional Logic {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/propositional-logic-sentential-logic/ |access-date=2024-04-28 |language=en-US}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=expressive completeness}}
{{defn |1=Synonym of [[functional completeness]].}}

{{term |1=[[extension (semantics)|extension]]}}
{{defn |1=The collection of objects or entities to which a term or concept applies, contrasted with its intension, which refers to the properties or characteristics defining those objects or entities.}}

{{term |1=[[extensional logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of logic where the truth of sentences and arguments depends solely on the extension of the terms involved, disregarding their intension or conceptual content.}}

{{glossary end}}

==F==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=factivity}}
{{defn |1=The property of certain expressions or verbs that implies the truth of the propositions they refer to, often used in the context of knowledge and belief.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Newmeyer |first=Frederick J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SZRsDwAAQBAJ |title=English Aspectual Verbs |date=2017-12-04 |publisher=Walter de Gruyter GmbH & Co KG |isbn=978-3-11-081845-1 |pages=65 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Radford |first=Andrew |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a-74DwAAQBAJ |title=An Introduction to English Sentence Structure |date=2020-10-15 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-83954-9 |pages=348 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[fallacy]]}}
{{defn |1=An error in reasoning that results in an invalid argument or one that is not logically sound.}}

{{term |1=[[fallacy of composition]]}}
{{defn |1=The logical error of assuming that what is true of the parts must also be true of the whole.}}

{{term |1=[[fallacy of division]]}}
{{defn |1=The logical error of assuming that what is true of the whole must also be true of its parts.}}

{{term |1=[[fallacy of four terms]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical fallacy in syllogistic logic where a syllogism includes four (rather than the requisite three) distinct terms, making the argument invalid.}}

{{term |1=[[false dichotomy]]}}
{{defn |1=An [[informal fallacy]] that presents two options as the only possibilities when in fact more possibilities exist.}}

{{term |1=[[false dilemma]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of false dichotomy where two choices are presented as the only options when other alternatives are available, often used to force a decision.}}

{{term |1=[[falsemaker]]}}
{{defn |1=An entity or set of conditions that makes a proposition false. In metaphysics, it's considered the counterpart to a truthmaker, which validates the truth of a proposition.}}

{{term |1=[[falsity]]}}
{{defn |1=The quality or condition of being false or untrue.}}

{{term |1=[[falsum]]}}
{{defn |1=A symbol used in logic to represent falsity or a contradiction, often denoted as <math>\bot</math>.}}

{{term |1="Fido"-Fido principle}}
{{defn |1=The principle in philosophy of language suggesting that the meaning of a word is the object it refers to, exemplified by the idea that the meaning of "Fido" is the dog Fido itself.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rudolf Carnap > H. Tolerance, Metaphysics, and Meta-Ontology (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy) |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/carnap/tolerance-metaphysics.html |access-date=2024-04-28 |website=plato.stanford.edu |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Field of a relation|field]]}}
{{defn |1=The field of a function is the union of the domain and range of that function.}}

{{term |1=figure}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|syllogistic figure}}.}}

{{term |1=[[finitary]]}}
{{defn |1=Pertaining to methods or processes that involve a finite number of steps or elements.}}

{{term |1=finitary arithmetic}}
{{defn |1=An approach to arithmetic focusing on finitary methods, avoiding infinities and emphasizing constructions that can be completed in a finite number of steps.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Panza |first1=Marco |chapter=From Frege to Gödel (Through Hilbert) |date=2013 |title=Plato's Problem |pages=45–98 |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1057/9781137298133_3 |access-date=2024-04-28 |place=London |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan UK |language=en |doi=10.1057/9781137298133_3 |isbn=978-0-230-36549-0 |last2=Sereni |first2=Andrea|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=finitary formal system}}
{{defn |1=A formal system in which all operations, proofs, and expressions are finitary, relying only on objects that can be constructed or demonstrated in a finite number of steps.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hockney |first=Mike |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jgbzEAAAQBAJ |title=Hyperreason |date=2013-09-30 |publisher=Magus Books |pages=203 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Aigner-Horev |first1=Elad |title=Infinite matroid union |date=2012-07-09 |last2=Carmesin |first2=Johannes |last3=Fröhlich |first3=Jan-Oliver|arxiv=1111.0602 }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[finite character]]}}
{{defn |1=The property of certain mathematical or logical systems where every relevant feature or property can be determined by examining only a finite part of the system.}}

{{term |1=[[finite model theory]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of model theory that deals with the study of properties of structures (models) that have a finite domain.}}

{{term |1=finitely axiomatizable}}
{{defn |1=Referring to a theory that can be fully captured by a finite set of axioms.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Blossier |first1=Thomas |last2=Bouscaren |first2=Elisabeth |date=2010 |title=Finitely Axiomatizable Strongly Minimal Groups |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25676766 |journal=The Journal of Symbolic Logic |volume=75 |issue=1 |pages=25–50 |doi=10.2178/jsl/1264433908 |jstor=25676766 |issn=0022-4812}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ivanov |first=Alexandre |date=May 1999 |title=FINITELY AXIOMATIZABLE THEORIES (Siberian School of Algebra and Logic) |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1112/S0024609397244164 |journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=31 |issue=3 |pages=373 |doi=10.1112/S0024609397244164|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Ebbinghaus |first1=H.-D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4sbSBwAAQBAJ |title=Mathematical Logic |last2=Flum |first2=J. |last3=Thomas |first3=Wolfgang |date=2013-03-14 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4757-2355-7 |pages=174 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[finitism]]}}
{{defn |1=A philosophical view that rejects the existence of infinite entities and infinite processes, emphasizing only those quantities or procedures that are finite.}}

{{term |1=first-degree entailment (FDE)}}
{{defn |1=A logical system that allows for the existence of both true and false atomic propositions but does not require every proposition to be either true or false, rejecting the law of the excluded middle for certain propositions.<ref>{{Citation |chapter=First Degree Entailment |date=2008 |title=[[An Introduction to Non-Classical Logic|An Introduction to Non-Classical Logic: From If to Is]] |pages=142–162 |editor-last=Priest |editor-first=Graham |chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/an-introduction-to-nonclassical-logic/first-degree-entailment/4BBFFAE38831FA9CFF610C417C524273 |access-date=2024-04-28 |series=Cambridge Introductions to Philosophy |edition=2 |place=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/cbo9780511801174.011 |isbn=978-0-511-80117-4|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Omori |first1=Hitoshi |last2=Wansing |first2=Heinrich |date=2017-12-01 |title=40 years of FDE: An Introductory Overview |journal=Studia Logica |language=en |volume=105 |issue=6 |pages=1021–1049 |doi=10.1007/s11225-017-9748-6 |issn=1572-8730|doi-access=free }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[first-order logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A formal logical system involving quantifiers "for all" and "there exists," which can quantify over individuals but not over predicates or functions.}}

{{term |1=[[first-order theory]]}}
{{defn |1=A theory expressed in first-order logic, dealing with the relationships between individuals and properties or relations that individuals may have.}}

{{term |1=first-order variable}}
{{defn |1=A variable in first-order logic that represents an individual in the domain of discourse.}}

{{term |1=[[Fitch's paradox of knowability|Fitch paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A paradox in epistemic logic that arises from seemingly reasonable assumptions about knowledge and leads to the conclusion that all truths are known.}}

{{term |1=[[Fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]]}}
{{defn |1=In mathematics and logic, a value or element that is mapped to itself by a particular function or operation.}}

{{term |1=forced march sorites}}
{{defn |1=A type of [[sorites paradox]] involving a series of incremental steps or changes that lead to a contradiction, challenging the precision of vague predicates by forcing a march from one end of a spectrum to another.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Åkerman |first=Jonas |date=2013 |title=Forced-March Sorites Arguments and Linguistic Competence |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/42971334 |journal=Dialectica |volume=67 |issue=4 |pages=403–426 |doi=10.1111/1746-8361.12038 |jstor=42971334 |issn=0012-2017}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Hyde |first1=Dominic |title=Sorites Paradox |date=2018 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2018/entries/sorites-paradox/ |access-date=2024-04-28 |edition=Summer 2018 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Raffman |first2=Diana}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=formal consequence}}
{{defn |1=A conclusion that follows in virtue of {{glossary link internal|logical form}} alone, as distinguished from a {{glossary link internal|material consequence}}, which (also) depends on the content of the propositions.<ref name="Ashworth_Formal_Material">{{Cite book |last=Ashworth |first=E. J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FSAyBwAAQBAJ |title=Language and Logic in the Post-Medieval Period |date=2012-12-06 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-010-2226-2 |pages=128 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Gabbay_Formal_Material">{{Cite book |last1=Gabbay |first1=Dov M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c2nmqagEz6QC |title=Mediaeval and Renaissance Logic |last2=Woods |first2=John |date=2008-03-14 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-08-056085-4 |pages=475 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Buridan_Formal_Material">{{Cite book |last1=Hochschild |first1=Joshua P. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZkG8EAAAQBAJ |title=Metaphysics Through Semantics: The Philosophical Recovery of the Medieval Mind: Essays in Honor of Gyula Klima |last2=Nevitt |first2=Turner C. |last3=Wood |first3=Adam |last4=Borbély |first4=Gábor |date=2023-04-27 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-031-15026-5 |pages=265 |language=en}}</ref> See also {{glossary link internal|syntactic consequence}}.}}

{{term |1=[[formal fallacy]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical error in the form or structure of an argument, as opposed to a material fallacy which relates to the argument's content.}}

{{term |1=[[formal language]]}}
{{defn |1=A set of strings of symbols that are constructed according to specific syntactic rules, used in mathematics, computer science, and formal logic to precisely define expressions without ambiguity.}}

{{term |1=[[formal logic]]}}
{{defn |1=The study of inference with purely formal content, where no interpretation is given to the terms and only the logical form is considered.}}

{{term |1=[[formal proof]]}}
{{defn |1=A proof in which each step is justified by a rule of inference, constructed within a formal system to demonstrate the truth of a proposition.}}

{{term |1=[[Formal semantics (logic)|formal semantics]]}}
{{defn |1=The study of how formal systems, especially those used in logic and linguistics, are connected to conceptual or referential interpretations.}}

{{term |1=[[formal system]]}}
{{defn |1=A system of symbols and rules for manipulating these symbols, used to derive statements or theorems in a logical or mathematical domain.}}

{{term |1=[[formation rule]]s}}
{{defn |1=Rules that specify the correct ways in which the basic symbols of a formal language can be combined to form well-formed formulas.}}

{{term |1=[[Formula (logic)|formula]]}}
{{defn |1=An expression in a formal language that can be evaluated as true or false within a given interpretation, often involving variables and logical connectives.}}

{{term |1=[[Kripke semantics|frame]]}}
{{defn |1=In modal logic, a structure consisting of a set of possible worlds and a relation between those worlds, used to interpret modal propositions.}}

{{term |1=[[Frame semantics (linguistics)|frame semantics]]}}
{{defn |1=A theory in linguistics and logic that uses frames—conceptual structures for representing stereotypical situations—as a means of understanding how language conveys meaning.}}

{{term |1=[[Free choice sequences|free choice sequence]]}}
{{defn |1=A sequence (typically of natural numbers) where each term is chosen freely, not determined by any rule or algorithm, often used in discussions of constructivism and intuitionism.}}

{{term |1=[[free logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of logic that allows for terms that do not denote any existing object, differing from classical logic by not requiring every term to refer to something in the domain of discourse.}}

{{term |1=[[Free variables and bound variables|free variable]]}}
{{defn |1=A variable in a formula that is not bound by a quantifier and does not have a specific value assigned to it within the context of the formula.}}

{{term |1=[[Frege's theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A result in logic and mathematics demonstrating that arithmetic can be derived from logic through the introduction of the concept of a successor and the use of second-order quantification.}}

{{term |1=[[Function (mathematics)|function]]}}
{{defn |1=A relation between sets that associates every element of a first set with exactly one element of a second set, often represented as a mapping from elements of one set to elements of another.}}

{{term |1=[[fuzzy logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A [[many-valued logic]] which allows for degrees of truth and certainty.}}

{{glossary end}}

==G==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=[[gambler's fallacy]]}}
{{defn |1=The erroneous belief that if an event occurs more frequently than normal during the past, it is less likely to happen in the future (or vice versa), often arising in contexts of gambling and misinterpretation of statistics.}}

{{term |1=game-theoretic semantics}}
{{defn |1=An approach to semantics that interprets the meaning of linguistic expressions through the outcomes of certain idealized games played between a verifier and a falsifier, emphasizing the interactive process of establishing truth or falsehood.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Hodges |first1=Wilfrid |title=Logic and Games |date=2019 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2019/entries/logic-games/ |access-date=2024-04-28 |edition=Fall 2019 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Väänänen |first2=Jouko}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=gap}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|truth-value gap}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Geach-Kaplan sentence]]}}
{{defn |1=A type of sentence that raises issues in the philosophy of language and logic regarding context-dependence, referential opacity, and the limits of formal semantic analysis. Named after philosophers Peter Geach and David Kaplan.}}

{{term |1=[[generalized quantifier]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic and linguistics, a quantifier that can express more complex relationships than standard quantifiers like "all" or "some," allowing for the expression of concepts like "most," "many," and "few."}}

{{term |1=[[Glivenko's translation|Glivenko's theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A result in logic stating that if a formula is provable in classical logic, then its double negation is provable in intuitionistic logic, establishing a connection between the two logics.}}

{{term |1=glut}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|truth-value glut}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Gödel numbering]]}}
{{defn |1=A method of encoding mathematical and logical symbols and expressions as natural numbers, introduced by Kurt Gödel as part of his incompleteness theorems.}}

{{term |1=[[Gödel sentence]]}}
{{defn |1=A self-referential sentence constructed in formal systems to demonstrate Gödel's incompleteness theorems, asserting its own unprovability within the system.}}

{{term |1=[[Gödel-Dummett logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of intuitionistic logic that includes a principle of maximal elements, allowing for the expression of certain intermediate truth values between true and false.}}

{{term |1=[[Gödel's first incompleteness theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A theorem proving that in any consistent formal system that is capable of expressing basic arithmetic, there are propositions that cannot be proven or disproven within the system.}}

{{term |1=[[Gödel's second incompleteness theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A theorem establishing that no consistent system capable of doing arithmetic can prove its own consistency, building on the first incompleteness theorem.}}

{{term |1=[[Slingshot argument|Gödel's slingshot argument]]}}
{{defn |1=An argument concerning the semantics of reference and truth, challenging the coherence of theories that attempt to distinguish between facts and true propositions in a fine-grained manner.}}

{{term |1=[[Grelling–Nelson paradox|Grelling paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A paradox related to self-reference and linguistic categories, particularly whether the word "heterological," meaning not applicable to itself, applies to itself.}}
{{glossary end}}

==H==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=[[halting problem]]}}
{{defn |1=The decision problem of determining, from a description of an arbitrary computer program and an input, whether the program will finish running or continue to run forever. Proven to be undecidable by Alan Turing.}}

{{term |1=[[Logical harmony|harmony]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic and philosophy, the notion that the introduction and elimination rules for a logical connective should be in balance, ensuring that the connective does not introduce more than it can eliminate, and vice versa.}}

{{term |1=[[hasty generalization]]}}
{{defn |1=An [[informal fallacy]] in which a conclusion is not logically justified by sufficient or unbiased evidence; drawing a general conclusion from a too-small sample size.}}

{{term |1=[[Henkin semantics]]}}
{{defn |1=A generalization of standard first-order semantics that allows for models where the range of quantifiers can be restricted, named after Leon Henkin.}}

{{term |1=Henkin sentence}}
{{defn |1=A sentence that asserts its own provability,<ref>{{Citation |last1=Halbach |first1=Volker |chapter=The Henkin Sentence |date=2014 |title=The Life and Work of Leon Henkin |pages=249–263 |editor-last=Manzano |editor-first=María |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-319-09719-0_17 |access-date=2024-04-28 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-09719-0_17 |isbn=978-3-319-09718-3 |last2=Visser |first2=Albert |editor2-last=Sain |editor2-first=Ildikó |editor3-last=Alonso |editor3-first=Enrique|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Boolos |first1=George S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0LpsXQV2kXAC |title=Computability and Logic |last2=Burgess |first2=John P. |last3=Jeffrey |first3=Richard C. |date=2002-03-04 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-00758-0 |pages=236 |language=en}}</ref> possibly by applying the {{glossary link internal|provability predicate}} to itself.}}

{{term |1=[[hereditary property]]}}
{{defn |1=A property of objects in a mathematical or logical structure that, if applied to an object, also applies to all subobjects or elements of that object.}}

{{term |1=[[heterological]]}}
{{defn |1=Describing an adjective that does not apply to itself. For example, "long" is not long, so "long" is heterological.}}

{{term |1=[[hierarchy]]}}
{{defn |1=A system in which entities are ranked one above the other based on certain criteria, often used in the context of sets, classes, or organizational structures. In logic, an important one is {{glossary link internal|Tarskian hierarchy|Tarski's hierarchy}}. In [[set theory]], an important one is the [[cumulative hierarchy]].}}

{{term |1=[[higher-order logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of logic that extends first-order logic by allowing quantification over predicates and possibly other higher-order entities, not just individuals.}}

{{term |1=higher-order quantifier}}
{{defn |1=A quantifier that binds a {{glossary link internal|higher-order variable}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ghilardi |first1=Silvio |last2=Pagani |first2=Elena |date=2021-03-01 |title=Higher-Order Quantifier Elimination, Counter Simulations and Fault-Tolerant Systems |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10817-020-09578-5 |journal=Journal of Automated Reasoning |language=en |volume=65 |issue=3 |pages=425–460 |doi=10.1007/s10817-020-09578-5 |issn=1573-0670|hdl=2434/766980 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hofweber |first=Thomas |date=2022-12-08 |title=The Case Against Higher-Order Metaphysics |journal=Metaphysics Collaborative |language=en-US |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=29–50 |doi=10.5334/met.83|doi-access=free }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=higher-order vagueness}}
{{defn |1=Vagueness about the application of the concept of vagueness itself, particularly in the context of predicates that are borderline cases of borderline cases.<ref name="SEP_Vagueness" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Williamson |first=Timothy |date=1999 |title=On the Structure of Higher-Order Vagueness |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2659905 |journal=Mind |volume=108 |issue=429 |pages=127–143 |doi=10.1093/mind/108.429.127 |jstor=2659905 |issn=0026-4423}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=higher-order variable}}
{{defn |1=A variable in higher-order logic that represents a function, predicate, or relation, rather than an individual object.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hale |first=Bob |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=L7poAgAAQBAJ |title=Necessary Beings: An Essay on Ontology, Modality, and the Relations Between Them |date=2013-09-19 |publisher=OUP Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-164834-2 |pages=183 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Cook |first=Roy T. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Zps0E4zVmAMC |title=The Arché Papers on the Mathematics of Abstraction |date=2007-11-27 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4020-4265-2 |pages=355 |language=en}}</ref>
}}

{{term |1=[[Hilbert's program]]}}
{{defn |1=An ambitious project proposed by David Hilbert to provide a solid foundation for all of mathematics by formalizing it and proving it consistent using finitary methods.}}

{{term |1=[[holism]]}}
{{defn |1=The idea that systems and their properties should be analyzed as wholes, not just as a collection of parts, often discussed in the context of meaning, knowledge, and the philosophy of science.}}

{{term |1=[[homomorphism]]}}
{{defn |1=A structure-preserving map between two algebraic structures of the same type, such as groups, rings, or vector spaces, that respects the operations of the structures.}}

{{term |1=horn}}
{{defn |1=Refers to either of the two alternatives presented by a [[dilemma]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cresswell |first=Julia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J4i3zV4vnBAC |title=Oxford Dictionary of Word Origins |date=2010-09-09 |publisher=OUP Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-954793-7 |pages=128 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Miles |first=Murray |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iA8ZQX4jyHoC |title=Inroads: Paths in Ancient and Modern Western Philosophy |date=2003-01-01 |publisher=University of Toronto Press |isbn=978-0-8020-8531-3 |pages=644 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Hume's principle]]}}
{{defn |1=The principle that the number of objects in one collection is equal to the number of objects in another collection if and only if there is a one-to-one correspondence between the two collections.}}

{{term |1=[[hybrid logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A type of modal logic that incorporates additional syntactic elements to refer directly to worlds in its models, allowing for more expressive power than standard modal logics.}}

{{term |1=[[hypothetical syllogism]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of logical argument consisting of three propositions: two conditional statements and a conclusion that infers a relationship between the antecedent of the first conditional and the consequent of the second.}}

{{glossary end}}

==I==
{{glossary}}

{{term |1=[[Idempotence|idempotent]]}}
{{defn |1=A property of certain operations in which applying the operation multiple times has the same effect as applying it once. For example, the union of a set with itself is the set itself.}}

{{term |1=[[Identity (philosophy)|identity]]}}
{{defn |1=The relation that each entity bears only to itself; or, the principle that an entity is the same as itself.}}

{{term |1=[[identity function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that always returns its input as its output, for any given input.}}

{{term |1=[[identity of indiscernibles]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle stating that if two entities share all their properties, they must be identical.}}

{{term |1=[[iff]]}}
{{defn |1=An abbreviation for "if and only if," denoting a biconditional logical connective indicating mutual implication.}}

{{term |1=[[ignoratio elenchi]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical fallacy where an argument misses the point or addresses an issue different from the one that was raised, also known as missing the point.}}

{{term |1=[[Image of a function|image]]}}
{{defn |1=The set of all outputs of a function from a given set of inputs.}}

{{term |1=[[immediate inference]]}}
{{defn |1=A process of reasoning in which a conclusion is directly derived from a single premise without any intermediary steps.}}

{{term |1=[[Imperative mood|imperative]]}}
{{defn |1=A type of linguistic expression or logical form that expresses a command, request, or instruction.}}

{{term |1=[[imperative logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of logic that studies the formal properties of imperatives or commands, distinct from indicative statements.}}

{{term |1=[[Material conditional|implication]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical relation where the truth of one statement (the antecedent) brings about the truth of another statement (the consequent).}}

{{term |1=implicit definition}}
{{defn |1=A definition that specifies an entity or concept not by direct enumeration of its properties but by its relations to other entities or concepts.<ref name="Springer_Implicit" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=implicit definition |url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803095959415 |access-date=2024-04-28 |website=Oxford Reference |language=en }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[impossible proposition|impossibility]]}}
{{defn |1=The state or condition of something being not possible, either logically or physically.}}

{{term |1=[[impossible world]]}}
{{defn |1=A hypothetical construct in modal logic representing a way things could not possibly be, used to explore concepts of necessity and possibility.}}

{{term |1=[[impredicative definition]]}}
{{defn |1=A definition that refers to a set that includes the entity being defined, often leading to paradoxes in naive set theories.}}

{{term |1=[[inclusive disjunction]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical operation that returns true if at least one of its operands is true; corresponds to the logical OR.}}

{{term |1=[[inclusive logic|inclusive first-order logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A variant of first-order logic that allows for empty domains, in contrast to the standard requirement that domains contain at least one object.}}

{{term |1=[[inclusive or]]}}
{{defn |1=The disjunction operation in logic that is true if either or both of its operands are true.}}

{{term |1=[[Completeness (logic)|incompleteness]]}}
{{defn |1=The property of a logical or mathematical system where not all truths within the system can be proven using the system's rules.}}

{{term |1=[[incompleteness theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=Gödel's theorem stating that any consistent formal system capable of expressing basic arithmetic cannot be both complete and consistent.}}

{{term |1=[[inconsistency]]}}
{{defn |1=The state of containing contradictory elements, which cannot all be true at the same time within a logical framework.}}

{{term |1=[[inconsistent mathematics|inconsistent arithmetic]]}}
{{defn |1=An arithmetic system in which a contradiction can be derived, violating the principle of consistency.}}

{{term |1=[[indefinite description]]}}
{{defn |1=A description that does not uniquely identify a single individual or entity but refers to any member of a class that satisfies a certain condition.}}

{{term |1=indefinite extensibility}}
{{defn |1=The concept that certain collections (such as the set of all sets) cannot be comprehensively listed because any attempt to enumerate them leads to the possibility of generating new members.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hall |first=Geoffrey |date=2021-02-01 |title=Indefinite extensibility and the principle of sufficient reason |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11098-020-01441-y |journal=Philosophical Studies |language=en |volume=178 |issue=2 |pages=471–492 |doi=10.1007/s11098-020-01441-y |issn=1573-0883|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Priest |first=Graham |date=2013 |title=Indefinite Extensibility—Dialetheic Style |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/43649610 |journal=Studia Logica|volume=101 |issue=6 |pages=1263–1275 |doi=10.1007/s11225-013-9532-1 |jstor=43649610 |hdl=11343/282970 |issn=0039-3215|hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Linnebo |first=Øystein |date=Oct 2018 |title=Dummett on Indefinite Extensibility |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/phis.12122 |journal=Philosophical Issues |language=en |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=196–220 |doi=10.1111/phis.12122 |hdl=10852/70857 |issn=1533-6077|hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[independence result]]}}
{{defn |1=A finding in logic and mathematics that a particular statement cannot be proven or disproven within a given system, assuming the system's axioms are consistent.}}

{{term |1=[[independence-friendly logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A logic that extends first-order logic to allow for more nuanced expressions of quantifier scope and dependence, particularly in contexts of game-theoretical semantics.}}

{{term |1=independent}}
{{defn |1=Referring to a pair of propositions that are not {{glossary link internal|contrary}}, {{glossary link internal|subcontrary}}, {{glossary link internal|contradictory}}, {{glossary link internal|logically equivalent}}, or implied one by the other (either the first by the second, or the second by the first).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bacon |first1=John B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YBFa4FHyU8sC |title=Logic from A to Z: The Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy Glossary of Logical and Mathematical Terms |last2=Detlefsen |first2=Michael |last3=McCarty |first3=David Charles |date=2013-09-05 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-97104-6 |pages=54 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="LemmonLogic" />}}

{{term |1=[[indeterminacy of translation]]}}
{{defn |1=Inition proposed by W.V.O. Quine, suggesting that no unique translation between languages can be determined solely by empirical evidence, due to the underdetermination of theories by data.}}

{{term |1=[[Indexicality|indexical]]}}
{{defn |1=A type of expression whose reference can shift based on the context in which it is used, such as "I," "here," and "now."}}

{{term |1=[[indicative conditional]]}}
{{defn |1=A conditional statement used to express factual implications or predictions about real situations, as opposed to counterfactual or hypothetical statements.}}

{{term |1=[[indirect proof]]}}
{{defn |1=A method of proof in which the negation of the statement to be proven is assumed, and a contradiction is derived, thereby proving the original statement by contradiction.}}

{{term |1=[[indiscernibility]]}}
{{defn |1=The inability to distinguish between objects due to them sharing all properties, related to the principle of identity of indiscernibles.}}

{{term |1=[[Indiscernibility|indiscernibility of identicals]]}}
{{defn |1=The principle stating that if two entities are identical, then they share all the same properties.}}

{{term |1=[[indispensability argument]]}}
{{defn |1=An argument suggesting that if a mathematical entity is indispensable to our best scientific theories, then we ought to commit to its existence.}}

{{term |1=[[individual]]}}
{{defn |1=An entity regarded as indivisible or atomistic in nature, often discussed in the context of metaphysics, logic, and the philosophy of language.}}

{{term |1=induction}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|inductive argument}}, {{glossary link internal|induction on well-formed formulas}}, {{glossary link internal|mathematical induction}}, {{glossary link internal|strong mathematical induction}}, {{glossary link internal|transfinite induction}}, {{glossary link internal|weak mathematical induction}}}}

{{term |1=induction on well-formed formulas}}
{{defn |1=A method used in formal logic and mathematics to prove properties of all well-formed formulas by showing they hold for basic formulas and are preserved under the operations that generate new formulas.<ref name="CookDictionary" />}}

{{term |1=induction schema}}
{{defn |1=Synonym of [[mathematical induction]].}}

{{term |1=[[inductive argument]]}}
{{defn |1=An argument that provides probable support for its conclusion, as opposed to deductive arguments which provide conclusive support.}}

{{term |1=[[inductive proof]]}}
{{defn |1=A proof method used in mathematics to prove statements about all natural numbers or other well-ordered sets, based on the principle of induction.}}

{{term |1=[[inductive step]]}}
{{defn |1=In an inductive proof, the step that shows if a property holds for an arbitrary element <math>n</math>, it also holds for the next element <math>n+1</math>.}}

{{term |1=[[inference]]}}
{{defn |1=The process of deriving logical conclusions from premises known or assumed to be true.}}

{{term |1=[[Rule of inference|inference rule]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical rule that outlines the conditions under which certain conclusions can be validly drawn from premises.}}

{{term |1=[[inference to the best explanation]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of abductive reasoning that suggests we should accept the hypothesis that best explains the relevant evidence.}}

{{term |1=[[inferentialism]]}}
{{defn |1=The philosophical view that the meaning of a statement is determined by the rules governing its use and the inferences that can be drawn from it.}}

{{term |1=[[infinitary]]}}
{{defn |1=Pertaining to operations, languages, or logics that allow expressions of infinite length, such as infinitary logic.}}

{{term |1=[[infinitesimal]]}}
{{defn |1=A quantity that is closer to zero than any positive real number, yet not zero, used in non-standard analysis.}}

{{term |1=[[infix notation]]}}
{{defn |1=A notation in which the operator is placed between the operands, as in standard arithmetic expressions.}}

{{term |1=[[informal fallacy]]}}
{{defn |1=A flaw in reasoning that occurs in natural language arguments due to ambiguity, irrelevance, or other factors outside the formal structure of the argument.}}

{{term |1=[[Injective function|injection]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that maps distinct elements of its domain to distinct elements of its codomain, also known as an injective function or one-to-one function.}}

{{term |1=[[Injective function|injective]]}}
{{defn |1=Describing a function in which each element of the codomain is mapped to by at most one element of the domain.}}

{{term |1=[[inner model]]}}
{{defn |1=An inner model of a theory is a model that is obtained by taking a substructure of another model.}}

{{term |1=in rebus vagueness}}
{{defn |1=The view that [[vagueness]] is a feature of the world, rather than of language or of human knowledge.<ref name="VaguenessGuide" /> Contrast {{glossary link internal|epistemic vagueness}} and {{glossary link internal|semantic vagueness}}. See also {{glossary link internal|ontic vagueness}}.}}

{{term |1=[[insolubilia]]}}
{{defn |1=Unsolvable problems or paradoxes, especially those related to self-reference and logical contradiction, such as the liar paradox.}}

{{term |1=instantiation}}
{{defn |1=The process of replacing [[bound variables]] with constants, eliminating the quantifiers that had bound them.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Goodman |first=Michael F. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PGbMZWKbinQC |title=First Logic |date=1993 |publisher=University Press of America |isbn=978-0-8191-8888-5 |pages=222 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Heil |first=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dThCEAAAQBAJ |title=First-Order Logic: A Concise Introduction |date=2021-10-06 |publisher=Hackett Publishing |isbn=978-1-64792-010-4 |pages=288 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Copi |first1=Irving |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6eAqDwAAQBAJ |title=Essentials of Logic |last2=Cohen |first2=Carl |last3=Flage |first3=Daniel |date=2016-12-08 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-1-315-38901-1 |pages=309 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[intended interpretation]]}}
{{defn |1=The standard or conventional meaning assigned to the symbols and expressions of a formal language within a particular context or theory.}}

{{term |1=[[intension]]}}
{{defn |1=The inherent content or essential properties and meanings of a concept or term, as opposed to its extension, which refers to the range of things it applies to.}}

{{term |1=[[intensional definition]]}}
{{defn |1=A definition that specifies the essential properties of the term being defined, focusing on the concept's intension rather than its extension.}}

{{term |1=[[intensional logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A logic that deals with the intensional aspects of meaning, such as belief, necessity, and possibility, distinguishing between logically equivalent expressions that have different modal properties.}}

{{term |1=[[intermediate logic]]}}
{{defn |1=Any logical system that falls between intuitionistic logic and classical logic in strength, allowing for distinctions not permissible in classical logic.}}

{{term |1=[[Craig interpolation|interpolation theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A result stating that if a formula <math>A \rightarrow B</math> is provable, then there exists a formula <math>C</math> containing only the [[non-logical symbol]]s common to <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> such that <math>A \rightarrow C</math> and <math>C \rightarrow B</math> are both provable.}}

{{term |1=[[Interpretation (logic)|interpretation]]}}
{{defn |1=The assignment of meanings to the symbols and expressions of a formal language, or the way a particular set of terms is understood or construed.}}

{{term |1=[[interrogative]]}}
{{defn |1=Pertaining to questions or the act of questioning.}}

{{term |1=interrogative logic}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|erotetic logic}}.}}

{{term |1=[[introduction rule]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic, a rule that allows for the introduction of a connective into a proof, defining how that connective can be logically inferred.}}

{{term |1=[[intuitionism]]}}
{{defn |1=A philosophy of mathematics that denies the reality of the mathematical infinite and the completeness of mathematical truth, requiring constructive proofs.}}

{{term |1=[[intuitionistic logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A system of logic that reflects the principles of intuitionism, rejecting the law of excluded middle and requiring more constructive proofs of existence.}}

{{term |1=[[intuitionistic mathematics]]}}
{{defn |1=Mathematics based on intuitionistic logic, emphasizing constructive methods and rejecting non-constructive principles like the law of excluded middle.}}

{{term |1=[[Validity (logic)|invalid]]}}
{{defn |1=Referring to an argument whose conclusion does not logically follow from its premises.}}

{{term |1=[[Validity (logic)|invalid deductive argument]]}}
{{defn |1=A deductive argument that fails to provide conclusive support for its conclusion, due to a flaw in logical structure.}}

{{term |1=[[Inverse function|inverse]]}}
{{defn |1=A operation or function that reverses the effect of another operation or function.}}

{{term |1=[[Involution (mathematics)|involution]]}}
{{defn |1=An operation that is its own inverse, meaning applying it twice returns to the original state.}}

{{term |1=I-proposition}}
{{defn |1=In traditional logic, a particular affirmative categorical proposition, stating that some members of the subject class are members of the predicate class.<ref name="IEP_Square" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=I-proposition |url=https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/i-proposition |website=Collins Dictionary}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[irreflexivity]]}}
{{defn |1=A property of a relation where no element is related to itself.}}

{{term |1="is" of identity}}
{{defn |1=The use of the verb "is" to denote numerical identity between two entities.<ref name="VallicellaPredication">{{Cite web |last=Vallicella |first=Bill |author-link=William F. Vallicella |date=2011-12-20 |title=The 'Is' of Identity and the 'Is' of Predication |url=https://maverickphilosopher.typepad.com/maverick_philosopher/2011/12/the-is-of-identity-and-the-is-of-predication.html |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=Maverick Philosopher}}</ref><ref name="OntologyPredication">{{Cite web |title=The Frege-Russell 'Is' Ambiguity Thesis |url=https://www.ontology.co/is-ambiguity-thesis.htm |access-date=2024-04-28 |website=www.ontology.co}}</ref><ref name="VilkkoPredication">{{Cite journal |last1=Vilkko |first1=Risto |last2=Hintikka |first2=Jaakko |date=2006 |title=Existence and Predication from Aristotle to Frege |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40040975 |journal=Philosophy and Phenomenological Research |volume=73 |issue=2 |pages=359–377 |doi=10.1111/j.1933-1592.2006.tb00622.x |jstor=40040975 |issn=0031-8205}}</ref>}}

{{term |1="is" of predication}}
{{defn |1=The use of the verb "is" to signify that a property or characteristic is attributed to a subject.<ref name="VallicellaPredication" /><ref name="OntologyPredication" /><ref name="VilkkoPredication" />}}

{{term |1=[[Knights and Knaves|island of knights and knaves]]}}
{{defn |1=A fictional scenario used in logic puzzles where inhabitants are either knights, who always tell the truth, or knaves, who always lie, posing challenges to deductive reasoning.}}

{{term |1=[[isomorphism]]}}
{{defn |1=A bijective (one-to-one and onto) correspondence between two structures that preserves the operations and relations of the structures, indicating they have the same form or structure.}}

{{term |1=[[iteration]]}}
{{defn |1=The process of repeating a set of operations or a procedure multiple times, each time applying it to the result of the previous step.}}

{{term |1=iteration theorem}}
{{defn |1=Synonym for the [[Smn theorem|{{subsup|S|n|m}} theorem]].}}
{{glossary end}}

==J==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=[[joint denial]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical connective in propositional logic, equivalent to the [[Logical NOR|nor operator]], that is true if and only if both propositions it connects are false. It denies the joint assertion of both propositions.}}
{{glossary end}}

==K==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=[[Kleene logic|K3]]}}
{{defn |1=The [[three-valued logic]] K<sub>3</sub>, due to [[Stephen Cole Kleene]].}}

{{term |1=Kleene connectives}}
{{defn |1=Logical connectives defined using [[Kleene logic|Kleene's three-valued logic]], which includes a third truth value (undefined or unknown) in addition to true and false, accommodating indeterminate propositions.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Maienborn |first1=Claudia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h3acDwAAQBAJ |title=Semantics - Interfaces |last2=Heusinger |first2=Klaus |last3=Portner |first3=Paul |date=2019-02-19 |publisher=Walter de Gruyter GmbH & Co KG |isbn=978-3-11-058984-9 |pages=501 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Knights and Knaves|knaves]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic puzzles, individuals who always lie. Used in scenarios like the island of knights and knaves to explore logical deduction.}}

{{term |1=[[Knights and Knaves|knights]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic puzzles, individuals who always tell the truth. They are used alongside knaves in scenarios that challenge deductive reasoning.}}

{{term |1=[[Fitch's paradox of knowability|knowability paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A paradox arising from the assumption that if a statement is true, then it is possible to know that it is true, leading to contradictions in certain epistemic frameworks.}}

{{term |1=[[Knower paradox|knower's paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A paradox related to self-reference and epistemic logic, typically involving a statement that claims its own unprovability or unknowability.}}

{{term |1=[[Kreisel-Putnam logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A logic developed to handle higher-order quantification and modalities, reflecting discussions on the foundations of mathematics by Kreisel and Putnam.}}

{{term |1=[[Kripke semantics]]}}
{{defn |1=A framework for interpreting modal logic through the use of possible worlds, developed by Saul Kripke, allowing for the formal analysis of necessity, possibility, and other modal notions.}}

{{term |1=[[Kripke structure (model checking)|Kripke structure]]}}
{{defn |1=A mathematical structure used in modal logic and computer science to model systems that can be in various states and transition between them, forming the basis for Kripke semantics.}}
{{glossary end}}

==L==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=[[Lambda calculus|lambda-calculus]]}}
{{defn |1=A formal system in mathematical logic and computer science for expressing computation based on function abstraction and application, using variable binding and substitution.}}

{{term |1=[[Lambek calculus]]}}
{{defn |1=A mathematical system for modeling the syntax of natural languages, based on categorial grammar, emphasizing the role of operations and types.}}

{{term |1=[[language]]}}
{{defn |1=A system of communication that enables humans to cooperate, express ideas, emotions, and, in the context of formal languages, to construct and convey precise meanings. See {{glossary link internal|formal language}}, {{glossary link internal|metalanguage}}, {{glossary link internal|natural language}}, {{glossary link internal|object language}}, {{glossary link internal|sublanguage}}, {{glossary link internal|translation}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Law of noncontradiction|law of non-contradiction]]}}
{{defn |1=A fundamental principle of classical logic stating that contradictory statements cannot both be true in the same sense at the same time.}}

{{term |1=left field}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|domain}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Identity of indiscernibles|Leibniz's Law]]}}
{{defn |1=The principle of the [[identity of indiscernibles]], stating that if two entities share all the same properties, then they are identical.}}

{{term |1=[[Lemma (mathematics)|lemma]]}}
{{defn |1=A proposition proved or assumed to be true, used to prove other propositions or theorems.}}

{{term |1=[[liar paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A self-referential paradox involving a statement that declares itself to be false, leading to a contradiction if it is either true or false.}}

{{term |1=liar sentence}}
{{defn |1=A sentence that asserts its own falsity, such as "This sentence is false," which creates the basis for the [[liar paradox]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Liar Paradox {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/liar-paradox/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |language=en-US}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=limitation result}}
{{defn |1=A result that establishes a boundary or limit on what can be achieved within a particular logical or mathematical system, often related to incompleteness or undecidability.<ref name="CookDictionary" />}}

{{term |1=[[linear logic]]s}}
{{defn |1=A subfield of logic that emphasizes the concept of resources, where logical operations consume their arguments, differing from classical logic's treatment of assumptions as reusable.}}

{{term |1=[[linear order]]}}
{{defn |1=A total order on a set where every pair of elements is comparable, meaning for any two elements, one is either greater than, less than, or equal to the other.}}

{{term |1=[[linear ordering]]}}
{{defn |1=Another term for linear order, emphasizing the arrangement of elements in a sequence where each is comparable to the others in a single, unambiguous way.}}

{{term |1=[[Literal (mathematical logic)|literal]]}}
{{defn |1=Either a propositional variable (e.g., <math>P</math>) or its negation (e.g., <math>\lnot P</math>).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Genesereth |first1=Michael |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uGqgEAAAQBAJ |title=Introduction to Logic |last2=Kao |first2=Eric |date=2022-12-06 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-031-01798-8 |pages=40 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Löb paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A paradox in modal logic that arises from attempting to formalize a statement's provability within the system, leading to conclusions that appear counterintuitive or self-contradictory.}}

{{term |1=[[Löb's theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A theorem in mathematical logic that provides conditions under which a statement about its own provability is provable, related to Gödel's incompleteness theorems.}}

{{term |1=[[logic]]}}
{{defn |1=The systematic study of the form of valid inference, including the structures that allow or compel particular conclusions given certain premises.}}

{{term |1=[[logic gate]]}}
{{defn |1=A physical device implementing a Boolean function, used in digital circuits to perform logical operations on one or more binary inputs to produce a single binary output.}}

{{term |1=[[logical machine]]}}
{{defn |1=A mechanical device for performing formal logic such as the [[Stanhope Demonstrator]] or Jevon's [[logic piano]].}}

{{term |1=logic of attributes}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|monadic first-order logic}}.}}

{{term |1=logic of conditionals}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|conditional logic}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Logic of Paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical system that allows for some contradictions to be true, challenging the traditional law of non-contradiction and exploring the consequences of paradoxical statements.}}

{{term |1=logic of questions and answers}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|erotetic logic}}.}}

{{term |1=[[logic of relations]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of logic that deals with the study of relations, including their properties, composition, and inversion, and how they interact with logical operators.}}

{{term |1=logic of weak excluded middle}}
{{defn |1=An [[intermediate logic]] obtained by adding all instances of {{glossary link internal|weak excluded middle}} to [[Propositional calculus|propositional logic]].<ref>{{Citation |chapter=Substructural Logics and Residuated Lattices |date=2007 |title=Residuated Lattices: An Algebraic Glimpse at Substructural Logics |series=Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics |volume=151 |pages=75–139 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1016/S0049-237X(07)80007-3 |access-date=2024-04-27 |publisher=Elsevier |doi=10.1016/s0049-237x(07)80007-3|isbn=978-0-444-52141-5 |chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Bezhanishvili">{{Cite book |last1=Bezhanishvili |first1=Nick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J-I71B_qYlwC |title=Logic, Language, and Computation: 8th International Tbilisi Symposium on Logic, Language, and Computation, TbiLLC 2009, Bakuriani, Georgia, September 21-25, 2009. Revised Selected Papers |last2=Löbner |first2=Sebastian |last3=Schwabe |first3=Kerstin |last4=Spada |first4=Luca |date=2011-07-18 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-642-22302-0 |pages=64 |language=en}}</ref> Also called "KC" and "[[Vadim Yankov|Jankov]]'s logic".<ref name="Bezhanishvili" />}}

{{term |1=logical antirealism}}
{{defn |1=The philosophical position that logical truths do not correspond to an independent reality but are instead products of human conventions, language, or thought processes.<ref name="CookDictionary" />}}

{{term |1=[[logical connective]]}}
{{defn |1=A symbol or word used in logic to connect propositions or sentences, forming more complex expressions that convey relationships such as conjunction, disjunction, and negation.}}

{{term |1=[[logical consequence]]}}
{{defn |1=A relationship between statements where the truth of one or more premises necessitates the truth of a conclusion, based on the logical structure of the statements. See {{glossary link internal|semantic consequence}} and {{glossary link internal|syntactic consequence}}.}}

{{term |1=[[logical constant]]}}
{{defn |1=A symbol in logic that has the same meaning in all interpretations, such as connectives and quantifiers, as opposed to variables whose interpretations can vary.}}

{{term |1=[[logical equivalence]]}}
{{defn |1=The relationship between statements that are true under exactly the same conditions, allowing them to be substituted for one another in logical proofs.}}

{{term |1=logical falsehood}}
{{defn |1=A statement that is false under all possible interpretations, also known as a contradiction.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Martin |first=Robert M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZlG8wUM-kZIC |title=Introducing Symbolic Logic |date=2004-05-14 |publisher=Broadview Press |isbn=978-1-55111-635-8 |pages=12 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[logical form]]}}
{{defn |1=The abstract structure of a statement or argument, representing the logical relationships between its components independent of the specific content.}}

{{term |1=[[logical implication]]}}
{{defn |1=The logical relationship that holds between propositions when the truth of one (the antecedent) guarantees the truth of another (the consequent).}}

{{term |1=logical monism}}
{{defn |1=The philosophical position that there is only one correct logic or logical system that accurately captures the principles of valid reasoning.<ref name="SEP_LogicalPluralism">{{Citation |last1=Russell |first1=Gillian |title=Logical Pluralism |date=2023 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2023/entries/logical-pluralism/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=Fall 2023 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Blake-Turner |first2=Christopher |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[logical operator]]}}
{{defn |1=A symbol or function in logic that applies to one or more propositions, producing another proposition that expresses a logical operation such as negation, conjunction, or disjunction.}}

{{term |1=[[logical paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A statement or group of statements that lead to a contradiction or a situation that defies intuition, often highlighting limitations or problems within the logical system. Sometimes distinguished from {{glossary link internal|semantic paradox}}.}}

{{term |1=[[logical pluralism]]}}
{{defn |1=The view that there are multiple equally correct logics or systems of logic that capture different aspects of reasoning or argumentation.<ref name="SEP_LogicalPluralism" /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Beall |first1=J. C. |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/ocm60793942 |title=Logical pluralism |last2=Restall |first2=Greg |date=2006 |publisher=Clarendon Press; Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-928841-0 |location=Oxford : New York |oclc=ocm60793942}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=logical structure}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|logical form}}.}}

{{term |1=[[logical theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A proposition that has been proven to be true within a specific system of logic, based on the system's axioms and inference rules.}}

{{term |1=[[logical truth]]}}
{{defn |1=A statement that is true in all possible worlds or under all possible interpretations, due to its logical form rather than the content of its terms.}}

{{term |1=[[Validity (logic)|logical validity]]}}
{{defn |1=The property of an argument wherein if the premises are true, the conclusion necessarily follows, due to the structure of the argument rather than the specific nature of the premises or conclusion.}}

{{term |1=[[logically equivalent]]}}
{{defn |1=Referring to statements that have the same truth value in every possible scenario, indicating that they are interchangeable in logical reasoning.}}

{{term |1=[[logicism]]}}
{{defn |1=The philosophical belief that mathematics can be reduced to logic and that all mathematical truths can be derived from logical axioms and definitions.}}

{{term |1=[[Löwenheim–Skolem theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A theorem in mathematical logic that states any countable theory with an infinite model has models of all infinite cardinalities, highlighting the limitations of first-order logic in controlling the sizes of its models.}}

{{term |1=LP}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|Logic of Paradox}}.}}
{{glossary end}}

==M==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=main connective}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|dominant connective}}.}}

{{term |1=main operator}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|dominant connective}}.}}

{{term |1=major connective}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|dominant connective}}.<ref name="MakridisLogic">{{Cite book |last=Makridis |first=Odysseus |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DoBgEAAAQBAJ |title=Symbolic Logic |date=2022-02-21 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-67396-3 |pages=95 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[major premise]]}}
{{defn |1=The premise in a syllogism containing the major term, which is the predicate of the conclusion.}}

{{term |1=[[major term]]}}
{{defn |1=The term that appears as the predicate in the conclusion of a syllogism.}}

{{term |1=[[many-sorted logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A variant of first-order logic that allows for multiple domains of discourse, with variables and quantifiers distinguished by the sort or type of objects they range over.}}

{{term |1=[[many-valued logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical system that extends beyond classical two-valued true/false logic to include additional truth values, accommodating indeterminacy, uncertainty, or levels of truth.}}

{{term |1=[[markov's principle]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle in constructive mathematics stating that if it is impossible for a mathematical object not to have a certain property, then there exists an object with that property.}}

{{term |1=[[Logical biconditional|material biconditional]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical connective that is true if and only if both operands have the same truth value, also known as the "if and only if" operator.}}

{{term |1=[[material conditional]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical connective typically represented by "if...then...", which is true unless the antecedent is true and the consequent is false.}}

{{term |1=material consequence}}
{{defn |1=The relationship between statements where the truth of one (the antecedent) results in the truth of another (the consequent), based on the content of the statements rather than their {{glossary link internal|logical form}}.<ref name="Ashworth_Formal_Material" /><ref name="Gabbay_Formal_Material" /><ref name="Buridan_Formal_Material" /> Contrast {{glossary link internal|formal consequence}}. See also {{glossary link internal|semantic consequence}}. Not to be confused with {{glossary link internal|material implication}}.}}

{{term |1=[[material equivalence]]}}
{{defn |1=The relation between propositions that hold the same truth value; their truth or falsity under all possible conditions is identical.}}

{{term |1=[[Material conditional|material implication]]}}
{{defn |1=Another term for material conditional, emphasizing the implication based on the substantive content of the propositions involved.}}

{{term |1=[[materially equivalent]]}}
{{defn |1=Describing propositions that are true under exactly the same conditions or have the same truth value across all possible worlds.}}

{{term |1=mathematical abstractionism}}
{{defn |1=A philosophical stance that views mathematical entities as abstractions from physical objects or properties, rather than as inherently existing objects.<ref name="SEP_Nonexistent" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Abstractionism {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/abstractionism/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |language=en-US}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[mathematical induction]]}}
{{defn |1=A method of proof used in mathematics to prove statements about natural numbers, based on proving a base case and an inductive step.}}

{{term |1=mathematical induction schema}}
{{defn |1=Synonym of [[mathematical induction]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hanazawa |first=Masazumi |date=1990 |title=ON AXIOM SCHEMATA APPLICABLE TO THE FORMULAE WITH ɛ-SYMBOLS |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/43686680 |journal=Tsukuba Journal of Mathematics |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=91–98 |doi=10.21099/tkbjm/1496161321 |jstor=43686680 |issn=0387-4982}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=reasoning.html |url=http://www-cs-students.stanford.edu/~pdoyle/quail/notes/reasoning.html |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=www-cs-students.stanford.edu}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[mathematical logic]]}}
{{defn |1=The study of logic within the framework of mathematical reasoning, focusing on the mathematical properties of logical systems.}}

{{term |1=matrix}}
{{defn |1=The [[Quantifier (logic)|quantifier]]-free part of a formula in [[prenex normal form]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Chang |first1=Chin-Liang |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oGriBQAAQBAJ |title=Symbolic Logic and Mechanical Theorem Proving |last2=Lee |first2=Richard Char-Tung |date=2014-06-28 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0-08-091728-3 |pages=35 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Das |first=Subrata |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mRPSBQAAQBAJ |title=Computational Business Analytics |date=2013-12-14 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-4398-9073-8 |pages=31 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[maximal consistent set]]}}
{{defn |1=A set of formulas in a logical system that is consistent (no contradictions can be derived from it) and maximal (no additional formulas can be added without causing inconsistency).}}

{{term |1=Meinongianism}}
{{defn |1=A philosophical theory that posits the existence of [[Nonexistent objects|non-existent objects]], named after [[Alexius Meinong]], challenging traditional ontological categories.<ref name="SEP_Nonexistent">{{Citation |last=Reicher |first=Maria |title=Nonexistent Objects |date=2022 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2022/entries/nonexistent-objects/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=Winter 2022 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=mention}}
{{defn |1=In philosophy, especially in discussions of language, "mention" involves referencing a word or phrase itself rather than employing it for its semantic content. This typically occurs when discussing the word as a linguistic entity. In the [[Use–mention distinction|use-mention distinction]], "mention" is signified by the use of quotation marks or other indicators that the words are subjects of discussion rather than tools for communication. For example, in the sentence "The word 'books' consists of five letters," "books" is mentioned, not {{glossary link internal|use|used}}.}}

{{term |1=mere possibilia}}
{{defn |1=Hypothetical or possible entities that do not actually exist but could exist under different circumstances.<ref name="SEP_Actualism" />}}

{{term |1=[[metalanguage]]}}
{{defn |1=A language used to describe, discuss, or analyze another language (the object language), especially in the context of logic and linguistics.}}

{{term |1=[[metalogic]]}}
{{defn |1=The study of the properties of logical systems and languages, including their consistency, completeness, and decidability.}}

{{term |1=[[metamathematics]]}}
{{defn |1=The branch of mathematics that studies mathematical systems and theories from a higher-level perspective, often using methods from mathematical logic.}}

{{term |1=[[metatheorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A theorem about a mathematical theory or logical system, stating properties or results about the system itself.}}

{{term |1=[[metatheory]]}}
{{defn |1=The theoretical analysis of mathematical theories or logical systems, focusing on their properties, structure, and foundations.}}

{{term |1=[[middle term]]}}
{{defn |1=In a syllogism, the term that appears in both premises but not in the conclusion, serving as a link between the major and minor terms.}}

{{term |1=minimalism}}
{{defn |1=A {{glossary link internal|deflationism|deflationist}} view of truth, according to which all instances of [[Alfred Tarski|Tarski]]'s {{glossary link internal|T-schema}} are [[Triviality (mathematics)|trivially]] (or [[Analytic proposition|analytically]]) [[truth|true]].<ref>{{Citation |last1=Armour-Garb |first1=Bradley |title=Deflationism About Truth |date=2023 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/truth-deflationary/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=Summer 2023 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Stoljar |first2=Daniel |last3=Woodbridge |first3=James |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=minimization}}
{{defn |1=In [[General recursive function|recursive function theory]], the operation of searching for the smallest witness to a decidable predicate.<ref name="SEP_recursive" />}}

{{term |1=[[minor premise]]}}
{{defn |1=The premise in a syllogism that includes the minor term, which is the subject of the conclusion.}}

{{term |1=[[minor term]]}}
{{defn |1=The term that appears as the subject in the conclusion of a syllogism.}}

{{term |1=[[modal actualism]]}}
{{defn |1=The philosophical position that only actual, existing objects are possible, denying the existence of merely possible objects.}}

{{term |1=modal agnosticism}}
{{defn |1=A stance of neutrality or skepticism regarding the truth of modal propositions, especially concerning necessity and possibility.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Divers |first=John |date=2004 |title=Agnosticism about Other Worlds: A New Antirealist Programme in Modality |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40040771 |journal=Philosophy and Phenomenological Research |volume=69 |issue=3 |pages=660–685 |doi=10.1111/j.1933-1592.2004.tb00522.x |jstor=40040771 |issn=0031-8205}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Fallon |first1=Francis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=C7AEEAAAQBAJ |title=Agnosticism: Explorations in Philosophy and Religious Thought |last2=Hyman |first2=Gavin |date=2020-11-05 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-885912-3 |pages=33 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[modal fictionalism]]}}
{{defn |1=The view that modal statements (about possibility and necessity) can be treated as useful fictions without committing to the existence of possible worlds.}}

{{term |1=[[modal logic]]}}
