{{defn |1=A branch of logic that deals with modalities such as necessity, possibility, and related concepts, often formalized through the use of modal operators.}}

{{term |1=[[modal operator]]}}
{{defn |1=A [[logical operator]] that modifies the truth value of a statement by expressing modality, such as necessity (<math>\Box</math>) or possibility (<math>\Diamond</math>).}}

{{term |1=modal possibilism}}
{{defn |1=The view that possible but non-actual entities exist in some sense or in possible worlds, in contrast to [[actualism]].<ref name="SEP_Actualism">{{Citation |last=Menzel |first=Christopher |title=The Possibilism-Actualism Debate |date=2024 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2024/entries/possibilism-actualism/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=Summer 2024 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[modal realism]]}}
{{defn |1=The philosophical position that possible worlds are as real as the actual world, and that individuals can exist across different possible worlds.}}

{{term |1=[[modal logic|modality]]}}
{{defn |1=A quality of propositions that expresses mode or manner, particularly in terms of necessity, possibility, and other related concepts.}}

{{term |1=[[Model theory|model]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic and mathematics, a structure that interprets the symbols of a language and satisfies the statements of a theory or system.}}

{{term |1=[[model-theoretic consequence]]}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|semantic consequence}}.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jacquette |first=Dale |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pzf7_sT58PUC |title=A Companion to Philosophical Logic |date=2008-04-15 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-1-4051-4994-5 |pages=236 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Soames |first=Scott |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RtmwLZka0qgC |title=Philosophical Essays, Volume 2: The Philosophical Significance of Language |date=2009-03-09 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1-4008-3318-4 |pages=5 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Logical Consequence, Model-Theoretic Conceptions {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/logcon-m/ |access-date=2024-04-28 |language=en-US}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=model-theoretic validity}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|semantic validity}}.}}

{{term |1=[[model theory]]}}
{{defn |1=The branch of mathematical logic that studies the relationship between formal languages and their interpretations or models.}}

{{term |1=[[modus ponens]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule of inference that allows one to derive a conclusion from a conditional statement and its antecedent, formalized as if <math>P \rightarrow Q</math> and <math>P</math>, then <math>Q</math>.}}

{{term |1=[[modus tollens]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule of inference that allows one to derive a conclusion from a conditional statement and the negation of its consequent, formalized as if <math>P \rightarrow Q</math> and <math>\neg Q</math>, then <math>\neg P</math>.}}

{{term |1=molecule}}
{{defn |1=In logic and philosophy, often used metaphorically to refer to a compound entity or concept that is made up of simpler, atomic parts.<ref name="SCKleene_MathLogic">{{Cite book |last=Kleene |first=Stephen Cole |title=Mathematical logic |date=2002 |publisher=Dover Publications |isbn=978-0-486-42533-7 |edition=Dover |location=Mineola, N.Y}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[monadic first-order logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A variant of first-order logic restricted to predicates that take only one argument, focusing on properties of individual objects rather than relations between them.}}

{{term |1=monadic function}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|unary function}}.}}

{{term |1=monadic predicate}}
{{defn |1=A predicate that takes a single argument, used to express properties of objects or entities within a domain of discourse.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Blackburn |first=Simon |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Mno8CwAAQBAJ |title=The Oxford Dictionary of Philosophy |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-873530-4 |pages=311 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[monadic predicate logic]]}}
{{defn |1=First-order logic with predicates that only take one argument, allowing for the expression of properties of individuals.}}

{{term |1=monadic relation}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|unary relation}}.}}

{{term |1=monism}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|logical monism}}.}}

{{term |1=[[monomorphism]]}}
{{defn |1=A morphism in category theory that is left-cancellable, meaning if two compositions with it are equal, then the other morphisms must be equal, akin to an injective function in set theory.}}

{{term |1=[[monotonic logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A type of logic in which adding new premises to a set does not decrease the set of conclusions that can be derived, ensuring that conclusions are preserved under the addition of new information.}}

{{term |1=[[monotonicity]]}}
{{defn |1=The property of a function or process that preserves order, in logic, referring to systems where conclusions derived from a set of premises are not invalidated by adding more premises.}}

{{term |1=mood}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|syllogistic mood}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Multimodal logic|multi-modal logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A system of modal logic that incorporates more than one kind of modality, such as necessity, possibility, knowledge, and belief.}}

{{term |1=[[Many-valued logic|multivalent logic]]}}
{{defn |1=Another term for many-valued logic, emphasizing the presence of more than two truth values beyond the classical true and false.}}

{{term |1=[[Mutual exclusivity|mutually exclusive]]}}
{{defn |1=Referring to events or propositions that cannot both occur or be true at the same time, indicating a logical or statistical relationship of exclusion.}}
{{glossary end}}

==N==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=[[Sheffer stroke|nand]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical operation meaning "not and"; it produces a true result for all input combinations except the case where all inputs are true. It is a fundamental operation since any logical function can be constructed using only NAND operations.}}

{{term |1=[[n-ary function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that takes n arguments, where n is a natural number, generalizing the concept of binary functions to functions of any arity.}}

{{term |1=[[n-ary relation]]}}
{{defn |1=A relation that involves n elements, where n is a natural number, extending the concept of binary relations to relations between more than two entities.}}

{{term |1=[[natural deduction]]}}
{{defn |1=A system of logical inference that attempts to mirror the intuitive ways humans reason, consisting of a set of inference rules for introducing and eliminating logical connectives.}}

{{term |1=[[natural language]]}}
{{defn |1=A language that has developed naturally in human societies as a means of communication, as opposed to artificial or constructed languages.}}

{{term |1=[[natural number]]s}}
{{defn |1=The set of positive integers, often denoted by <math> \mathbb{N} </math>, and typically including zero. Used as the basis for counting and ordering.}}

{{term |1=[[Necessity and sufficiency|necessary condition]]}}
{{defn |1=A condition that must be satisfied for a statement to be true but is not sufficient on its own to guarantee the statement's truth.}}

{{term |1=necessitation rule}}
{{defn |1=In [[modal logic]], a rule stating that if a proposition is a theorem, then its necessity is also a theorem.<ref name="SEP_ModalLogic" />}}

{{term |1=[[necessary proposition|necessity]]}}
{{defn |1=A modal quality indicating that a proposition is true in all possible worlds or under all possible circumstances.}}

{{term |1=[[necessity of identity]]}}
{{defn |1=The principle stating that if two objects are identical, they are necessarily identical in all possible worlds.}}

{{term |1=[[negation]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical operation that inverts the truth value of a proposition; it turns a true statement into a false one and vice versa.}}

{{term |1=negation completeness}}
{{defn |1=The property of a logical system where every statement or its negation is provable within the system.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Margaris |first=Angelo |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q3mObeaklrIC |title=First Order Mathematical Logic |date=1990-01-01 |publisher=Courier Corporation |isbn=978-0-486-66269-5 |pages=143 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Stoll |first=Robert Roth |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y1mMCgAAQBAJ |title=Set Theory and Logic |date=1979-10-01 |publisher=Courier Corporation |isbn=978-0-486-63829-4 |pages=239 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=negation consistency}}
{{defn |1=The consistency of a logical system in which no statement is both provable and disprovable, including its negation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Robles |first=Gemma |date=2008 |title=The Basic Constructive Logic for Negation-Consistency |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41217804 |journal=Journal of Logic, Language and Information |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=161–181 |doi=10.1007/s10849-007-9056-z |jstor=41217804 |issn=0925-8531}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Robles |first=Gemma |date=2008 |title=EXTENSIONS OF THE BASIC CONSTRUCTIVE LOGIC FOR NEGATION-CONSISTENCY B Kc4 DEFINED WITH A FALSITY CONSTANT |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/44084882 |journal=Logique et Analyse |volume=51 |issue=201 |pages=57–80 |jstor=44084882 |issn=0024-5836}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Robles |first=Gemma |date=April 2008 |title=The Basic Constructive Logic for Negation-Consistency |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10849-007-9056-z |journal=Journal of Logic, Language and Information |language=en |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=161–181 |doi=10.1007/s10849-007-9056-z |issn=0925-8531|url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=negation elimination}}
{{defn |1=A rule in natural deduction that allows the derivation of a conclusion by eliminating a negation, under certain conditions.}}

{{term |1=[[negation introduction]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule in natural deduction that allows for the introduction of negation into a proof, typically by deriving a contradiction from the assumption that the negation is false.}}

{{term |1=[[negation normal form]]}}
{{defn |1=A way of expressing logical formulas where negation is only applied directly to atomic propositions, and the only other allowed connectives are conjunction and disjunction.}}

{{term |1=negative proposition}}
{{defn |1=A proposition that asserts the non-existence or absence of something, or denies some property of an object.<ref>{{Cite web |title="Chapter 5" {{!}} Logic: Deductive and Inductive {{!}} Carveth Read, M.A. {{!}} Lit2Go ETC |url=https://etc.usf.edu/lit2go/37/logic-deductive-and-inductive/460/chapter-5/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=etc.usf.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://faculty.fiu.edu/~harrisk/Notes/Critical%20Thinking/Categorical%20Claims,%20Venn%20Diagrams%20and%20Logical%20Relations.htm |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=faculty.fiu.edu|title=Logic and Categorical Claims}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[neo-Fregeanism]]}}
{{defn |1=A philosophical stance revisiting Frege's logicism with the aim of grounding mathematics, particularly arithmetic and analysis, in logic through the use of Hume's Principle and other axioms.}}

{{term |1=[[neo-logicism]]}}
{{defn |1=A movement in the philosophy of mathematics seeking to revive logicism, the project of founding mathematics on logic, through new insights and approaches, particularly in the wake of criticisms of traditional logicism.}}

{{term |1=[[New Foundations]]}}
{{defn |1=A system of set theory proposed by W.V. Quine with a distinctive axiom schema intended to avoid the paradoxes of naïve set theory while allowing a universal set.}}

{{term |1=[[nominalism]]}}
{{defn |1=The philosophical view that abstract concepts, general terms, or universals have no independent existence but exist only as names or labels for groups of individual objects.}}

{{term |1=non-alethic modal logic}}
{{defn |1=A form of modal logic that deals with modes of truth beyond the alethic modes of necessity and possibility, such as deontic (duty and permission) or epistemic (knowledge and belief) modalities.<ref>{{Citation |last=Ballarin |first=Roberta |title=Modern Origins of Modal Logic |date=2023 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2023/entries/logic-modal-origins/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=Fall 2023 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Kment |first=Boris |title=Varieties of Modality |date=2021 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/spr2021/entries/modality-varieties/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=Spring 2021 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[non-classical logic]]}}
{{defn |1=Any logical system that diverges from the principles of classical logic, including intuitionistic logic, many-valued logics, modal logics, and others that challenge classical assumptions or introduce new principles.}}

{{term |1=[[Noncommutative logic|non-commutative logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical system in which the order of application of operations affects the outcome, contrasting with classical logic where operations like conjunction and disjunction are commutative.}}

{{term |1=[[Nondeterministic polynomial time|non-deterministic polynomial time]]}}
{{defn |1=The complexity class NP, consisting of decision problems for which a 'yes' answer can be verified by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time, given the correct certificate or witness.}}

{{term |1=[[Nondeterministic Turing machine|non-deterministic turing machine]]}}
{{defn |1=A theoretical model of computation that, at each step, can make a 'choice' from multiple possibilities, allowing it to explore many possible branches of execution simultaneously.}}

{{term |1=non-standard logic}}
{{defn |1=Logics that diverge from or extend classical logic, including non-classical logics, many-valued logics, and modal logics, among others.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Peter Suber, "Non-Standard Logics" |url=http://legacy.earlham.edu/~peters/courses/logsys/nonstbib.htm |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=legacy.earlham.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Berleur |first1=Jacques |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eGjTBwAAQBAJ |title=The Information Society: Evolving Landscapes |last2=Clement |first2=Andrew |last3=Sizer |first3=Richard |last4=Whitehouse |first4=Diane |date=2013-11-11 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4757-4328-9 |pages=392 |language=en}}</ref> Also called {{glossary link internal|non-classical logic|non-classical logics}}.}}

{{term |1=[[non-standard model]]}}
{{defn |1=A model of a theory that satisfies the axioms of the theory but has properties not intended by the original formulation, often revealing the theory's consistency or independence results.}}

{{term |1=[[Normal form (abstract rewriting)|normal form]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic, a standardized way of expressing logical formulas, such as conjunctive normal form (CNF) or disjunctive normal form (DNF), to facilitate analysis or computation.}}

{{term |1=[[normal modal logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A class of modal logics that include the necessitation rule and the distribution axiom, allowing for the derivation of necessary truths from given axioms and rules of inference.}}

{{term |1=[[NP-completeness|NP]]}}
{{defn |1=A complexity class (nondeterministic polynomial time) that includes decision problems for which a 'yes' answer can be verified in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine.}}

{{term |1=[[NP-completeness|NP-complete]]}}
{{defn |1=A class of decision problems in NP for which any problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time, and whose solution can be verified in polynomial time; considered among the hardest problems in NP.}}

{{term |1=numerical quantifier}}
{{defn |1=A quantifier that specifies the exact number of instances for which a predicate holds within a domain of discourse, such as 'exactly three', 'at least five'.<ref>{{Cite web |title=JML Reference Manual: Predicates and Specification Expressions |url=https://www.cs.ucf.edu/~leavens/JML/jmlrefman/jmlrefman_12.html |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=www.cs.ucf.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |title=Part One: Numbers and Quantifiers |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/3/oa_monograph/chapter/2963349 |journal=Indiana University Press |date=1973 |language=en |pages=26–105|isbn=978-0-253-04940-7 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Troiani |first1=Vanessa |last2=Peelle |first2=Jonathan E. |last3=Clark |first3=Robin |last4=Grossman |first4=Murray |date=Jan 2009 |title=Is it logical to count on quantifiers? Dissociable neural networks underlying numerical and logical quantifiers |url=https://profiles.wustl.edu/en/publications/is-it-logical-to-count-on-quantifiers-dissociable-neural-networks |journal=Neuropsychologia |language=English |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=104–111 |doi=10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2008.08.015 |issn=0028-3932 |pmid=18789346|pmc=2637397 }}</ref>}}
{{glossary end}}

==O==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=object language}}
{{defn |1=The language that is being studied, analyzed, or used to construct statements in a logical system, as opposed to the [[metalanguage]] used to talk about the object language.<ref name="SEP_TarskiTruth">{{Citation |last=Hodges |first=Wilfrid |title=Tarski's Truth Definitions |date=2022 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/tarski-truth/ |access-date=2024-04-26 |edition=Winter 2022 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Lasersohn |first=Peter |title=object language |url=https://blogs.illinois.edu/view/8885/2063680752 |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=blogs.illinois.edu |language=en-US}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=objectual quantifier}}
{{defn |1=A type of quantifier in formal logic that quantifies over objects in the domain of discourse, as opposed to substituting variables with constants or other expressions.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://academic.oup.com/book/32524/chapter/270277984 |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=academic.oup.com |title=Context and the Attitudes|doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199557950.003.0003}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Linsky |first=Leonard |date=1972 |title=Two Concepts of Quantification |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2214771 |journal=Noûs |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=224–239 |doi=10.2307/2214771 |jstor=2214771 |issn=0029-4624|url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Obverse (logic)|obverse]]}}
{{defn |1=In traditional logic, the process of negating the predicate of a categorical proposition and changing its quality (affirmative to negative, or vice versa) without altering its truth value.}}

{{term |1=[[obversion]]}}
{{defn |1=The operation of forming the obverse of a categorical proposition, resulting in an equivalent statement with a negated predicate and opposite quality.}}

{{term |1=[[one-to-one function|one-to-one]]}}
{{defn |1=A function or mapping from one set to another where each element of the first set is associated with a unique element of the second set; also known as injective.}}

{{term |1=ontic vagueness}}
{{defn |1=Vagueness inherent in the nature of reality itself, as opposed to {{glossary link internal|semantic vagueness|semantic}} or {{glossary link internal|epistemic vagueness}} which relate to language or knowledge, respectively.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-94-007-7978-5 |title=Vague Objects and Vague Identity |series=Logic, Epistemology, and the Unity of Science |date=2014 |volume=33 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-94-007-7978-5|isbn=978-94-007-7977-8 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Barnes |first=Elizabeth |date=2010 |title=Ontic Vagueness: A Guide for the Perplexed |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40959694 |journal=Noûs |volume=44 |issue=4 |pages=601–627 |doi=10.1111/j.1468-0068.2010.00762.x |jstor=40959694 |issn=0029-4624}}</ref> See also {{glossary link internal|in rebus vagueness}}.}}

{{term |1=[[onto]]}}
{{defn |1=A function or mapping from one set to another where every element of the second set is associated with at least one element of the first set; also known as surjective.}}

{{term |1=[[open formula]]}}
{{defn |1=A formula in a formal language that contains free variables, meaning it cannot be determined as true or false until the variables are bound or specified.}}

{{term |1=open pair}}
{{defn |1=A paradox about a pair of statements that deny each other.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Woodbridge |first1=James A. |last2=Armour-Garb |first2=Bradley |date=2005 |editor-last=Sorensen |editor-first=Roy |title=Semantic Pathology and the Open Pair |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40040896 |journal=Philosophy and Phenomenological Research |volume=71 |issue=3 |pages=695–703 |doi=10.1111/j.1933-1592.2005.tb00482.x |jstor=40040896 |issn=0031-8205}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Goldstein |first=Laurence |date=2009 |title=A Consistent Way with Paradox |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27734452 |journal=Philosophical Studies|volume=144 |issue=3 |pages=377–389 |doi=10.1007/s11098-008-9215-3 |jstor=27734452 |issn=0031-8116}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[open term]]}}
{{defn |1=An expression in a formal language that contains [[Free variables and bound variables|free variables]], which does not denote a specific object or truth value until the variables are instantiated.}}

{{term |1=o-proposition}}
{{defn |1=In traditional logic, a particular negative categorical proposition, stating that some members of the subject class are not members of the predicate class.<ref name="IEP_Square" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=O-proposition |url=https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/o-proposition |website=Collins Dictionary}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[logical or|or]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical connective (disjunction) that links propositions in a way that the compound proposition is true if at least one of the linked propositions is true.}}

{{term |1=ordered logic}}
{{defn |1=A logic without {{glossary link internal|weakening}} and {{glossary link internal|permutation}}.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Van Nieuwenborgh |first1=Davy |chapter=An Ordered Logic Program Solver |date=2005 |title=Practical Aspects of Declarative Languages |volume=3350 |pages=128–142 |editor-last=Hermenegildo |editor-first=Manuel V. |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-540-30557-6_11 |access-date=2024-04-27 |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-30557-6_11 |isbn=978-3-540-24362-5 |last2=Heymans |first2=Stijn |last3=Vermeir |first3=Dirk |editor2-last=Cabeza |editor2-first=Daniel|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Buccafurri |first1=Francesco |last2=Leone |first2=Nicola |last3=Scarcello |first3=Francesco |date=1996-01-01 |title=On the expressive power of ordered logic |url=https://content.iospress.com/articles/ai-communications/aic9-1-01 |journal=AI Communications |language=en |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=4–13 |doi=10.3233/AIC-1996-9101 |issn=0921-7126}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[ordered n-tuple]]}}
{{defn |1=A sequence of elements in which the order of the elements matters, generalizing the concept of an ordered pair to sequences of any length.}}

{{term |1=[[ordered pair]]}}
{{defn |1=A fundamental structure in mathematics and logic that consists of two elements arranged in a specific order, typically represented as (a, b).}}

{{term |1=[[ostensive definition]]}}
{{defn |1=A definition that explains the meaning of a term or symbol by pointing to examples and counterexamples of the concept it represents.}}
{{glossary end}}

==P==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=[[pairing function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that uniquely associates pairs of numbers with a single number, allowing pairs to be encoded as single values.}}

{{term |1=[[paraconsistent logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A non-classical logic that allows for contradictions to exist without deriving absurdity, useful in modeling inconsistent but non-trivial systems.}}

{{term |1=[[paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A statement or situation that contradicts itself or defies intuition, often challenging existing understandings of logic and truth.}}

{{term |1=[[paradoxes of material implication]]}}
{{defn |1=Paradoxes that arise from the counterintuitive consequences of the material conditional, especially when the antecedent is false or when there is no causal or necessary connection between the antecedent and consequent.}}

{{term |1=[[parameter]]}}
{{defn |1=A parameter is an expression whose referent is assumed to be fixed relative to a particular situation, but whose value can vary across situations.}}

{{term |1=partial logic}}
{{defn |1=A logical system that allows for statements that are neither true nor false, accommodating undefined terms or indeterminate truth values.<ref>{{Citation |last=Blamey |first=Stephen |chapter=Partial Logic |date=2002 |title=Handbook of Philosophical Logic |pages=261–353 |editor-last=Gabbay |editor-first=Dov M. |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-94-017-0458-8_5 |access-date=2024-04-27 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-94-017-0458-8_5 |isbn=978-90-481-5927-7 |editor2-last=Guenthner |editor2-first=F.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Barba |first=Juan |date=1993 |title=A Modal Reduction for Partial Logic |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/30227069 |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |volume=22 |issue=4 |pages=429–435 |doi=10.1007/BF01052534 |jstor=30227069 |issn=0022-3611}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[particular proposition]]}}
{{defn |1=In traditional logic, a proposition that asserts something about some members of a class, as opposed to all members.}}

{{term |1=[[Peano arithmetic]]}}
{{defn |1=A formal system for arithmetic based on axioms proposed by Giuseppe Peano, foundational for the theory of natural numbers.}}

{{term |1=[[Peirce's law]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle in logic ((<math>P \rightarrow Q) \rightarrow P) \rightarrow P</math> that is valid in classical but not in intuitionistic logic, named after Charles Sanders Peirce.}}

{{term |1=permutation}}
{{defn |1=The [[structural rule]] that allows one to exchange two formulas that are on the same side of the arrow.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jäger |first=Gerhard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dc-KMCWvTq4C |title=Anaphora and Type Logical Grammar |date=2005-08-26 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4020-3904-1 |pages=27 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Lecomte |first=Alain |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tle7CgAAQBAJ |title=Meaning, Logic And Ludics |date=2011-03-22 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-1-908978-24-0 |pages=99 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=permutation invariant}}
{{defn |1=A property of a function or relation that remains unchanged when the elements of its arguments are permuted.<ref>{{Cite thesis |title=Communication complexity of permutation-invariant functions |url=https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/99861 |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |date=2015 |degree=Thesis |first=Pritish |last=Kamath|hdl=1721.1/99861 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fukshansky |first1=Lenny |last2=Garcia |first2=Stephan |last3=Sun |first3=Xun |date=2015-01-01 |title=Permutation invariant lattices |url=https://scholarship.claremont.edu/pomona_fac_pub/437 |journal=Pomona Faculty Publications and Research|arxiv=1409.1491 }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[persuasive definition]]}}
{{defn |1=A definition intended to influence attitudes or stir emotions by embedding an evaluative component, often used in ethical or political arguments.}}

{{term |1=[[petitio principii]]}}
{{defn |1=Also known as begging the question, an [[informal fallacy]] where the conclusion of an argument is assumed in one of the premises.}}

{{term |1=Philonian conditional}}
{{defn |1=Another term for the material conditional, emphasizing its use in propositional logic to represent "if...then..." statements without implying a causal relation.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Bobzien |first1=Susanne |title=Dialectical School |date=2023 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2023/entries/dialectical-school/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=Fall 2023 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Duncombe |first2=Matthew |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[philosophical logic]]}}
{{defn |1=The study of the more abstract or theoretical aspects of logic, often concerning questions about reference, modality, quantification, and the structure of propositions and arguments.}}

{{term |1=[[philosophy of logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of philosophy that examines the nature and scope of logic, including the assumptions, methodologies, and implications of various logical systems.}}

{{term |1=[[Platonism (mathematics)|platonism]]}}
{{defn |1=In the philosophy of mathematics, the view that abstract mathematical objects exist independently of human thought.}}

{{term |1=[[Plato's beard]]}}
{{defn |1=A metaphorical expression attributed to Willard Van Orman Quine, referring to the problem of non-existent entities and their properties.}}

{{term |1=[[plural quantification]]}}
{{defn |1=Quantification over multiple objects or entities considered together, extending beyond singular quantification to express statements about sets or groups.}}

{{term |1=pluralism}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|logical pluralism}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Polish notation]]}}
{{defn |1=A prefix notation for logic and arithmetic where operators precede their operands, eliminating the need for parentheses to indicate order of operation.}}

{{term |1=polyadic first-order logic}}
{{defn |1=First-order logic extended to include predicates with more than one argument, allowing for the expression of relations between multiple objects.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Makridis |first=Odysseus |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DoBgEAAAQBAJ |title=Symbolic Logic |date=2022-02-21 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-67396-3 |pages=302 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Lucas |first=J. R. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Q42EAgAAQBAJ |title=Conceptual Roots of Mathematics |date=2002-09-11 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-62227-6 |pages=80 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=possibility}}
{{defn |1=A [[modal logic|modality]] indicating that a proposition may be true, even if it is not actually true; the capacity for some state of affairs to occur.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ben-Menahem |first=Yemima |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rRB1EAAAQBAJ |title=Rethinking the Concept of Law of Nature: Natural Order in the Light of Contemporary Science |date=2022-06-13 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-96775-8 |pages=157 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Allan |first=Keith |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3_1snsgmqU8C |title=Concise Encyclopedia of Semantics |date=2010-04-06 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-08-095969-6 |pages=931 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[possible world]]}}
{{defn |1=A hypothetical total way things might have been or could be, used in modal logic to analyze possibility, necessity, and other modal concepts.}}

{{term |1=Post consistency}}
{{defn |1=A theory is "Post consistent" (or absolutely consistent) if and only if there is at least one statement in the language of the theory that is not a theorem; otherwise, it is "Post inconsistent".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Epstein |first=Richard L. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8AmnDwAAQBAJ |title=Propositional Logics 3rd edition |date=2018-11-05 |publisher=Advanced Reasoning Forum |isbn=978-0-9834521-7-1 |pages=66 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Hackstaff |first=L. H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0ivpCAAAQBAJ |title=Systems of Formal Logic |date=2012-12-06 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-010-3547-7 |pages=199 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Post hoc ergo propter hoc|post hoc, ergo propter hoc]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical fallacy that assumes that if one event occurs after another, then the first event must be the cause of the second.}}

{{term |1=[[postulate]]}}
{{defn |1=A proposition accepted as true to provide a logical basis.}}

{{term |1=[[pragmatics]]}}
{{defn |1=The study of how context influences the interpretation of meaning in language, beyond the literal meaning of words or the structure of sentences.}}

{{term |1=[[Predicate (mathematical logic)|predicate]]}}
{{defn |1=A function or relation that asserts a property about or a relationship between individuals or objects in a domain of discourse.}}

{{term |1=predicate functor}}
{{defn |1=In logic, a symbol that represents a function from individuals or tuples of individuals to truth values, essentially a generalization of a predicate.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bacon |first=Andrew |date=2019 |title=Is reality fundamentally qualitative? |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/45094266 |journal=Philosophical Studies|volume=176 |issue=1 |pages=259–295 |doi=10.1007/s11098-017-1015-1 |jstor=45094266 |issn=0031-8116}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[predicate functor logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical system that combines elements of predicate logic with the concept of functors, allowing for a more expressive representation of properties and relations.}}

{{term |1=predicate term}}
{{defn |1=The second term of a proposition in a [[syllogism]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Syllogistic Terminology |url=https://philosophy.lander.edu/logic/syll_terms.html |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=philosophy.lander.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Categorical Syllogism |url=http://www.philosophypages.com/lg/e08a.htm |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=www.philosophypages.com}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[prefix notation]]}}
{{defn |1=A way of writing mathematical and logical expressions where the operator precedes its operands, facilitating unambiguous interpretation without parentheses.}}

{{term |1=prelinearity axiom}}
{{defn |1=The formula (P → Q) ∨ (Q → P).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Flaminio |first1=Tommaso |last2=Rivieccio |first2=Umberto |date=September 2022 |title=Prelinearity in (quasi-)Nelson logic |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fss.2022.03.021 |journal=Fuzzy Sets and Systems |volume=445 |pages=66–89 |doi=10.1016/j.fss.2022.03.021 |issn=0165-0114|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite conference
 | last1 = Codara | first1 = Pietro
 | last2 = D'Antona | first2 = Ottavio M.
 | last3 = Marra | first3 = Vincenzo
 | contribution = Propositional Gödel Logic and Delannoy Paths
 | doi = 10.1109/FUZZY.2007.4295542
 | pages = 1–5
 | publisher = IEEE
 | title = FUZZ-IEEE 2007, IEEE International Conference on Fuzzy Systems, Imperial College, London, UK, 23–26 July, 2007, Proceedings
 | year = 2007| isbn = 978-1-4244-1209-9
 }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[premise]]}}
{{defn |1=A statement in an argument that provides support or evidence for the conclusion.}}

{{term |1=[[prenex normal form]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of logical expression where all quantifiers are moved to the front, standardizing the structure of first-order logical statements.}}

{{term |1=[[primitive recursion]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of recursion where a function is defined in terms of itself, using simpler cases, with a base case to stop the recursion.}}

{{term |1=primitive recursive function}}
{{defn |1=A function computable by a primitive recursive algorithm, representing a class of functions that can be defined by initial functions and operations of composition and primitive recursion.<ref name="SEP_recursive">{{Citation |last1=Dean |first1=Walter |title=Recursive Functions |date=2024 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2024/entries/recursive-functions/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=Summer 2024 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Naibo |first2=Alberto |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=primitive recursive relation}}
{{defn |1=A relation that can be defined by primitive recursive functions, characterizing a subset of computable relations.<ref name="SEP_recursive" />}}

{{term |1=principal connective}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|dominant connective}}.<ref name="MakridisLogic" />}}

{{term |1=[[probability calculus]]}}
{{defn |1=The branch of mathematics dealing with probability, including the laws and formulas that govern random variables and events.}}

{{term |1=[[Probabilistic logic|probability logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical system that incorporates probabilistic elements to deal with uncertainty, extending classical logic to handle degrees of belief or likelihood.}}

{{term |1=[[probability theory]]}}
{{defn |1=The mathematical study of randomness and uncertainty, focusing on the analysis of random variables, events, and processes.}}

{{term |1=[[Formal proof|proof]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical or mathematical argument that demonstrates the truth of a statement or theorem, based on axioms, definitions, and previously established theorems.}}

{{term |1=[[proof by cases]]}}
{{defn |1=A proof technique that divides the proof into several cases, showing that the statement to be proved holds in each case.}}

{{term |1=[[proof by induction]]}}
{{defn |1=A method of mathematical proof used to establish the truth of an infinite number of cases, based on a base case and an inductive step.}}

{{term |1=[[proof theory]]}}
{{defn |1=The branch of mathematical logic that studies the structure and properties of mathematical proofs, aiming to understand and formalize the process of mathematical reasoning.}}

{{term |1=proof-theoretic consequence}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|syntactic consequence}}.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Sannella |first1=Donald |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=85CLRvu5QxUC |title=Foundations of Algebraic Specification and Formal Software Development |last2=Tarlecki |first2=Andrzej |date=2012-01-05 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-642-17336-3 |pages=53 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Zalta |first=E. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dHTvCAAAQBAJ |title=Abstract Objects: An Introduction to Axiomatic Metaphysics |date=2012-12-06 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-009-6980-3 |pages=30 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[proof-theoretic semantics]]}}
{{defn |1=An alternative to truth-condition semantics (also known as [[Model theory|model-theoretic]] semantics), focusing on proof rather than on truth.<ref name="SEP_ProofTheoreticSemantics" />}}

{{term |1=proof-theoretic validity}}
{{defn |1=Referring to a valid proof in {{glossary link internal|proof-theoretic semantics}}.<ref name="SEP_ProofTheoreticSemantics" />}}

{{term |1=property}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|concept}}.}}

{{term |1=[[proposition]]}}
{{defn |1=A declarative statement that is capable of being true or false, serving as the basic unit of meaning in logic and philosophy.}}

{{term |1=[[propositional attitude]]}}
{{defn |1=A mental state expressed by verbs such as believe, desire, hope, and know, followed by a proposition, reflecting an individual's attitude towards the truth of the proposition.}}

{{term |1=propositional connective}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|logical connective}}.}}

{{term |1=[[propositional function]]}}
{{defn |1=An expression that becomes a proposition when values are assigned to its variables, essentially a predicate that can take one or more arguments.}}

{{term |1=[[propositional variable|propositional letter]]}}
{{defn |1=A variable in propositional logic that represents a specific, undefined proposition, used as a placeholder in logical formulas.}}

{{term |1=[[propositional logic]]}}
{{defn |1=The branch of logic that deals with propositions as units and uses propositional connectives to construct complex statements, focusing on the truth-values of propositions.}}

{{term |1=[[Pro-sentence|prosentential]]}}
{{defn |1=Pertaining to the theory that some expressions function as whole propositions rather than referring to objects or describing properties.}}

{{term |1=prosentential theory of truth}}
{{defn |1=A theory that regards truth as a prosentential operator, simplifying the analysis of truth statements without invoking propositions as entities.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Truth, Prosentential Theory of {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://iep.utm.edu/truthpro/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |language=en-US}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[provability logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A branch of modal logic concerned with the properties of provability and modalities that express notions of necessity as provability within a formal system.}}

{{term |1=provability predicate}}
{{defn |1=A predicate, often called "[[Bew (mathematical logic)|Bew]]", that expresses the concept of a statement being provable within a given formal system.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Visser |first1=Albert |last2=Zoethout |first2=Jetze |date=June 2019 |title=Provability logic and the completeness principle |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apal.2019.02.001 |journal=Annals of Pure and Applied Logic |volume=170 |issue=6 |pages=718–753 |doi=10.1016/j.apal.2019.02.001 |issn=0168-0072|arxiv=1804.09451 }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=pseudo modus ponens}}
{{defn |1=Synonym for {{glossary link internal|assertion}}, the axiom that (A ∧ (A → B)) → B.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Weber |first=Zach |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qchCEAAAQBAJ |title=Paradoxes and Inconsistent Mathematics |date=2021-10-21 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-83441-4 |pages=114 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Başkent |first1=Can |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PZPHDwAAQBAJ |title=Graham Priest on Dialetheism and Paraconsistency |last2=Ferguson |first2=Thomas Macaulay |date=2020-01-01 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-25365-3 |pages=355 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=punctuation}}
{{defn |1=In logic, refers to [[Bracket|parentheses and brackets]].<ref name="beallbasics2ed">{{Cite book |last=Beall |first=Jeffrey C. |title=Logic: the basics |date=2017 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-138-85227-3 |edition=2nd |location=London New York |pages=61}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=pure first-order logic}}
{{defn |1=The system of first-order logic that contains no function symbols or identity, only predicate symbols.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Smullyan |first=Raymond M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UHzmCwAAQBAJ |title=Recursion Theory for Metamathematics |date=1993 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-508232-6 |pages=47 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=pure predicate logic}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|pure first-order logic}}.}}

{{term |1=Putnam's model-theoretic argument}}
{{defn |1=An argument by Hilary Putnam challenging the conventional understanding of reference and truth, suggesting that semantic externalism leads to radical skepticism about the meanings of terms and the contents of thoughts.<ref>{{Citation |last=Khlentzos |first=Drew |title=Challenges to Metaphysical Realism |date=2021 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/spr2021/entries/realism-sem-challenge/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=Spring 2021 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University}}</ref>}}
{{glossary end}}

==Q==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=quality}}
{{defn |1=Refers to whether a [[categorical proposition]] is affirmative or negative.<ref name="comfsm" /><ref name="elemen38" /><ref name="lander-quantqual" />}}

{{term |1=quantified modal logic}}
{{defn |1=An extension of modal logic that includes quantifiers such as "all" and "some", allowing for expressions involving necessity or possibility applied to individuals or properties quantitatively.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Actualism > The Simplest Quantified Modal Logic (SQML) (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy/Summer 2020 Edition) |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archIves/sum2020/entries/actualism/SQML.html |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=plato.stanford.edu}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Quantifier (logic)|quantifier]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical operator that specifies the quantity of specimens in the domain of discourse that satisfy an open formula, such as "all", "some", or "exists".}}

{{term |1=[[quantifier shift fallacy]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical fallacy involving the incorrect interchange of the position of two quantifiers, or a quantifier and a modal operator, leading to invalid conclusions.}}

{{term |1=quantity}}
{{defn |1=Refers to a [[categorical proposition]]'s being universal or particular.<ref name="comfsm" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Elements of Logic 37 |url=https://www3.nd.edu/~maritain/jmc/etext/logic-37.htm |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=www3.nd.edu}}</ref><ref name="lander-quantqual" />}}

{{term |1=[[quantum logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A non-classical logic that attempts to capture the peculiarities of quantum mechanics, challenging traditional logical principles such as the law of excluded middle and distributivity.}}

{{term |1=Quine's dictum}}
{{defn |1=The principle that "To be is to be the value of a variable", emphasizing ontological commitment in terms of quantification and the variables of quantified theory.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hugly |first1=Philip |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZW_vCAAAQBAJ |title=Intensionality and Truth: An Essay on the Philosophy of A.N. Prior |last2=Sayward |first2=C. |date=2012-12-06 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-009-0293-0 |pages=177 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Kriegel |first=Uriah |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YT5MDwAAQBAJ |title=Brentano's Philosophical System: Mind, Being, Value |date=2018-02-09 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-250909-3 |pages=146 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Murphey |first=Murray |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6AiL1JQJAzQC |title=The Development of Quine's Philosophy |date=2011-12-23 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-007-2423-5 |pages=196 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Q.E.D.|quod erat demonstrandum (QED)]]}}
{{defn |1=A Latin phrase meaning "which was to be demonstrated", traditionally used at the end of a mathematical proof or logical argument to signify its completion.}}

{{term |1=[[quotation]]}}
{{defn |1=The practice of repeating words or text from another source, often indicated in writing by quotation marks. In logic, it involves [[Use–mention distinction|referring to the expression itself rather than its meaning]].}}

{{glossary end}}

==R==
{{glossary}}

{{term |1=[[ramified theory of types]]}}
{{defn |1=An extension of the simple theory of types that includes a hierarchy of levels, allowing for the distinction between objects and functions at different orders to avoid paradoxes such as Russell's paradox.}}

{{term |1=[[ramsey sentence]]}}
{{defn |1=A way of expressing the empirical content of a theory by replacing its theoretical terms with existential quantifiers, named after Frank P. Ramsey.}}

{{term |1=[[Ramsey test]]}}
{{defn |1=A criterion for evaluating the acceptability of conditional statements in terms of belief revision: if adding the antecedent to one's stock of beliefs requires adding the consequent for consistency, then the conditional is accepted.}}

{{term |1=[[Range of a function|range]]}}
{{defn |1=The set of all possible outputs or values that a function can produce, given all possible inputs.}}

{{term |1=[[recursion]]}}
{{defn |1=The process of defining something in terms of itself, often used in mathematics and computer science to define functions, sequences, and structures.}}

{{term |1=recursion theorem}}
{{defn |no=1|1=[[Master theorem (analysis of algorithms)]]}}
{{defn |no=2|1=[[Kleene's recursion theorem]]}}

{{term |1=recursive definition}}
{{defn |1=A definition of a function, set, or other mathematical object that is defined in terms of itself, using a base case and a rule for generating subsequent elements.}}

{{term |1=[[Recursive function (computability)|recursive function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that can be computed by a procedure that calls itself, directly or indirectly, with a base case to prevent infinite recursion.}}

{{term |1=[[recursive function theory]]}}
{{defn |1=The study of recursive functions and their properties, including their computability and classification into hierarchies of complexity.}}

{{term |1=[[recursive relation]]}}
{{defn |1=A relation defined on a set where the relation is specified in terms of itself, allowing for the construction of complex relational structures from simpler ones.}}

{{term |1=recursively axiomatizable theory}}
{{defn |1=A theory for which there exists a recursive set of axioms that can generate all theorems of the theory through logical deduction.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Lassaigne |first1=Richard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t8_iBwAAQBAJ |title=Logic and Complexity |last2=Rougemont |first2=Michel de |date=2012-12-06 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-0-85729-392-3 |pages=116 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Ellis |first=Gerard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5pt0c_xphIEC |title=Conceptual Structures: Applications, Implementation and Theory: Third International Conference on Conceptual Structures, ICCS '95, Santa Cruz, CA, USA, August 14 - 18, 1995. Proceedings |date=1995-07-21 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-540-60161-6 |pages=21 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Wang |first=Hao |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FhWtBAAAQBAJ |title=Popular Lectures on Mathematical Logic |date=2014-09-22 |publisher=Courier Corporation |isbn=978-0-486-17104-3 |pages=74 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[red herring]]}}
{{defn |1=An [[informal fallacy]] or rhetorical strategy that diverts attention from the original issue or argument by introducing an irrelevant topic.}}

{{term |1=[[reductio ad absurdum]]}}
{{defn |1=A method of argument that demonstrates the falsity of a statement by showing that it logically leads to a contradiction or absurd conclusion.}}

{{term |1=[[redundancy theory of truth]]}}
{{defn |1=A theory of truth that suggests stating that a proposition is true is redundant and does not add anything to the proposition's content.}}

{{term |1=reference}}
{{defn |1=The relation between words, phrases, or symbols and the objects, concepts, or events they denote or stand for.<ref name="RoutledgeSenseReference">{{Citation |last=Marti |first=Genoveva |title=Sense and reference |date=2016 |encyclopedia=Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://www.rep.routledge.com/articles/thematic/sense-and-reference/v-1 |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=1 |place=London |publisher=Routledge |doi=10.4324/9780415249126-x038-1 |isbn=978-0-415-25069-6|url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[referential opacity]]}}
{{defn |1=A property of expressions wherein substituting a co-referential term does not necessarily preserve truth, typically occurring in intensional contexts like belief reports.}}

{{term |1=[[Reflexive relation|reflexivity]]}}
{{defn |1=The property of a relation where every element is related to itself, such as the equality relation.}}

{{term |1=[[refutation]]}}
{{defn |1=The process of disproving or showing the falseness of a statement, argument, or theory.}}

{{term |1=register computable}}
{{defn |1=Computable by a [[register machine]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hinman |first=Peter G. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6UBZDwAAQBAJ |title=Fundamentals of Mathematical Logic |date=2018-10-08 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-4398-6427-2 |pages=441 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Craig |first=Edward |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1wL-MriFm2YC |title=Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy |date=1998 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-0-415-18710-7 |pages=808 |language=en}}</ref>
}}

{{term |1=[[register machine]]}}
{{defn |1=A theoretical model of computation that uses a set of registers to store numbers and a program of instructions to perform calculations, serving as an alternative to the Turing machine model.}}

{{term |1=[[relational semantics]]}}
{{defn |1=An approach to interpreting logical languages where the meaning of sentences is defined in terms of relations between possible worlds or states of affairs, commonly used in modal and temporal logics.}}

{{term |1=relative consistency proof}}
{{defn |1=A proof showing that if a mathematical system <math>S</math> is consistent, then an extension of <math>S</math> by adding new axioms is also consistent, used to compare the foundational strength of different theories.<ref name="CookDictionary" />}}

{{term |1=[[relevance logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A non-classical logic that seeks to capture the notion that the premises of a valid argument must be relevant to the conclusion, avoiding paradoxes of material implication.}}

{{term |1=representation}}
{{defn |1=A '''n+1'''-ary predicate '''P''' ''represents'' an '''n'''-ary function '''f''' if, and only if, it is the case that: <math>Px_1, x_2, \ldots x_n, y</math> is true if, and only if, <math>f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) = y</math>. Similarly, a unary predicate '''P''' ''represents'' a set '''S''' if, and only if, it is the case that: '''Px''' is true if, and only if, '''x''' is a member of '''S'''.<ref name="CookDictionary" />}}

{{term |1=[[reverse mathematics]]}}
{{defn |1=A program in mathematical logic that seeks to determine which axioms are necessary to prove theorems of mathematics by proving theorems from the weakest possible systems.}}

{{term |1=revision theory of truth}}
{{defn |1=A theory proposing a non-classical approach to the concept of truth, suggesting that truth values of propositions can be revised in light of paradoxes, notably the liar paradox.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Kremer |first1=Philip |title=The Revision Theory of Truth |date=2023 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/truth-revision/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=Summer 2023 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Rivello |first2=Edoardo |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[rigid designator]]}}
{{defn |1=A term that refers to the same object in all possible worlds where that object exists, used in discussions of necessity and identity across possible worlds.}}

{{term |1=[[Robinson arithmetic]]}}
{{defn |1=A fragment of Peano arithmetic that omits the axiom schema of induction, serving as a foundation for arithmetic that is weaker but still expressive.}}

{{term |1=[[Ross' paradox|Ross paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A paradox in deontic logic arising from imperatives that imply counterintuitive obligations, demonstrating challenges in formalizing moral and ethical reasoning.}}

{{term |1=[[rule of inference]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical rule that justifies the transition from a set of premises to a conclusion, forming the basis of deductive reasoning.}}

{{term |1=[[rule of replacement]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule in formal logic allowing for the substitution of equivalent expressions within logical proofs, maintaining the validity of the argument.}}
{{glossary end}}

==S==
{{glossary}}

{{term |1=salve veritate}}
{{defn |1=A Latin phrase meaning "with truth unchanged", used in logic and philosophy to indicate a transformation or substitution that preserves the [[truth value]] of statements.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Chapman |first=Siobhan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GtTGBQAAQBAJ |title=Philosophy for Linguists: An Introduction |date=2002-11-01 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-62457-7 |pages=30 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Satisfiability|satisfaction]]}}
{{defn |1=In model theory, the relation between a structure and a sentence where the structure makes the sentence true, according to the interpretation of the sentence's symbols in that structure.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Corcoran |first1=John |title=Schema |date=2022 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2022/entries/schema/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |edition=Fall 2022 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Hamid |first2=Idris Samawi |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[satisfiability]]}}
{{defn |1=The property of a logical formula if there exists at least one interpretation under which the formula is true.}}

{{term |1=schema}}
{{defn |1=A template or pattern representing a class of similar statements or propositions, often used in the formulation of logical axioms and rules.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Thalheim |first=Bernhard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SBjycgTuEmMC |title=Conceptual Modeling - ER '96: 15th International Conference on Conceptual Modeling, Cottbus, Germany, October 7 - 10, 1996. Proceedings. |date=1996-09-25 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-540-61784-6 |pages=62 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Pacholski |first1=Leszek |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1r0drWA4bREC |title=Computer Science Logic: 8th Workshop, CSL '94, Kazimierz, Poland, September 25 - 30, 1994. Selected Papers |last2=Tiuryn |first2=Jerzy |date=1995-07-18 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-540-60017-6 |pages=106 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Textor |first=Mark |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YwXHBQAAQBAJ |title=Routledge Philosophy GuideBook to Frege on Sense and Reference |date=2010-09-13 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-136-93054-6 |pages=45 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Scope (logic)|scope]]}}
{{defn |1=The part of a logical formula to which an operator, quantifier, or modifier applies, determining the extent of its operation.}}

{{term |1=Scott}}
{{defn |1=[[Dana Scott]]}}

{{term |1=sea battle}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|Aristotle's sea battle}}.}}

{{term |1=[[second-order logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A logic that extends first-order logic by allowing quantification over predicates and relations, in addition to quantification over individuals.}}

{{term |1=[[Contradiction|self-contradictory]]}}
{{defn |1=A property of a statement or proposition that contradicts itself, making it impossible to be true.}}

{{term |1=[[self-reference]]}}
{{defn |1=The act of referring to oneself or itself, used in discussions of paradoxes, reflexivity, and the foundations of mathematics and logic.}}

{{term |1=[[Semantic theory of truth|semantic conception of truth]]}}
{{defn |1=A theory of truth based on the correspondence between statements and facts or states of affairs in the world, emphasizing the role of meaning and interpretation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tarski |first=Alfred |date=1944 |title=The Semantic Conception of Truth: and the Foundations of Semantics |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2102968 |journal=Philosophy and Phenomenological Research |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=341–376 |doi=10.2307/2102968 |jstor=2102968 |issn=0031-8205|url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=semantic consequence}}
{{defn |1=The relation that holds between a set of premises and a conclusion formulated within a certain [[formal language]], such that, for this language, there is no possible [[Interpretation (logic)|interpretation]] that evaluates the premises as true and the conclusion as false.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Boundas |first=Constantin V. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9jAkDQAAQBAJ |title=Edinburgh Companion to Twentieth-Century Philosophies |date=2007-06-19 |publisher=Edinburgh University Press |isbn=978-0-7486-2929-9 |pages=241 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Epstein |first=R. L. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=02_rCAAAQBAJ |title=The Semantic Foundations of Logic Volume 1: Propositional Logics |date=2013-11-11 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-009-0525-2 |pages=31 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Giaquinto |first=Marcus |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gyNbrpYXzxoC |title=The Search for Certainty : A Philosophical Account of Foundations of Mathematics: A Philosophical Account of Foundations of Mathematics |date=2002-06-06 |publisher=Clarendon Press |isbn=978-0-19-158817-4 |pages=256 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[semantic paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A [[paradox]] that arises due to some peculiarity of semantic concepts, such as truth, falsity, and definability, as distinguished from logical or set-theoretical concepts. The distinction between semantical and logical paradoxes is controversial and was invented by [[Frank Ramsey (mathematician)|Ramsey]].<ref name="BunninYu">{{Cite book |last1=Bunnin |first1=Nicholas |title=The Blackwell dictionary of Western philosophy |last2=Yu |first2=Jiyuan |date=2004 |publisher=Blackwell Pub |isbn=978-1-4051-0679-5 |location=Malden, MA |pages=503}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=MacBride |first1=Fraser |title=Frank Ramsey |date=2023 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2023/entries/ramsey/ |access-date=2024-04-29 |edition=Winter 2023 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Marion |first2=Mathieu |last3=Frápolli |first3=María José |last4=Edgington |first4=Dorothy |last5=Elliott |first5=Edward |last6=Lutz |first6=Sebastian |last7=Paris |first7=Jeffrey |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[semantic tableau]]}}
{{defn |1=A method of proof in logic that uses a tree structure to systematically explore the truth or falsity of logical expressions by breaking them down into simpler components.}}

{{term |1=semantic vagueness}}
{{defn |1=The view that [[vagueness]] is a feature of language, rather than of the world or of human knowledge.<ref name="VaguenessGuide" /> Contrast {{glossary link internal|in rebus vagueness}} and {{glossary link internal|epistemic vagueness}}.}}

{{term |1=semantic value}}
{{defn |1=The meaning or content assigned to a linguistic expression in semantics, including truth values for sentences in logical languages.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bar-Elli |first=Gilead |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ImMiAAAAQBAJ |title=The Sense of Reference: Intentionality in Frege |date=2013-02-06 |publisher=Walter de Gruyter |isbn=978-3-11-081303-6 |pages=3 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Barros |first1=J. Acacio de |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mM2wDwAAQBAJ |title=Quanta and Mind: Essays on the Connection between Quantum Mechanics and Consciousness |last2=Montemayor |first2=Carlos |date=2019-09-19 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-21908-6 |pages=206 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=semantic validity}}
{{defn |1=A formula is called semantically valid, or a {{glossary link internal|tautology}}, if it is true under every [[Interpretation (logic)|interpretation]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Knowledge Representation and Reasoning: Basics of Logics |url=https://www.emse.fr/~zimmermann/Teaching/KRR/generalities.html |access-date=2024-03-28 |website=www.emse.fr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=6. Semantics of Propositional Logic — Logic and Proof 3.18.4 documentation |url=https://leanprover.github.io/logic_and_proof/semantics_of_propositional_logic.html |access-date=2024-03-28 |website=leanprover.github.io}}</ref><ref name="chowdharyAI">{{cite book |last=Chowdhary |first=K.R. |date=2020 |title=Fundamentals of Artificial Intelligence |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-81-322-3972-7  |language=en |pages=31–34 |doi=10.1007/978-81-322-3972-7 |isbn=978-81-322-3970-3|url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=semantically closed language}}
{{defn |1=A language that contains its own truth predicate, allowing statements about the truth of sentences formulated within the same language.<ref name="PhilosopyOfLogicElsevier">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1xEVkzuX5e0C |title=Philosophy of Logic |date=2006-11-29 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-08-046663-7 |pages=259, 1038 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Simmons |first=Keith |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h_tdDwAAQBAJ |title=Semantic Singularities: Paradoxes of Reference, Predication, and Truth |date=2018-05-24 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-250919-2 |pages=6 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Semantics of logic|semantics]]}}
{{defn |1=The study of meaning in language, including the interpretation of words, phrases, sentences, and texts, and the study of the principles that govern the assignment of meanings.}}

{{term |1=semi-decidable theory}}
{{defn |1=A theory for which there exists an algorithm that can enumerate all its theorems, but there may not be an algorithm to decide non-theorems.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Büchi |first1=J. R. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PWl7CwAAQBAJ |title=Decidable Theories: Vol. 2: The Monadic Second Order Theory of All Countable Ordinals |last2=Siefkes |first2=D. |date=2006-11-14 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-46946-9 |pages=7 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=sense}}
{{defn |1=The aspect of meaning that pertains to the inherent content or connotation of an expression, distinct from its reference or denotation.<ref name="RoutledgeSenseReference" />}}

{{term |1=sensible formula}}
{{defn |1=A formula with no [[Scope (logic)|vacuous quantifiers]].<ref name="BostockIntermediate">{{Cite book |last=Bostock |first=David |title=Intermediate logic |date=1997 |publisher=Clarendon Press; Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-875141-0 |location=Oxford : New York |pages=81}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Yang |first=Syraya Chin-mu |chapter=A universally free modal logic |date=Aug 2011 |title=Proceedings of the 11th Asian Logic Conference |pages=159–180 |chapter-url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/9789814360548_0010 |access-date=2025-10-14 |publisher=WORLD SCIENTIFIC |doi=10.1142/9789814360548_0010 |isbn=978-981-4360-53-1|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[sentence letter]]}}
{{defn |1=A symbol used in propositional logic to represent an arbitrary proposition, serving as a placeholder in logical formulas.}}

{{term |1=[[Propositional calculus|sentential logic]]}}
{{defn |1=Another term for propositional logic, focusing on the logical relationships between whole sentences or propositions rather than their internal structure.}}

{{term |1=[[sequence]]}}
{{defn |1=An ordered list of objects or terms, each of which is identified by its position in the list, used in mathematics and logic to define functions, sets, and series.}}

{{term |1=[[sequent]]}}
{{defn |1=In sequent calculus, a formal representation of a logical deduction, consisting of a sequence of formulas that precede a turnstile and a sequence of formulas that follow it, indicating premises and conclusion.}}

{{term |1=[[sequent calculus]]}}
{{defn |1=A formal system for deriving logical entailments, representing deductions as sequences of formulas, and emphasizing the structural rules of logical derivation.}}

{{term |1=[[Serial relation|seriality]]}}
{{defn |1=The property of a relation where for every element in the domain, there exists an element in the codomain that is related to another element in a specific way, particularly in the context of binary relations and modal logic.}}

{{term |1=[[S4 (logic)|S4]]}}
{{defn |1=A modal logic system characterized by the axioms that necessitate reflexivity and transitivity for the accessibility relation, implying that if something is necessary, then it is necessarily necessary.}}

{{term |1=sharpening}}
{{defn |1=The process of making a vague or imprecise concept more precise or clearly defined, often discussed in the context of semantic vagueness.<ref name="VaguenessGuide" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Wright |first=Crispin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=g1c1EAAAQBAJ |title=The Riddle of Vagueness |date=2021 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-927733-9 |pages=139 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=John |last2=Varzi |first2=Achille C. |date=2000 |title=Unsharpenable Vagueness |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/43154328 |journal=Philosophical Topics |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.5840/philtopics200028110 |jstor=43154328 |issn=0276-2080}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Sheffer stroke]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical operation equivalent to the nand (not and) function; it is [[Functional completeness|functionally complete]], meaning all other logical operations can be constructed from it.}}

{{term |1=[[Signature (logic)|signature]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic and algebra, a set of symbols along with their arities, defining the kinds of operations, functions, and relations considered in a structure or theory.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Vialar |first=Thierry |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Eq4UDgAAQBAJ |title=Handbook of Mathematics |date=2016-12-07 |publisher=BoD - Books on Demand |isbn=978-2-9551990-0-8 |pages=693 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=simple type theory}}
{{defn |1=A [[type theory]] that divides objects into a simple hierarchy of objects, classes of objects, classes of classes of objects, etc. The adjective "simple" is used to contrast it with [[ramified type theory]], which further stratifies these simple types into ''orders''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sommaruga |first=Giovanni |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RGrxCAAAQBAJ |title=History and Philosophy of Constructive Type Theory |date=2013-03-09 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-015-9393-9 |pages=57 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=single turnstile}}
{{defn |1=A symbol used in logic (<math>\vdash</math>) to denote syntactic entailment, indicating that a formula or set of formulas derives or proves another formula within a formal system.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jeremy |first=Horne |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZfYoDwAAQBAJ |title=Philosophical Perceptions on Logic and Order |date=2017-05-19 |publisher=IGI Global |isbn=978-1-5225-2444-1 |pages=149 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[singular proposition]]}}
{{defn |1=A proposition that makes a statement about a specific individual or unique object, as opposed to general statements about classes or categories.}}

{{term |1=[[singular term]]}}
{{defn |1=A term in logic that refers to a single object or entity, distinguishing it from general terms that may refer to classes of objects or properties.}}

{{term |1=situation}}
{{defn |1=In logic and philosophy, a set of circumstances or a state of affairs to which truth-values of statements are relative, often used in {{glossary link internal|situation semantics}}.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Contexts |url=https://www.jfsowa.com/ontology/contexts.htm |access-date=2024-04-26 |website=www.jfsowa.com}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[situation semantics]]}}
{{defn |1=An approach to semantics that analyzes meaning in terms of situations, rather than attempting to account for meaning solely in terms of truth conditions at possible worlds.}}

{{term |1=[[skolemization]]}}
{{defn |1=A technique in first-order logic for eliminating existential quantifiers by introducing Skolem functions, used in the process of converting formulas to a standard form.}}

{{term |1=[[Skolem-Lowenheim theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A theorem stating that if a first-order theory has an infinite model, then it has models of every infinite cardinality, highlighting the flexibility of first-order semantics.}}

{{term |1=[[Skolem normal form]]}}
{{defn |1=A way of expressing first-order logic formulas where all existential quantifiers are moved inside and replaced by Skolem functions, leaving only universal quantifiers at the front.}}

{{term |1=[[Skolem's paradox|Skolem paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=The apparent paradox arising from the Skolem-Lowenheim theorem, where countable models can be found for theories that intuitively require uncountably many objects, challenging notions of absolute size in set theory.}}

{{term |1=[[slingshot argument]]}}
{{defn |1=An argument aiming to show that all true statements refer to the same "fact" or "entity", raising questions about the correspondence theory of truth and the nature of facts.}}

{{term |1=[[slippery slope]]}}
{{defn |1=An [[informal fallacy]] or rhetorical argument suggesting that a relatively small first step or minor decision will lead to a chain of related events culminating in a significant (often negative) outcome, without sufficient justification for such inevitability.}}

{{term |1=[[Smn theorem|s-m-n theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A fundamental theorem in the theory of computable functions that provides a method for constructing a specific computable function from a given computable function, highlighting the universality and flexibility of computable functions.}}

{{term |1=sophism}}
{{defn |1=An argument or form of reasoning deemed fallacious, misleading, or deceptive, historically associated with the Sophists in ancient Greece, who were known for their rhetorical skill and relativistic views on truth and morality.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Number game - Paradoxes, Fallacies {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/number-game/Paradoxes-and-fallacies |access-date=2024-04-26 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=sophisma}}
{{defn |1=A puzzle or paradoxical question that challenges conventional wisdom or logical reasoning, often used in medieval logic to teach students about logical fallacies and the complexities of language.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Pironet |first1=Fabienne |title=Sophismata |date=2023 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2023/entries/sophismata/ |access-date=2024-04-26 |edition=Fall 2023 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Spruyt |first2=Joke |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[sorites paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A paradox arising from vague predicates and the problem of heap, illustrating how a series of seemingly acceptable premises can lead to a paradoxical or absurd conclusion.}}

{{term |1=sorites series}}
{{defn |1=A sequence of propositions associated with the [[sorites paradox]], each adding a small amount to the previous one, challenging the boundary between truth and falsehood for vague concepts.}}

{{term |1=[[Soundness|sound deductive argument]]}}
{{defn |1=An argument where the logical structure ensures the truth of the conclusion if the premises are true, and where the premises are indeed true, making the argument both valid and sound.}}

{{term |1=[[soundness]]}}
{{defn |1=The property of a logical system wherein every theorem that can be derived using the system's rules is true in every interpretation of the system.}}

{{term |1=[[square of opposition]]}}
{{defn |1=A diagram representing the logical relationships between the four types of categorical propositions (A, E, I, O) in traditional logic, showing their contradictions, contraries, subcontraries, and subalternations.}}

{{term |1=[[Statement (logic)|statement]]}}
{{defn |1=An assertion that something is or is not the case, capable of being true or false; the basic unit of discourse in logic.}}

{{term |1=[[stipulative definition]]}}
{{defn |1=A definition that assigns a meaning to a word for the first time, or proposes a new meaning for an existing word, without claiming to capture an already established usage.}}

{{term |1=[[straw man]]}}
{{defn |1=An [[informal fallacy]] in which an opponent's argument is overstated or misrepresented in order to be more easily attacked or refuted.}}

{{term |1=[[strict conditional]]}}
{{defn |1=A conditional statement interpreted in terms of necessity, such that the truth of the antecedent necessarily implies the truth of the consequent, unlike the material conditional.}}

{{term |1=[[Strict conditional|strict implication]]}}
{{defn |1=A relation between propositions where the truth of the first (the antecedent) necessarily brings about the truth of the second (the consequent), often associated with modal logic.}}

{{term |1=strong completeness}}
{{defn |1=The property of a logical system where if a formula is semantically valid (true in all interpretations), then it is syntactically derivable within the system.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Piecha |first1=Thomas |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TP7NCgAAQBAJ |title=Advances in Proof-Theoretic Semantics |last2=Schroeder-Heister |first2=Peter |date=2015-10-24 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-319-22686-6 |pages=242 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Boolos |first=George |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2BvlvetSrlgC |title=Logic, Logic, and Logic |date=1998 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-53767-5 |pages=52 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=strong counterexample}}
{{defn |1=Within [[intuitionistic logic]] and [[Intuitionism|intuitionistic mathematics]], a strong counterexample is a proof of the negation of an instance of some variant of the [[law of excluded middle]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ross |first=Timothy J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3zcgIKPl8L0C |title=Fuzzy Logic with Engineering Applications |date=2005-04-08 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-470-86076-2 |pages=163 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Placek |first=Tomasz |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ho7TBgAAQBAJ |title=Mathematical Intuitionism and Intersubjectivity: A Critical Exposition of Arguments for Intuitionism |date=2013-03-09 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-015-9315-1 |pages=81 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=strong inductive argument}}
{{defn |1=An argument that, if the premises are true, provides strong support for the conclusion, making it highly probable but not necessarily true.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Martin |first=Robert M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VSsNQYnL09gC |title=Scientific Thinking |date=1997-03-31 |publisher=Broadview Press |isbn=978-1-55111-130-8 |pages=35 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=strong Kleene connectives}}
{{defn |1=Connectives in three-valued logic proposed by Stephen Cole Kleene, designed to deal with indeterminate or undefined values in a logical system.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Maienborn |first1=Claudia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OSMnaYWeruwC |title=Semantics. Volume 3 |last2=Heusinger |first2=Klaus von |last3=Portner |first3=Paul |date=2012-12-19 |publisher=Walter de Gruyter |isbn=978-3-11-025338-2 |pages=2438 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Strong induction|strong mathematical induction]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of mathematical induction that allows one to assume the proposition for all smaller instances simultaneously when proving it for any given instance.}}

{{term |1=strong negation}}
{{defn |no=1|1={{glossary link internal|exclusion negation}}}}
{{defn |no=2|1={{glossary link internal|choice negation}}}}

{{term |1=strong paraconsistency}}
{{defn |1=Strong paraconsistency is the view that there are [[possible world]]s where contradictions are true, or where some statements are both true and false.
