Compare {{glossary link internal|weak paraconsistency}}, the view that true contradictions, and worlds that contain them, are merely a formal tool used to study reasoning.<ref name="dialetheism_appl">{{Cite book |last1=Rieger |first1=Adam |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eZPHDwAAQBAJ |title=Dialetheism and its Applications |last2=Young |first2=Gareth |date=2020-01-01 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-30221-4 |pages=120 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=strongly connected}}
{{defn |1=A relation R is strongly connected (or total) if and only if, for all x and y, either Rxy, or Ryx.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Suppes |first=Patrick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JZu8AQAAQBAJ |title=Introduction to Logic |date=2012-07-12 |publisher=Courier Corporation |isbn=978-0-486-13805-3 |pages=110 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[structural rule]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic, especially in proof theory, a rule that concerns the manipulation of the components of sequents or deductions without reference to their internal logical structure, such as contraction, weakening, and exchange.}}

{{term |1=subaltern}}
{{defn |1=In traditional syllogistic logic, a term describing the relationship between two categorical propositions where the truth of the first (the universal) implies the truth of the second (the particular), but not vice versa.<ref name="IEP_Square" />}}

{{term |1=[[subalternation]]}}
{{defn |1=The logical relationship between a universal statement and its corresponding particular statement, where the truth of the universal necessitates the truth of the particular.}}

{{term |1=[[Subcontrary|subcontraries]]}}
{{defn |1=In traditional logic, a pair of particular statements (I and O propositions) that cannot both be false together, though both can be true under the square of opposition.}}

{{term |1=[[subcontrary]]}}
{{defn |1=Referring to the relationship between two statements that can both be true but cannot both be false at the same time.}}

{{term |1=[[subformula]]}}
{{defn |1=A part of a formula in logic that is itself a formula, often considered in the context of the formula's syntactic structure.}}

{{term |1=[[subject term]]}}
{{defn |1=The term in a categorical proposition that denotes the subject about which something is asserted.}}

{{term |1=[[subjunctive conditional]]}}
{{defn |1=A conditional statement expressing what would be the case if its antecedent were true, used to explore hypothetical situations and their consequences.}}

{{term |1=[[sublanguage]]}}
{{defn |1=A subset of a language that uses a restricted vocabulary or simpler grammatical structures, often for a specific purpose or domain.}}

{{term |1=sublogic}}
{{defn |1=A logical system that is a subset of a more comprehensive logic, retaining some but not all of the operations and principles of the larger system.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dvurecenskij |first=Anatolij |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z3zvCAAAQBAJ |title=Gleason's Theorem and Its Applications |date=2013-06-29 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-015-8222-3 |pages=74 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=subordinate connective}}
{{defn |1=A [[logical connective]] that occurs within the {{glossary link internal|scope}} of another logical connective.<ref name="LemmonLogic" />}}

{{term |1=[[Substitution (logic)|substitution]]}}
{{defn |1=The act of replacing a variable or expression within a logical formula with another, maintaining logical consistency.}}

{{term |1=substitution-instance}}
{{defn |1=The [[well-formed formula]] which results from a given well-formed formula by replacing one or more of the variables occurring in the well-formed formula throughout by some other well-formed formulas, it being understood that each variable so replaced is replaced by the same well-formed formula wherever it occurs.<ref name="LemmonLogic" /><ref name="SEP_FreeLogic">{{Citation |last=Jansana |first=Ramon |title=Algebraic Propositional Logic |date=2022 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2022/entries/logic-algebraic-propositional/ |access-date=2024-06-14 |edition=Summer 2022 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=substitutional quantifier}}
{{defn |1=A type of quantifier interpreted as ranging over expressions or names rather than over objects directly, used in certain theories of reference and meaning.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Halbach |first1=Volker |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x4sFCgAAQBAJ |title=Principles of Truth |last2=Horsten |first2=Leon |date=2013-04-30 |publisher=Walter de Gruyter |isbn=978-3-11-033272-8 |pages=52 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[substructural logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A class of non-classical logics that relax or modify structural rules found in classical logic, such as relevance logic and linear logic.}}

{{term |1=[[subtheory]]}}
{{defn |1=A theory contained within a larger theory, sharing some but not all of its axioms and theorems, and focusing on a subset of its domain.}}

{{term |1=[[successor function]]}}
{{defn |1=A fundamental function in arithmetic and logic that maps any natural number to the next larger natural number, denoted as <math>S(n) = n+1</math>.}}

{{term |1=[[suffix notation]]}}
{{defn |1=A way of writing expressions where operators follow their operands, also known as reverse Polish notation, used in some calculators and programming languages for its efficiency.}}

{{term |1=[[supertask]]}}
{{defn |1=A task that consists of an infinite sequence of operations completed in a finite amount of time, often discussed in the context of philosophical paradoxes and theoretical physics.}}

{{term |1=supertrue}}
{{defn |1=A term used in certain theories of truth, such as {{glossary link internal|supervaluational semantics}}, to describe propositions that remain true across all precisifications or interpretations of vague terms.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Salles |first=Sagid |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c0AjEAAAQBAJ |title=Vagueness as Arbitrariness: Outline of a Theory of Vagueness |date=2021-03-12 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-66781-8 |pages=102 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=supervaluational semantics}}
{{defn |1=A semantic theory designed to handle vagueness by considering multiple precisifications of vague terms, with a proposition deemed supertrue if it is true under all precisifications.<ref name="PhilosopyOfLogicElsevier" />}}

{{term |1=[[Supposition theory|supposition]]}}
{{defn |1=In medieval logic, a relation between an expression and the object or concept that the expression is being used to talk about, where the supposition of the expression need not be its literal reference.}}

{{term |1=[[suppressed evidence]]}}
{{defn |1=An [[informal fallacy]] that occurs when relevant information is omitted from an argument, potentially leading to a misleading or unjustified conclusion.}}

{{term |1=[[Surjective function|surjection]]}}
{{defn |1=A function from one set to another where every element of the target set is mapped to by at least one element of the domain set, also known as an onto function.}}

{{term |1=[[syllogism]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of deductive reasoning consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion, traditionally used in Aristotelian logic to infer relationships between categories.}}

{{term |1=syllogistic figure}}
{{defn |1=The form of a syllogism, determined by the position of the middle term in its premises, categorized into four figures that structure the syllogistic argument differently.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Figure {{!}} Description & Classification {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/figure-syllogistic |access-date=2024-04-26 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=syllogistic mood}}
{{defn |1=The type of a syllogism, defined by the nature of its premises (universal affirmative, universal negative, particular affirmative, particular negative) and how they combine to form a conclusion.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mood {{!}} Emotions, Cognitive Science, Reasoning {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/mood-logic |access-date=2024-04-26 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=syllogistic terms}}
{{defn |1=The three terms in a [[syllogism]]: the {{glossary link internal|major term}} (predicate of the conclusion), the {{glossary link internal|minor term}} (subject of the conclusion), and the {{glossary link internal|middle term}} (appears in both premises but not in the conclusion). See also {{glossary link internal|barbara}}.}}

{{term |1=symmetry}}
{{defn |1=A property of binary relations where if one element is related to another, then the second is related to the first, such as the relation of equality.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Johnsonbaugh |first=Richard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KJwvt2Zz2R8C |title=Discrete Mathematics |date=2009 |publisher=Prentice Hall |isbn=978-0-13-159318-3 |pages=156 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[syncategorematic term]]s}}
{{defn |1=Terms that do not stand for objects or have a reference by themselves but contribute to the meaning of expressions in which they occur, such as conjunctions, prepositions, and quantifiers.}}

{{term |1=syntactic consequence}}
{{defn |1=The relation that holds between premises and the conclusions derivable from them based on [[axiom]]s and [[inference rules]] within a [[formal system]].<ref>{{Citation |last1=Ferguson |first1=Thomas Macaulay |chapter=syntactic consequence |date=2016-06-23 |title=A Dictionary of Logic |chapter-url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/acref/9780191816802.001.0001/acref-9780191816802-e-440 |access-date=2024-03-23 |publisher=Oxford University Press |language=en |doi=10.1093/acref/9780191816802.001.0001 |isbn=978-0-19-181680-2 |last2=Priest |first2=Graham|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> Contrast {{glossary link internal|semantic consequence}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Syntax (logic)|syntax]]}}
{{defn |1=The set of rules, principles, and processes that govern the structure of sentences in a given language, distinguishing between correct and incorrect forms of expression.}}

{{glossary end}}

==T==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=Tarskian hierarchy}}
{{defn |1=A hierarchical structure of languages proposed by Alfred Tarski to avoid paradoxes in semantic theories, where each level of language can only reference levels below it, preventing self-reference.<ref name="SEP_TarskiTruth" />}}

{{term |1=[[Tarski's undefinability theorem|Tarski's indefinability theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A theorem stating that truth cannot be consistently defined within the same language it applies to, requiring a meta-language for a definition of truth to avoid paradoxes.}}

{{term |1=[[Tautology (logic)|tautology]]}}
{{defn |1=A statement or formula that is true in every possible interpretation, often used in propositional logic to refer to formulas that are logically true.}}

{{term |1=[[temperature paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A paradox where, from "the temperature is ninety" and "the temperature is rising", it is concluded that "ninety is rising", which seems invalid but can actually be valid under some formalization schemes.}}

{{term |1=temporal modal logic}}
{{defn |1=A branch of modal logic that deals with modalities related to time, such as 'always', 'sometimes', and 'never', allowing for reasoning about temporal aspects of propositions.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Howard |first1=Barringer |title=Modal Varieties of Temporal Logic |date=2005 |pages=119–165 |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-6526(05)80006-9 |access-date=2024-04-26 |publisher=Elsevier |doi=10.1016/s1574-6526(05)80006-9 |last2=Dov |first2=Gabbay|series=Foundations of Artificial Intelligence |volume=1 |isbn=978-0-444-51493-6 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[term logic]]}}
{{defn |1=An approach to logic focusing on the relations between terms in propositions and the inferences that can be drawn from them, characteristic of Aristotelian logic.}}

{{term |1=[[Ternary operation|ternary function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that takes three arguments or inputs, in contrast to unary and binary functions.}}

{{term |1=[[ternary relation]]}}
{{defn |1=A relation involving three elements, where the relation specifies how the elements are connected or related.}}

{{term |1=ternary semantics}}
{{defn |1=A ternary semantics is a [[Possible world semantics|possible worlds semantics]] that makes use of a [[ternary relation]] on [[possible world]]s instead of, or in addition to, the more standard binary [[accessibility relation]]. Ternary semantics have been most widely applied in the development of [[Relevance logic|relevant logics]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Mares |first=Edwin |title=Relevance Logic |date=2024 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2024/entries/logic-relevance/ |access-date=2024-04-26 |edition=Summer 2024 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[theorem]]}}
{{defn |1=A statement or proposition that has been formally proven on the basis of previously established statements or axioms within a logical or mathematical system.}}

{{term |1=[[theory]]}}
{{defn |1=A coherent set of propositions or statements, especially one that forms a comprehensive explanation of some aspect of the natural world or an abstract concept.}}

{{term |1=[[three-valued logic]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical system that introduces a third truth value (such as 'unknown', 'indeterminate', or 'both true and false') in addition to the classic binary true and false values.}}

{{term |1=[[tilde]]}}
{{defn |1=The symbol '~' used in logic to denote negation, indicating that the proposition it precedes is false.}}

{{term |1=[[Type–token distinction|token]]}}
{{defn |1=An instance of a type, such as a particular occurrence of a word or phrase, in contrast to the abstract concept or category it represents.}}

{{term |1=tolerant}}
{{defn |1=In the theory of [[vagueness]], a predicate is considered tolerant if, and only if, small changes in the relevant underlying properties of an object do not affect the justice with which the predicate applies to it. Thus, the predicate "bald" is tolerant, since one hair more or less does not transform a clear instance of baldness into a clear instance of non-baldness.<ref name="VaguenessGuide" />}}

{{term |1=tonk}}
{{defn |1=A fictional [[logical connective]] introduced to illustrate the importance of preserving inference rules in defining logical operators, showing that arbitrary rules can lead to absurdity.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Boghossian |first1=Paul |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AKwmGycd6yYC |title=New Essays on the A Priori |last2=Peacocke |first2=Christopher |date=2000-10-26 |publisher=Clarendon Press |isbn=978-0-19-152907-8 |pages=247 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Makridis |first=Odysseus |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DoBgEAAAQBAJ |title=Symbolic Logic |date=2022-02-21 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-67396-3 |pages=220 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="WrongWithTonk" />}}

{{term |1=[[Tee (symbol)|top]]}}
{{defn |1=In logic, a symbol (⊤) representing the highest or maximal element in a lattice or order, often used to denote a [[Tautology (logic)|tautology]] or universally true proposition in propositional logic.}}

{{term |1=[[topos]]}}
{{defn |1=See ''elementary topos''}}

{{term |1=[[Topos|topos theory]]}}
{{defn |1=The study of toposes, which are categories that behave like the category of sets and provide a foundation for much of mathematics, allowing for generalized notions of computation and logic.}}

{{term |1=[[total function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that is defined for every element of its domain, ensuring that there is an output for each input.}}

{{term |1=transition function}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|action table}}.}}

{{term |1=[[transitive closure]]}}
{{defn |1=The smallest transitive relation that contains a given relation, effectively adding the minimum necessary elements to make the original relation transitive.}}

{{term |1=[[Transitive relation|transitivity]]}}
{{defn |1=A property of a relation where if the relation holds between A and B, and between B and C, then it also holds between A and C, ensuring a kind of consistency or continuity in the relation across elements.}}

{{term |1=[[translation]]}}
{{defn |1=A translation is a function from the expressions of one language to the expressions of another language. Translations are typically intended to preserve either the meanings or the truth conditions of the translated expressions.}}

{{term |1=translation lemma}}
{{defn |1=Synonym for the [[Smn theorem|{{subsup|S|n|m}} theorem]].}}

{{term |1=[[Transposition (logic)|transposition]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical rule that allows the equivalent transformation of a conditional statement <math>P \rightarrow Q</math> into its contrapositive <math>\neg Q \rightarrow \neg P</math>, preserving truth.}}

{{term |1=[[Transworld identity|trans-world identity]]}}
{{defn |1=A concept in modal logic and metaphysics concerning the identity of individuals across different possible worlds, addressing questions of persistence and change.}}

{{term |1=tribar}}
{{defn |1=A name for the symbol ≡, used for [[Logical biconditional|logical equivalence]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kahane |first=Howard |url=https://www.google.com.br/books/edition/Logic_and_Philosophy/crMPEAAAQBAJ |title=Logic and Philosophy: A Modern Introduction |last2=Hausman |first2=Alan |last3=Boardman |first3=Frank |date=2020-12-18 |publisher=Hackett Publishing |isbn=978-1-62466-936-1 |pages=50 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=trichotomy}}
{{defn |1=A relation R is trichotomous (or comparable) if and only if, for any objects x and y, either Rxy, or Ryx, or x = y.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Oberste-Vorth |first1=Ralph W. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_iv4DwAAQBAJ |title=Bridge to Abstract Mathematics |last2=Lawrence |first2=Bonita A. |date=2012 |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. |isbn=978-0-88385-779-3 |pages=93 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Law of trichotomy|trichotomy law]]}}
{{defn |1=A law in order theory and mathematics stating that for any two elements in a certain set, exactly one of three relationships (greater than, less than, or equal to) must hold.}}

{{term |1=[[Triviality (mathematics)|triviality]]}}
{{defn |1=The state or quality of being trivial, in logic and mathematics, often referring to statements, propositions, or problems that are oversimplified or of little interest or importance.}}

{{term |1=[[truth]]}}
{{defn |1=A concept in logic and philosophy concerning the property of statements, beliefs, or propositions corresponding to reality or fact, or being in accord with the actual state of affairs.}}

{{term |1=[[truth condition]]s}}
{{defn |1=The conditions under which a statement or proposition is considered to be true, playing a central role in the semantic analysis of language.}}

{{term |1=[[truth function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that takes truth values as input and produces a truth value as output, used in logic to model the truth conditions of logical connectives.}}

{{term |1=truth-functional}}
{{defn |1=Pertaining to an operator or connective in logic whose output truth value depends solely on the input truth values, without regard to the content of the propositions involved.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Haack |first=Susan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0GsZ8SBQrUcC |title=Philosophy of Logics |date=1978-07-27 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-29329-7 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=truth-in-a-model}}
{{defn |1=A concept in [[Semantic theory of truth|semantic theories of truth]] indicating that a statement or proposition is true relative to a particular [[Interpretation (logic)|model or interpretation]] of the [[formal language|language]] in which it is expressed.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jr |first=Henry E. Kyburg |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PI29RoPxWq8C |title=Science and Reason |date=1990-11-15 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-536274-9 |pages=21 |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Truthmaker theory|truthmaker]]}}
{{defn |1=An entity or set of entities in the world that makes a proposition true, grounding truth in aspects of reality.}}

{{term |1=[[truth predicate]]}}
{{defn |1=A predicate that assigns the property of being true to propositions, often discussed in relation to Tarski's semantic conception of truth and the liar paradox.}}

{{term |1=[[truth table]]}}
{{defn |1=A table used in logic to show the truth value of a compound statement for every possible combination of truth values of its components, instrumental in analyzing logical expressions.}}

{{term |1=truth-teller}}
{{defn |1=The converse of the liar paradox, a statement that asserts its own truth, raising questions about self-reference and the nature of truth.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Contents: Paradoxes |url=https://spot.colorado.edu/~huemer/analytical5.htm |access-date=2024-04-26 |website=spot.colorado.edu}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[truth-tree]]}}
{{defn |1=Synonym of [[Method of analytic tableaux|analytic tableaux]].}}

{{term |1=[[truth value]]}}
{{defn |1=The value indicating the truth or falsity of a proposition or statement, typically represented as true or false in classical logic, but possibly more varied in many-valued logics.}}

{{term |1=truth-value gap}}
{{defn |1=A situation where a statement or proposition cannot be assigned a traditional truth value of true or false, often due to vagueness or undefined terms.<ref name="Logic Without Gaps or Gluts">{{Cite book |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-94624-1 |title=Logic Without Gaps or Gluts |series=Synthese Library |date=2022 |volume=458 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-94624-1|isbn=978-3-030-94623-4 }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=truth-value glut}}
{{defn |1=A condition in which a statement or proposition is paradoxically both true and false simultaneously, associated with dialetheism and contradictions.<ref name="Logic Without Gaps or Gluts">{{Cite book |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-94624-1 |title=Logic Without Gaps or Gluts |series=Synthese Library |date=2022 |volume=458 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-94624-1|isbn=978-3-030-94623-4 }}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[T-schema]]}}
{{defn |1=The Tarski schema for defining truth, stating that 'P' is true if and only if P, where 'P' is a placeholder for a proposition and P is the proposition itself.}}

{{term |1=[[tu quoque]]}}
{{defn |1=A logical fallacy that attempts to discredit an opponent's position by asserting the opponent's failure to act consistently with that position, essentially accusing them of hypocrisy.}}

{{term |1=[[Turing-computable function|Turing computable function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that can be calculated by a [[Turing machine]], representing the class of functions that are computable in principle, according to the {{glossary link internal|Church–Turing thesis}}.}}

{{term |1=Turing thesis}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|Church–Turing thesis}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Turnstile (symbol)|turnstile]]}}
{{defn |1=A symbol used in logic (<math>\vdash</math>) to denote syntactic entailment or provability, indicating that the statement or set of statements to the right is a logical consequence of the statements to the left within a given formal system.}}

{{term |1=type}}
{{defn |no=1|1=(In [[type theory]].) A category or class of entities that share certain characteristics, used in logic and mathematics to distinguish between different kinds of objects, expressions, or variables, preventing certain kinds of logical paradoxes.}}
{{defn |no=2|1=(In the [[Type–token distinction|type-token distinction]].) A universal, as opposed to a particular..}}

{{term |1=[[type theory]]}}
{{defn |1=A framework in mathematical logic and computer science that uses types to classify expressions and objects, aiming to avoid paradoxes like Russell's paradox by organizing objects into hierarchies or levels and restricting operations to objects of the same type.}}
{{glossary end}}

==U==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=[[Unary operation|unary function]]}}
{{defn |1=A function that operates on a single input or argument, common in mathematics and logic for representing operations like negation or the absolute value function.}}

{{term |1=[[unary relation]]}}
{{defn |1=A relation that applies to a single element, used to characterize properties or attributes that an element may or may not possess.}}

{{term |1=[[Universal instantiation|universal elimination]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule of inference in predicate logic that allows for the derivation of a specific statement about an individual from a general statement that applies to all members of a category.}}

{{term |1=[[Universal generalization|universal introduction]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule of inference in predicate logic that allows for the generalization of a statement to all members of a category if the statement is shown to hold for an arbitrary but specific individual.}}

{{term |1=universal proposition}}
{{defn |1=A statement in logic that asserts something about all members of a certain category, typically formulated using a [[Universal quantification|universal quantifier]].}}

{{term |1=[[Universal quantification|universal quantifier]]}}
{{defn |1=A symbol in predicate logic (<math>\forall</math>) used to indicate that the statement it precedes holds for all individuals in the domain of discourse.}}

{{term |1=universal variable}}
{{defn |1=A variable in predicate logic that is bound by a [[Universal quantification|universal quantifier]], representing any and all individuals in the domain of discourse.}}

{{term |1=[[universe of discourse]]}}
{{defn |1=The set of all objects, individuals, or values that are relevant in a particular logical or mathematical discussion, serving as the domain over which quantifiers range.}}

{{term |1=upward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem}}
{{defn |1=Part of the {{glossary link internal|Löwenheim–Skolem theorem}}.}}

{{term |1=[[Soundness|unsound deductive argument]]}}
{{defn |1=An argument that is either invalid in its logical form or contains at least one false premise, and therefore does not guarantee the truth of its conclusion.}}

{{term |1=use}}
{{defn |1=In philosophy, particularly in the analysis of language, "use" refers to the actual application of a word or a phrase in a sentence to convey meaning. In the [[Use–mention distinction|use-mention distinction]], "use" involves employing words to refer to things, actions, qualities, or concepts in the world. For example, in the sentence "I enjoy reading books," the word "books" is used to refer to objects that can be read; it is not merely {{glossary link internal|mention|mentioned}}.}}

{{glossary end}}

==V==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=vacuous quantifier}}
{{defn |1=A vacuous [[Quantifier (logic)|quantifier]] is one that doesn't bind any variables, such as the second quantifier in <math>\forall x \forall y Rxx</math>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Peter Suber, "Predicate Logic Terms and Symbols" |url=http://legacy.earlham.edu/~peters/courses/log/terms3.htm |access-date=2024-04-22 |website=legacy.earlham.edu}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=vagueness}}
{{defn |1=The characteristic of terms, concepts, or propositions that lack clear boundaries or precision in meaning, leading to indeterminate or borderline cases.<ref name="SEP_Vagueness" />}}

{{term |1=[[Validity (logic)|valid]]}}
{{defn |no=1|1=A deductive argument whose structure ensures that if all the premises are true, then the conclusion must also be true, demonstrating logical validity.}}
{{defn |no=2|1=In [[Semantics of logic|model-theoretic semantics]], a formula that is true under all [[Interpretation (logic)|interpretations]].}}
{{defn |no=3|1=In [[proof-theoretic semantics]], a formula that is either an explicit rule of inference of a system, or that does not allow one to prove anything that could not be proved using the explicit rules of inference.<ref>{{Citation |last=Schroeder-Heister |first=Peter |title=Proof-Theoretic Semantics |date=2024 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2024/entries/proof-theoretic-semantics/ |access-date=2024-04-22 |edition=Summer 2024 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=valuation}}
{{defn |1=Another name for an [[Interpretation (logic)|interpretation of a formal language]], coming from the fact that it assigns semantic values (such as [[truth value]]s) to the language's formulas.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Leblanc |first=Hugues |title=Truth, syntax and modality: proceedings of the Temple University Conference on Alternative Semantics |date=1973 |publisher=North-Holland |others=Conference on Alternative Semantics, Temple University, Association for symbolic logic |isbn=978-0-7204-2269-6 |series=Studies in logic and the foundations of mathematics |location=Amsterdam |pages=297}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=variable assignment}}
{{defn |1=Sometimes, an [[Interpretation (logic)|interpretation of a formal language]] for [[First-order logic|first-order]] or [[higher-order logic]] is called simply a "variable assignment",<ref>{{Cite book |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.3233/faia377 |title=Formal Ontology in Information Systems |date=2023-12-21 |publisher=IOS Press |isbn=978-1-64368-468-0 |editor-last=Aussenac-Gilles |editor-first=Nathalie |series=Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and Applications |volume=377 |pages=42 |doi=10.3233/faia377 |editor-last2=Hahmann |editor-first2=Torsten |editor-last3=Galton |editor-first3=Antony |editor-last4=Hedblom |editor-first4=Maria M.}}</ref> or "variable assignment function".<ref>{{Cite book |title=Foundations of data mining and knowledge discovery |date=2005 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |isbn=978-3-540-26257-2 |editor-last=Lin |editor-first=Tsau Y. |series=Studies in computational intelligence |location=Berlin; New York |pages=92}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Vel (symbol)|vel]]}}
{{defn |1=The Latin word for "or", used in logic as a name for ∨, the [[descending wedge]] symbol. The symbol is used to denote a disjunction that is inclusive, meaning at least one of the disjuncts must be true for the whole expression to be true.}}

{{term |1=verification constraint}}
{{defn |1=See {{glossary link internal|epistemic constraint}}.}}

{{term |1=verity}}
{{defn |1=The verity (or "degree of truth") of a statement is the semantic value of that statement within degree-theoretic semantics, which assigns degrees between 0 and 1 to statements.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Walters |first1=Lee |title=Conditionals, paradox, and probability: themes from the philosophy of Dorothy Edgington |last2=Hawthorne |first2=John P. |date=2021 |publisher=Oxford University press |isbn=978-0-19-178107-0 |location=Oxford New York (N.Y.) |pages=239}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Tee (symbol)|verum]]}}
{{defn |1=''Verum'' ([[Latin]] for "true") is another name for the <math>\top</math> symbol,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Polkowski |first=Lech T. |date=2023 |title=Logic: Reference Book for Computer Scientists |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-42034-4 |journal=Intelligent Systems Reference Library |volume=245 |pages=180 |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-42034-4 |isbn=978-3-031-42033-7 |issn=1868-4394|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which represents a primitive, necessarily true statement, and is sometimes considered a [[nullary]] [[logical connective|connective]].}}

{{term |1=[[vicious circle principle]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle against definitions or arguments that are circular, ensuring that the thing being defined is not used in its own definition or premise in a way that presupposes its conclusion.}}

{{glossary end}}

==W==
{{glossary}}
{{term |1=[[Completeness (logic)#Semantic completeness|weak completeness]]}}
{{defn |1=The property of a logical system where if a statement is semantically valid (true under all interpretations), then there is a proof of the statement within the system.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Formal logic - Interdefinability, Operators {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/formal-logic/Interdefinability-of-operators |access-date=2024-04-22 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=weak counterexample}}
{{defn |1=Within [[intuitionistic logic]] and [[Intuitionism|intuitionistic mathematics]], a weak counterexample is a situation in which we have no positive evidence for the (intuitionistic) truth of some instance of the law of excluded middle, <math>p \lor \neg p</math>.<ref>{{Citation |last=van Atten |first=Mark |title=Luitzen Egbertus Jan Brouwer |date=2020 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/spr2020/entries/brouwer/ |access-date=2024-04-22 |edition=Spring 2020 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Luitzen Egbertus Jan Brouwer > Weak Counterexamples (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy) |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/brouwer/weakcounterex.html |access-date=2024-04-22 |website=plato.stanford.edu |language=en}}</ref>}}

{{term |1=[[Law of excluded middle#Law of the weak excluded middle|weak excluded middle]]}}
{{defn |1=A principle in intuitionistic logic stating that for any proposition P, either P is provable or not-P is provable, but not necessarily both, reflecting a more nuanced view of truth than the classical law of excluded middle.}}

{{term |1=weak Kleene connectives}}
{{defn |1=[[Three-valued logic#Kleene and Priest logics|Connectives defined in the three-valued logic of Kleene]], which do not fully determine the truth value of compound statements if any component statement is undefined.}}

{{term |1=weak mathematical induction}}
{{defn |1=A form of [[mathematical induction]] that only assumes the truth of the statement for the immediately preceding case to prove its truth for any natural number, as opposed to strong induction, which assumes the statement for all smaller numbers.}}

{{term |1=[[weak negation]]}}
{{defn |1=A form of negation in some non-classical logics where the negation of a proposition does not assert the truth of the opposite proposition but rather the absence of truth of the original proposition.}}

{{term |1=weak paraconsistency}}
{{defn |1=Weak paraconsistency is the view that true contradictions, and worlds that contain them, are merely a formal tool used to study reasoning. Compare {{glossary link internal|strong paraconsistency}}, the view that there are [[possible world]]s where contradictions are true, or where some statements are both true and false.<ref name="dialetheism_appl" />}}

{{term |1=[[Weakening (logic)|weakening]]}}
{{defn |1=A rule in both propositional and predicate logic allowing the addition of propositions to a derivation without affecting its validity, reflecting the idea that if something follows from a set of premises, it also follows from any larger set of premises.}}

{{term |1=[[Wedge (symbol)|wedge]]}}
{{defn |1=A symbol used in logic (<math>\wedge</math>) to represent logical conjunction, indicating that both connected statements are true.}}

{{term |1=[[well-formed formula]]}}
{{defn |1=A string of symbols in a formal language that follows the syntactic rules of the language, making it a meaningful or grammatically correct expression within the context of that system.}}

{{term |1=wff}}
{{defn |1=Short for {{glossary link internal|well-formed formula}}. Pronounced "woof",<ref name="GenslerLogic">{{Cite book |last=Gensler |first=Harry |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YjuCAgAAQBAJ |title=Introduction to Logic |date=2002-09-11 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-58880-0 |pages=35 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hall |first1=Cordelia |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QZgKCAAAQBAJ |title=Discrete Mathematics Using a Computer |last2=O'Donnell |first2=John |date=2013-04-17 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4471-3657-6 |pages=44 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Agler |first=David W. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nhQHlwV5NSIC |title=Symbolic Logic: Syntax, Semantics, and Proof |date=2013 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-4422-1742-3 |pages=41 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Simpson |first=R. L. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w2doAwAAQBAJ |title=Essentials of Symbolic Logic - Third Edition |date=2008-03-17 |publisher=Broadview Press |isbn=978-1-77048-495-5 |pages=14 |language=en}}</ref> or sometimes "wiff",<ref>{{Cite book |last=Laderoute |first=Karl |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LwyXEAAAQBAJ |title=A Pocket Guide to Formal Logic |date=2022-10-24 |publisher=Broadview Press |isbn=978-1-77048-868-7 |pages=59 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Maurer |first1=Stephen B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SWds5v8UUc4C |title=Discrete Algorithmic Mathematics, Third Edition |last2=Ralston |first2=Anthony |date=2005-01-21 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-56881-166-6 |pages=625 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Martin |first=Robert M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0sOpx5-90d4C |title=The Philosopher's Dictionary - Third Edition |date=2002-05-06 |publisher=Broadview Press |isbn=978-1-77048-215-9 |pages=323 |language=en}}</ref> "weff",<ref>{{Cite book |last=Date |first=Christopher |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HMIay77Pkv0C |title=The Relational Database Dictionary, Extended Edition |date=2008-10-14 |publisher=Apress |isbn=978-1-4302-1042-9 |pages=211 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Date |first=C. J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TB5UCwAAQBAJ |title=The New Relational Database Dictionary: Terms, Concepts, and Examples |date=2015-12-21 |publisher=O'Reilly Media, Inc. |isbn=978-1-4919-5171-2 |pages=241 |language=en}}</ref> or "whiff".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Simpson |first=R. L. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=exeO4UNCJ8cC |title=Essentials of Symbolic Logic |date=1998-12-10 |publisher=Broadview Press |isbn=978-1-55111-250-3 |pages=12 |language=en}}</ref> (All sources supported "woof". The sources cited for "wiff", "weff", and "whiff" gave these pronunciations as alternatives to "woof". Gensler<ref name="GenslerLogic" /> gives "wood" and "woofer" as examples of how to pronounce the vowel in "woof".) Plural "wffs".<ref name="GenslerLogic" />}}
{{glossary end}}

==Y==
{{glossary}}

{{term |1=[[Yablo's paradox|Yablo paradox]]}}
{{defn |1=A paradox involving an infinite sequence of sentences, each of which states that all following sentences in the sequence are false. Unlike the [[liar paradox]], it does not rely on self-reference, raising questions about the nature of paradoxes and infinity.}}

{{glossary end}}

==Z==
{{glossary}}

{{term |1=[[Zeno's paradoxes|Zeno paradoxes]]}}
{{defn |1=A series of paradoxes proposed by the ancient Greek philosopher Zeno of Elea to challenge the coherence of the concepts of plurality, motion, and the continuum, including the famous paradoxes of Achilles and the tortoise, and the dichotomy.}}
{{glossary end}}
